artigo.texto: SamsungSDI has secured an additional supply volume of LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) worth 3 to 4 trillion won from U.S.-based Jupiter Power, signaling a major step in expanding its medium- and long-term order book. After already securing production volumes through 2028, the company has also landed large-scale, long-term contracts starting in 2029, broadening its growth foundation in the U.S. ESS market. As of the 16th, SamsungSDI's cumulative U.S. power ESS order book has grown to over 76 GWh (gigawatt-hours), including an additional 16 GWh contract with Jupiter Power. The existing order volume of more than 60 GWh secured by the end of October this year alone is sufficient to keep the U.S. SPE (Star Plus Energy) and Ulsan production lines running at full capacity through 2028. This new contract covers supply over three years starting in 2029, marking another achievement for SamsungSDI in securing long-term supply volumes. To meet growing ESS demand, SamsungSDI is accelerating the expansion of its local production capacity in the United States. In early October, the company began mass production of prismatic LFP batteries for ESS at its SPE plant in Indiana, and started shipping battery cells from mid-October. The produced cells will undergo module and battery box processes before being delivered to customers as finished SBB (Samsung Battery Box) products starting in December. SamsungSDI is working to expand supply capacity by converting existing electric vehicle (EV) battery production lines into ESS LFP battery facilities. It is additionally converting two of the four production lines at its U.S. SPE Plant 1. The company also plans to utilize the U.S. Synergy Cells plant, acquired through the full buyout of its joint venture stake with GM (General Motors) in August, as an ESS production hub. Synergy Cells is currently optimizing designs to convert existing EV facilities into high-capacity LFP battery production lines for ESS. Mass production is scheduled to begin from late 2028 to early 2029, followed by phased expansion of production lines. This expansion of the ESS business is also closely tied to efforts to capture the battery market for AI (artificial intelligence) data centers. SamsungSDI is accelerating its market push by leveraging its status as the world's only company capable of supplying all three essential battery solutions for data centers: BESS (battery energy storage systems), UPS (uninterruptible power supplies), and BBU (battery backup units). As a result, performance has shown signs of recovery. SamsungSDI's cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters of this year reached 456 billion won, turning profitable compared to an operating loss of 1.4232 trillion won in the same period last year. Building on its improved performance, SamsungSDI is strategizing to accelerate its next-generation all-solid-state battery business. All-solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid ones, offering enhanced safety. The company is developing the technology with a target of commercialization in the second half of next year. Since September, it has been supplying all-solid-state battery cell and pack samples for humanoid robots to multiple customers for performance evaluation. It is currently at the stage of refining product specifications for next year's mass production through iterative performance improvements and verification based on customer requirements. The company is also working in parallel to establish a stable supply chain for key materials such as cathode materials and solid electrolytes. A SamsungSDI official stated, "This order reflects recognition of our global technological competitiveness by securing large volumes early on," adding, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

artigo.texto: As far as we know, San Francisco has three data centers. Two are in Bayview, and one is in Soma. They’re relatively small in terms of energy and water use. The two associated places on Paul Avenue have been around for decades, since the days when we called them “server farms.” The City Planning Department admits other centers may exist, on a smaller scale, since the department has no formal inventory of this type of land use. The Board of Supes recently approved a 45-day moratorium on new centers, and the Land Use and Transportation Committee will consider Monday/16 a year-long extension. The Planning Department has done a study on the issue, and its findings suggests that the city needs at least a moratorium, if not an outright ban. From an environmental justice perspective, data centers are a public nuisance—and to no surprise, all are in low-income neighborhoods with high concentrations of people of color. I don’t think we’re going to see a data center in Pacific Heights. The city also has a major capacity problem. According to the report, big data centers use as much as 50 megawatts of power, which is enough for 25,000 homes. The city’s under immense pressure to approve more housing—and the grid doesn’t have much space available. The current capacity of the power lines coming into San Francisco is 1 gigawatt. Peak usage is about 900 megawatts, and that’s rising, as more residents, businesses, and vehicles are shifting to electric power. A 50 MW data center would overwhelm the grid. PG&E can’t handle this load. Expanding the power lines coming into San Francisco could take at least eight years, and would cost hundreds of millions of dollars. If the city had a municipal utility, it could control new data centers: The City of Santa Clara, which already has 55 existing data centers, has its own municipal utility (Silicon Valley Power, SVP) that stopped taking new applications for service from data centers (but not other development) in 2023 while it assessed the ability to provide power for these uses and while they await the completion of a major transmission expansion project expected to be completed in the next couple years. Then there’s water. From the report: SFPUC has concerns for existing and potential future data centers about the types of chemicals (and their concentrations and amounts) that are being used for cooling systems; whether wastewater discharges from data centers are within the local temperature limit of 125 °F; and whether the combined sewer system has the capacity to handle the data center’s wastewater flow, especially during wet weather. Depending on the water quality, there’s a risk of causing additional corrosion to sewers. SFPUC uses site-specific wastewater discharge permits to regulate non-domestic and temporary discharges into the City’s combined sewer system. Mayor Daniel Lurie loves AI, and if the companies he sees as the city’s economic future want local data centers, I suspect he will by sympathetic. Of course, it we don’t build them here, we’re just outsourcing the problem to other communities. The committee will consider the planning report Monday/16, and the full board will discuss a year-long moratorium Tuesday/17. I don’t use self-checkout. I hate having to take pictures of checks on my phone and sending them to the bank. People used to get paid to do that work; now they’ve lost their jobs, and I’m supposed to do it, for no pay. It’s hard to find an open bank branch with real tellers these days, and sometimes it costs money to get a human on the phone for customer service. When I have an internet outage, my provider’s phone system tells me to seek help on the web; dude, I can’t get to the web. That’s the problem. Not everyone is young and tech-savvy. Some people need people, real people, to help them with their groceries or prescriptions or banking. And the more technology replaces people, the more we are going to have to deal with massive unemployment. The Government Audit and Oversight Committee will consider Thursday/19 a measure that would place limits on self-checkout facilities at grocery stores and pharmacies. The measure would require one employee-staffed checkout center for every three self-check centers, would limit self-check to 15 items, and would mandate one employee to supervise every self-check operations center. The measure has six co-sponsors, enough to ensure it will pass, but not enough to override a mayoral veto. That hearing starts at 10am. Thanks to the AI boom and radical economic inequality, evictions are soaring in San Francisco; landlords are looking for any possible loophole to get rid of rent-controlled tenants who are paying below market rate. One tactic: Cite a “nuisance.” Some landlords in Chinatown tried to use that tool to evict renters who hung their laundry out to dry on a clothesline. It’s been used to evict tenants who have bicycles in public spaces. The Land Use and Transportation Committee will consider Monday/16 an ordinance that would restrict “nuisance” evictions. Among other things, it would ban evictions for damage to the property if the tenants paid to have the place repaired. That hearing starts at 10 am. A final note: I’m not surprised that the Chron would allow the head of a hotel lobbying group to write an oped promoting the economic interests of the giants of the hospitality industry. I’m not even surprised by the doom-and-gloom rhetoric: If this amendment were to pass, unions would be able to hold hotels and the city hostage, and San Francisco’s hospitality and reputational recovery would come to a screeching halt. The union and its representatives would be able to use the threat of a legal filing to gain leverage with hotels during contract negotiations. As a result, investments in new hotels and investments in renovations will dry up, and San Francisco will become a no-invest zone once again. artigo.texto: HD Hyundai Energy Solution and HD Hyundai Electric said Monday that they will jointly participate in 'RE+ 26,' North America's largest clean energy exhibition, held at the Las Vegas Convention Center in the United States, showcasing their integrated energy business capabilities spanning from solar power generation to energy storage, conversion, and transmission and distribution. HD Hyundai Energy Solution will unveil its 'TOPCon Multi-Cut (G12R TOPCon Multi-Cut)' module for the North American market for the first time. Multi-cut is a technology that divides large-area solar cells into multiple pieces to reduce power loss generated during current flow. Through this, the company achieved a module efficiency of 24.4% by increasing power density. It plans to gradually apply ultra-precision multi-cut technology to its production lines to strengthen the competitiveness of its high-efficiency products. HD Hyundai Electric will introduce battery energy storage systems (BESS) and power grid stabilization technologies. The company will showcase major domestic and international project cases, including the 96th-megawatt-class Anmyeondo BESS project in Sinan, South Korea, and the 100th-megawatt-class Rutile BESS project in Texas, United States. It will also present Grid-Forming technology, which actively controls voltage and frequency to enhance power supply stability, as well as a product lineup of power equipment targeting the North American power grid and data center markets. In the United States, the utilization of energy storage systems is rapidly increasing alongside the expansion of solar power generation. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. solar power generation increased by 18.3% year-on-year from January to August this year. More than 16% of new large-scale solar facilities built through September this year were installed together with battery storage systems. The importance of grid stabilization technology and the expansion of transmission and distribution infrastructure is also growing due to increasing power demand and the expanded integration of renewable energy into the power grid. The two companies are strengthening their business foundations for targeting the North American market. HD Hyundai Electric is expanding its local business base through the expansion of its North American production subsidiary and the expansion of its BESS business via its Texas subsidiary. HD Hyundai Energy Solution is responding to changes in U.S. supply chain regulations, including requirements related to Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC), based on its domestic integrated cell and module production system. An official from HD Hyundai said, "In the North American market, not only product technological capability but also stable supply capacity and project execution capabilities have emerged as key competitive factors." He added, "Taking this exhibition as an opportunity, we will expand cooperation with local customers and partners and discover practical business opportunities."

artigo.texto: The Greek energy group targets 1 GW of renewable generation and 500 MW of battery storage by 2030, highlighting the growing importance of grid flexibility and energy storage in renewable infrastructure development. HELLENiQ ENERGY plans to invest more than €1 billion in Romania by 2030, expanding its solar, wind and battery energy storage operations as part of its regional growth strategy. The company aims to reach 1 GW of installed renewable generation capacity and 500 MW of battery energy storage system (BESS) power capacity, positioning Romania as its second-largest renewable energy growth market after Greece. The investment program forms part of the group’s Vision 2035+ strategy and reflects a broader transformation of its energy portfolio, in which renewable generation is increasingly linked to storage infrastructure and electricity grid integration. A renewable portfolio combining solar and wind assets HELLENiQ ENERGY currently operates four photovoltaic parks in the Romanian counties of Teleorman, Giurgiu, Olt and Dolj, with a combined installed capacity of 211 MW. These facilities generate electricity equivalent to the annual consumption of more than 155,000 households. The portfolio will be expanded with a 96 MW wind farm in Galați County, scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027. Additional wind and solar projects at advanced development stages exceed 500 MW of renewable generation capacity, alongside another 500 MW of planned battery storage power capacity. This combination of technologies is intended to diversify generation profiles and reduce dependence on a single renewable energy source. Battery storage becomes central to the generation strategy The planned 500 MW of BESS capacity represents one of the main components of the company’s Romanian expansion. Battery systems can absorb electricity during periods of high renewable generation and discharge it when demand increases or market conditions become more favorable. However, storage power capacity alone does not determine how much energy a battery installation can deliver. Its actual storage capability depends on the installed energy capacity, measured in megawatt-hours (MWh), and its discharge duration. HELLENiQ previously identified a potential Romanian storage configuration of 500 MW and 1,500 MWh. The company has also been assessing battery integration into existing photovoltaic assets through a potential 170 MW / 680 MWh installation. These developments illustrate how battery storage can be incorporated into both new hybrid renewable projects and operating solar facilities. Grid connection constraints influence project economics One of the most important aspects of the expansion concerns electricity infrastructure. According to reporting by Romanian energy publication Energynomics, based on statements from company executives, two recently completed photovoltaic parks initially operated with restrictions on electricity injection while additional grid reinforcement works were being carried out. This highlights an important distinction in renewable project development: completing a generating facility does not necessarily guarantee immediate access to the full available grid connection capacity. Battery storage can help manage excess generation and shift electricity delivery toward periods of higher commercial value. However, it cannot replace the transmission infrastructure upgrades required to accommodate additional renewable capacity. For HELLENiQ ENERGY, reaching its 2030 targets in Romania will therefore depend not only on project construction, but also on grid access, operational availability and the ability to commercialize the electricity generated. artigo.texto: O governo da Bolívia iniciou negociações com o Kawari Fund para estruturar a venda de créditos de carbono provenientes da preservação florestal, transformando a manutenção de ecossistemas em um fluxo de receita financeira direta. O mecanismo, discutido durante a COP31, visa conectar investidores internacionais às comunidades indígenas que atuam na vigilância e proteção dos recursos naturais. A operação baseia-se na iniciativa REDD+ (Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação florestal), que atrai capital estrangeiro mediante a comprovação da redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O projeto piloto foi concentrado no Distrito Autônomo Indígena Charua Iyambae, onde a fase atual consiste em consultas obrigatórias para garantir a conformidade dos direitos das comunidades locais antes da implementação do fluxo financeiro. Para viabilizar a atratividade do ativo para os compradores de créditos, o Ministro da Produção Sustentável, Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Oscar Mario Justiniano, trabalha na criação de uma estrutura de governança que elimine intermediários. O objetivo é que o pagamento pelos créditos de carbono chegue diretamente ao orçamento das famílias que operam como patrulhas florestais. Segundo Vanessa Jiménez, representante do Kawari Fund, a transparência nos relatórios de destino dos fundos é a condição necessária para que investidores internacionais mantenham o aporte de capital no país. A conversão da floresta em ativo financeiro depende de um processo de verificação técnica, conduzido pela Fundação Amigos da Natureza (FAN) e pela União Internacional para a Conservação da Natureza (CI). Essas entidades são responsáveis pelo monitoramento e a certificação da quantidade de carbono sequestrado, etapa indispensável para que as empresas compradoras possam registrar legalmente as cotas em seus balanços de emissões. Caso o modelo piloto no distrito Charua Iyambae seja validado, a Bolívia pretende expandir a escala da operação, estabelecendo um preço por tonelada de CO2 absorvido que se converta em renda estável para as populações residentes nas áreas florestais. artigo.texto: South Korea's Mplus Wins approximately $15 Million Solid-State Battery Assembly and Electrode Equipment Order from Global Battery Maker Mplus, a South Korean specialist in secondary-battery assembly equipment, has won an order worth approximately 20 billion won (approximately $15.0 million) from a global battery company for assembly and electrode-line equipment used in solid-state battery mass production. According to industry sources on the 16th, the contract covers equipment for the customer's solid-state battery production line, and its significance lies in Mplus securing an official supply track record in the next-generation battery mass-production equipment segment. The equipment to be supplied will use assembly machinery developed in-house by Mplus, incorporating core process technologies such as notching, stacking and precision dispensing. The company is also developing its own roll press technology capable of replacing the warm isostatic press (WIP), which is regarded as a representative pressing process for solid-state batteries. Through this, Mplus aims to build a full lineup of equipment covering all processes required for solid-state battery production. Solid-state batteries are next-generation secondary batteries that replace conventional liquid electrolytes with solid ones. They can improve safety and energy density, but their manufacturing processes are highly demanding, and equipment technology capable of supporting stable mass production is seen as the key to commercialization. As major automakers target the launch of vehicles equipped with solid-state batteries by 2030, battery manufacturers are accelerating facility investment in pilot and mass-production lines. Note: The counterparty and detailed delivery terms were not disclosed. Mplus is also accelerating the diversification of its order portfolio. After recently targeting the multi-purpose specialty battery equipment market, including defense applications, with a European global battery company, it has now also secured this solid-state equipment order, expanding its customer base from a focus on electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESS) into next-generation and specialty battery segments. A company official said, "This order is meaningful in that we have secured an official supply reference in the next-generation solid-state battery mass-production equipment segment," adding, "If the customer's shift to solid-state battery mass production gets into full swing, it could lead to follow-on large orders." The official added, "We also expect additional order opportunities as the customer expands production going forward." Industry observers expect order opportunities for related equipment makers to expand as the solid-state battery market moves beyond the R&D stage into a phase of preparation for commercialization. In particular, they say a track record of supplying initial production lines could serve as a gauge of competitiveness in future mass-production equipment orders. Mplus manufactures assembly equipment — including notching, stacking, tab welding and packaging for pouch-type, prismatic and solid-state batteries — as well as electrode-line facilities. The company is also expanding its new business portfolio, including autonomous mobile robots (AIMRs) and control systems for the physical AI (artificial intelligence) era. This contract remains at the equipment supply stage, so its immediate contribution to earnings may be limited, but it is significant as a bridgehead for securing additional orders when the shift to solid-state battery mass production takes place. Solid-state batteries are still in the early stages of mass production and process standards have not yet been established, so companies that supply equipment for initial lines are seen as potentially holding an advantageous position in subsequent equipment orders. However, some note that with the customer unidentified and the mass-production schedule unconfirmed, whether follow-on orders materialize depends on the pace of the customer's investment execution. artigo.texto: NTT Eyes Space Optical Communications Network, Lunar Power Supply and Space Data Centers NTT President Akira Shimada said in a November 16 lecture in Tokyo that the company will build a space optical communications network linking satellites to each other and to ground communications equipment via optical signals. The company aims to mount electronic components compatible with its next-generation high-speed communications platform IOWN on satellites and other communications devices, creating a system that efficiently delivers satellite-acquired data to ground receiving stations by routing it through another satellite positioned closer to the receiver. Shimada also outlined plans to work on space data centers and power-generation infrastructure on the lunar surface. "NTT will use the technology it has cultivated to weave an optical information network across space," Shimada said, stressing the significance of extending the company's communications control technology into the space domain. Optical communications can transmit far larger volumes of data than radio waves, but are vulnerable to weather and atmospheric conditions, including blockage by clouds. NTT will need technology to accurately transmit data to satellites moving at speeds that circle the Earth in about 90 minutes, as well as the ability to select communications routes that connect multiple satellites and ground equipment along the shortest path. Shimada also said that "the major social roles space will play are communications and observation." Analyzing high-resolution imagery captured by satellites can be used to assess conditions during wildfires and disasters, as well as to survey the distribution of wildlife and vegetation. NTT also anticipates demand for satellite communications as a supplement in mountainous areas and remote islands where terrestrial networks are hard to reach. NTT plans to deploy ground communications equipment around the world by fiscal 2029. Partnership with ispace to study lunar infrastructure NTT announced the same day that it has signed a partnership agreement with space venture ispace (Chuo Ward, Tokyo). The two companies will pursue research, development, demonstration and study toward future commercialization of infrastructure technologies including high-speed optical communications in cislunar space—the region between Earth and the Moon—and wireless laser power transmission on the lunar surface. As lunar exploration advances, a wide variety of data will be generated, including sensor data and activity logs in addition to measurement data. Communications and power infrastructure will be essential to transmit this data to Earth and share it on the Moon as well. From an economic security standpoint, experts have also pointed to the importance of Japan taking the lead in building and managing such infrastructure. While expanding its optical communications research into space, NTT has been developing laser wireless power transmission technology with an eye toward applications beyond communications. ispace, through the lunar landers and rovers its group develops and operates, is working to provide lunar transportation and lunar data services. It plans "Mission 3," targeting a lunar landing in 2028, and aims to commercialize communications and positioning services using lunar orbiters, with plans to launch its first orbiter as early as 2027 under "Mission 2.5." The two companies will combine NTT's optical technologies, including optical communications and laser power transmission, with ispace's expertise in lunar transportation, exploration and mission operations to verify the applicability of optical technology to the lunar environment. Private-sector entry accelerates in U.S.-China-led space race The United States and China are vying for leadership in space development, with countries competing over the number of satellites launched. SpaceX, led by entrepreneur Elon Musk, is pursuing a plan to expand its satellite constellation to 42,000. China has set out a vision of deploying more than 200,000 satellites by the mid-2030s, and South Korea plans to build a network of 7,000 communications satellites. Major IT companies such as Amazon.com are also entering the field, intensifying competition over the use of low-Earth-orbit satellites. The concept of placing computing infrastructure in space is also gaining traction as an alternative to ground-based data centers, which are increasingly struggling to secure power and cooling water. NTT's space data center initiative is seen as aimed at capturing this demand. Market impact For NTT, space optical communications represent an attempt to open a new revenue stream from IOWN-related technology. With Japan's domestic communications market maturing, satellite communications and space infrastructure are drawing attention as areas with significant growth potential. If the partnership with ispace moves from demonstration to commercialization, it could raise the profile of Japanese companies in international competition over lunar transportation and data communications. At the same time, SpaceX and Chinese state-owned enterprises boast overwhelming launch volumes for low-Earth-orbit satellites, and international coordination over the use of frequencies and orbits remains a challenge. Putting an optical communications network into practical use requires the mass deployment of satellites and the buildout of ground equipment, raising questions about the scale of investment required. How NTT's expansion into space contributes to its earnings structure will depend on the progress of demonstrations and the timing of commercialization. artigo.texto: POWER POINT The demise of data centers has been greatly exaggerated. So says every utility CEO and energy-focused investor we spoke with at the Edison Electric Institute's annual conference in Arizona. Here's why... There is a lot of misleading, misdirected, or straight-up incorrect information floating around about data centers and the AI buildout. I'm not going to dive into the old water-use story — you can do your own research on that — but rather focus this week on what the insiders know: Some newly elected politicians either don't have the power to stop the buildouts or, if they do, the buildout will likely just continue somewhere else. Ohio and Georgia are important states to watch with their new incoming political class, but for the sheer importance in size and scope, I'll focus on the energy and data center capital: Texas. Incoming Governor Gina Hinojosa and incoming Senator James Talarico both campaigned on promises to go after what they believe to be affordability issues around data centers. I say "what they believe to be" because it's unclear how much data centers may raise your electricity bill, if at all. First and foremost, data centers are largely a state issue, meaning officials elected to federal office have little control over outcomes, at least for now. In Texas, any cancellations or moratoriums on new builds will come from the statehouse in Austin. That's where current Governor Greg Abbott has already, and rather quietly, put his own "pause" on data center permitting. That delay has been underway for a few weeks. Also, in Texas, the Governor has less direct power than in some other states. The power the governor does have largely derives from the authority to appoint those in charge of the all-important permitting process. In the Lone Star State, that power lies with two agencies: the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the even lesser-known Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ). The PUCT regulates Texas' electricity, telecom, and water industries. It helps oversee growth of anything electricity-grid-related. So if a data center wants to connect to the public utility grid, it needs the commission's approval. Its chair — a pro-growth chap named Thomas Gleeson —is also on the board of Texas' electric grid powerhouse ERCOT and will serve his term with the utility commission through September 2029. Yes, three years from now. That agency gets involved when a data center or power provider wants to connect to the electricity grid. But what about facilities that are off the grid and have their own dedicated power sources? Texas has less control over what happens then. That said, it does have to authorize certain environmental permits, and that responsibility largely lies with the TCEQ. The TCEQ was "BBI" (my own little term for "boring, but important") until data centers came along. It's not exactly the Alamo, but this obscure group — run by a regulator named Brooke Paup — is largely the "last stand" for permitting on those new builds. Paup was also appointed by Gov. Abbott and serves through next year. In other words, unless she and Gleeson step down or there is some way to oust them, the regulatory environment in Texas may not change much. The bottom line in this brief foray into the Texas regulatory swamp is to highlight that there are things for investors to consider around the data center/energy world that may not be at the top of the headlines. Important Note → Be mindful that I am an East Coast-based financial broadcaster and journalist, not an expert on Texas regulation or how the state operates. There may very well be things I don't know, things my sources aren't aware of, or other ways in which the new Governor and state House can assert power. For one, she recently said she may try to freeze electricity rates. Hint: that would be a terrible idea unless you want to damage the growth of badly needed new power sources like wind and solar. Disclaimer is done. Let's assume I am wrong on Texas and there is a larger push to slow or stop data center growth in the state. Conversations with some pretty smart people lead me to believe that if those facilities aren't built in that state, they will be built in another: Louisiana, Oklahoma, or another state. Sources tell me that Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and his team are already working the phones, telling companies that his state would love to welcome new business. Same for Oklahoma. Both are gas-rich, have plenty of power, and are only too happy to grab any data center dollars. Now, a huge caveat. Let's acknowledge that not all data centers are going to be built… and never were. There are way too many plans to make them all happen. Some DCs were shelved before the election. Some others may soon be canceled, either for reasons of public pushback or otherwise. It's also not clear if we even need all the planned compute. There will be a time when companies realize they have enough — or at least enough for now — and turn off the spending taps. Goldman Sachs lays it out in a new note late this week: "The midterm election results pose only modest risks to AI investment, for now. We expect newly elected Democratic governors in states that account for over a third of planned US data center capacity to impose moratoria on new data centers. However, these will likely only impact projects not yet permitted, leaving the vast majority of planned 2027 construction unaffected. We therefore expect data center construction spending to remain strong next year, though moratoria that are stricter or longer-lasting than we expect pose downside risks." The firm adds that it still sees spending on AI-related hardware coming in around $1.4 trillion by the end of next year. In other words, the spending boom is going to keep going, at least for now. artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution is set to launch an offensive in the North American AI power infrastructure market by unveiling an integrated energy solution that covers everything from power storage to supply and management for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On Nov. 15, LG Energy Solution announced its participation in ‘RE+ 2026,’ North America’s largest renewable energy exhibition, which will be held in Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, from the 17th to the 19th (local time). This year’s exhibition theme is “Energy for the Future of AI – Reliability, Resilience, and Intelligence.” LG Energy Solution has prepared an exhibition space of 279 square meters, approximately 20% larger than last year, where it will showcase integrated power infrastructure for AI data centers and next-generation battery technology. The core of the exhibition is “AI Data Center Integrated Power Infrastructure,” which combines Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS), Battery Backup Units (BBU), and Energy Management Systems (EMS). A key feature is that it provides power storage and supply, as well as functions to respond to emergencies such as power outages, all within a single system. The company will also introduce its recent achievement of being selected as a partner in NVIDIA’s “DSX Ready BESS” program. In the field of grid-scale Energy Storage Systems (ESS), LG Energy Solution will unveil the “JF3 AC LINK,” based on Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries. This product utilizes LFP batteries produced locally in the United States and increases energy density per site by approximately 26% compared to existing products. It is designed to supply power stably to data centers and large-scale power grids by applying digital twin technology (a technique that replicates real-world facilities or systems in a virtual computer space to analyze and predict operating conditions) and AI-based power stabilization technology. As for next-generation battery technology, the company will showcase a system combining sodium-ion batteries with Solid-State Transformers (SST). This technology combines the thermal stability of sodium-ion batteries with the power conversion function of SSTs to respond to frequent charging and discharging cycles as well as sudden changes in power demand. In addition, LG Energy Solution will exhibit next-generation “JP6 UPS Rack” systems and BBU products utilizing cylindrical 2170 batteries. These products supply power immediately to servers during a power outage while enhancing data center space utilization through high-density battery design. LG Energy Solution also plans to emphasize its production capacity of over 50 GWh secured in North America. The company is expanding its business scope from system design and construction to operation, optimization, and asset management by leveraging Vertech, a specialized legal entity for the ESS business, and the integrated software platform “AEROS Suite.” Kang Chang-beom, vice president of LG Energy Solution’s ESS Battery Business Division, said, “The growth of the AI industry demands new energy solutions that encompass stable power storage and supply, as well as efficient operation.” He added, “By combining local production competitiveness in North America with differentiated technological capabilities, system construction expertise, and intelligent operational capabilities, we will accelerate our growth into an energy platform company.”

artigo.texto: Projeto de data centers da Atlas Energy pode movimentar R$ 40 bilhões em Uberaba Uberaba, no Triângulo Mineiro, pode receber cerca de R$ 40 bilhões em investimentos destinados à instalação de infraestrutura para data center na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE). O projeto foi formalizado pela Atlas Renewable Energy e deve ser protocolado, até o fim de 2026, no Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE). Segundo a Prefeitura de Uberaba, estudos preliminares indicam aportes superiores a R$ 10 bilhões na etapa inicial, destinados a obras e infraestrutura, e outros R$ 30 bilhões em equipamentos de tecnologia da informação em uma fase posterior. Ao Diário do Comércio, o secretário de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Turismo e Inovação de Uberaba, Celso Neto, afirmou que as conversas com a Atlas Renewable Energy começaram no início deste ano. Desde então, segundo ele, o município e a empresa têm mantido tratativas para adequar o projeto às exigências do Conselho Nacional das ZPEs. Clique aqui para seguir o canal do Diário do Comércio no WhatsApp “Foi uma negociação bastante tranquila e construtiva. Nossa cidade conta com a única ZPE do Sul e Sudeste do País e temos um plano claro e definido de atrair pelo menos um grande projeto de datacenter para ela”, destaca Neto. Ele acrescenta que o cronograma de implantação da infraestrutura de data center em Uberaba dependerá do aval do conselho e do cumprimento das demais exigências regulatórias. “Como depende da aprovação de um órgão do governo federal (o CZPE), não conseguimos prever exatamente quando teremos uma definição deles. Todavia, até o final deste ano, todas as obrigações do município, da ZPE Uberaba e da empresa estarão sanadas”, afirma o secretário. O que atraiu projeto de data center para Uberaba Segundo Neto, os benefícios tributários federais da Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) de Uberaba abriram caminho para as conversas com a Atlas Renewable Energy. Entre os atrativos do município, ele cita a infraestrutura logística e a proximidade de capitais e centros consumidores em um raio de cerca de 500 quilômetros (km). Neto destaca ainda a atuação do Parque Tecnológico de Uberaba e a oferta de formação profissional pelas universidades e pelo Sistema S, que reúne entidades como o Senai e o Senac, voltadas à qualificação de trabalhadores. Além das condições de formação e inovação, o secretário cita a gestão municipal do licenciamento ambiental, que, na avaliação dele, aproxima a prefeitura dos empreendedores e dá mais previsibilidade ao processo. Atlas avalia projeto em Uberaba e já sinalizou interesse em Paracatu As ZPEs, são áreas de livre comércio com o exterior que oferecem benefícios tributários, administrativos e cambiais à exportação de bens e serviços. Segundo a Prefeitura, a ZPE de Uberaba é uma das quatro do País alfandegadas pela Receita Federal e aptas a receber investimentos. A Atlas Renewable Energy, que avalia a instalação de infraestrutura para data center na ZPE de Uberaba, desenvolve, financia, constrói e opera projetos de energia renovável de grande escala na América Latina. “Uberaba tem características que a tornam uma região de grande potencial para o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura digital sustentável no País. Seguimos avaliando a iniciativa em diálogo com o Município e com os órgãos competentes”, afirma o presidente da Atlas Renewable Energy no Brasil, Fábio Bortoluzo. Vale lembrar que o grupo Atlas também está ligado a um projeto de data center em Paracatu, no Noroeste de Minas. A Central Fotovoltaica Giovana SPE 1 S.A, empresa do grupo, apresentou ao governo federal três pedidos de conexão à rede de transmissão de energia para instalar um complexo no município. O projeto também também poderia mobilizar um aporte bilionário e figurar entre os maiores do setor no País. Ainda não está claro se Uberaba e Paracatu são alternativas para um mesmo investimento ou se os dois projetos podem avançar em paralelo. artigo.texto: EcoPro is stepping up efforts to strengthen its global competitiveness by showcasing its secondary battery materials ecosystem in Pohang, North Gyeongsang Province, and its next-generation battery materials technologies. EcoPro said Sunday that it participated in the International Battery Expo 2026 Pohang, held for three days from Nov. 13 at Manindang Gymnasium in Pohang. Now in its second year, the expo is a specialized exhibition showcasing technologies and future visions across the entire battery industry, from materials and components to recycling used batteries. EcoPro organized its exhibition booth around seven themes, including cooperation with the Pohang community, global supply chains, high-nickel cathode materials and next-generation battery materials. Since 2017, EcoPro has invested approximately 3.3 trillion won in Pohang to build a secondary battery materials ecosystem linking precursor and cathode material production with used battery recycling. The company is strengthening its supply chain competitiveness through a closed-loop system that connects raw material procurement, production and recycling. The company also introduced its global production network. It is building an integrated supply chain linking its BNSI nickel smelter in Indonesia, its cathode materials plant in Debrecen, Hungary, and its domestic production facilities, connecting raw material sourcing with finished product manufacturing. EcoPro also showcased its next-generation battery materials technologies. Its lineup included high-nickel ternary cathode materials, known for their high energy density, as well as mid-nickel cathode materials, materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. The company also presented its solid electrolyte technology, a key material for all-solid-state batteries, outlining its strategy to expand its product portfolio. High-nickel cathode materials, in particular, are expected to find wider applications beyond electric vehicles in emerging industries requiring high energy density, including humanoid robots, urban air mobility (UAM) and aerospace. EcoPro also highlighted its contributions to the local community. Through social initiatives such as supporting childbirth in vulnerable households, providing safety umbrellas for children and developing community welfare villages, the company has been recognized as a community-contributing company for seven consecutive years. "Having grown in Pohang, EcoPro feels a strong responsibility to contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of Korea's battery industry alongside the local community," EcoPro CEO Choi Sang-woon said. "We will do our utmost to boost our global competitiveness through continued investment and technological innovation while helping revitalize the local economy and create quality jobs."

artigo.texto: Apresentando o mercado de carbono do Vietnã à comunidade internacional. A TPO - Vietnam acaba de lançar um portal de informações sobre o mercado de carbono na Turquia, com o objetivo de compartilhar publicamente informações importantes sobre as políticas, regulamentações e operações do mercado de carbono vietnamita com a comunidade internacional. No âmbito da 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), o Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente do Vietnã, o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) e o Escritório das Nações Unidas de Serviços para Projetos (UNOPS) organizaram o evento “Promovendo o Mercado de Carbono do Vietnã: Transparência, Eficiência e Cooperação Internacional” . O ponto alto do evento foi o lançamento do Portal de Informações sobre o Mercado de Carbono. Este canal disponibiliza publicamente informações importantes sobre políticas, regulamentações e operações de mercado, auxiliando empresas, investidores e demais partes interessadas a acessar informações e participar do mercado de carbono emergente no Vietnã. Nos últimos anos, o Vietnã fez progressos significativos no estabelecimento de um mercado de carbono doméstico, com o lançamento da Bolsa de Carbono em 29 de junho de 2026. Durante o período de 2025–2026, o Governo aprovou uma quota piloto total de emissões de aproximadamente 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente, atribuída a 110 instalações nas indústrias de energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento. A fase piloto do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) terá duração até o final de 2028, com o objetivo de que o mercado entre em operação oficialmente a partir de 2029. Segundo o Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, o Vietnã reconhece que o mercado de carbono não é apenas uma ferramenta para gerenciar emissões, mas também precisa criar incentivos para que as empresas inovem em tecnologia, melhorem a eficiência energética e invistam em soluções para a redução de emissões. Desde 2022, o PNUD tem apoiado a Agência de Mudanças Climáticas no desenvolvimento de políticas, estruturas institucionais e roteiros para a implementação de mercados de carbono, além de fortalecer sua capacidade de participar de mecanismos de cooperação internacional, conforme o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. O PNUD também apoiou o desenvolvimento do Sistema Nacional de Registro de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono (VCRS) e sua conexão com a Bolsa de Valores de Hanói e a Corporação de Custódia e Liquidação de Valores Mobiliários do Vietnã. Você também pode gostar Juntamente com o novo portal, esses sistemas formam uma base crucial de infraestrutura digital para operar um mercado de carbono transparente no Vietnã. Leticia Guimarães, Chefe de Mercados Globais de Carbono do PNUD, afirmou que, em todo o mundo , cada vez mais países estão desenvolvendo mercados de carbono como uma ferramenta importante para a redução de emissões de forma economicamente viável e para a mobilização de financiamento climático. A Sra. Leticia Guimarães avaliou que o Vietnã fez progressos notáveis no desenvolvimento de seu mercado de carbono, transformando gradualmente sua Contribuição Nacionalmente Determinada (NDC) e seu compromisso de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 em ações concretas. É importante destacar que o projeto-piloto do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (ETS, na sigla em inglês) inclui atualmente 110 instalações nos setores de energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, que representam aproximadamente 40% do total de emissões de gases de efeito estufa do país. A Sra. Leticia Guimarães acredita que os próximos dois a três anos serão um período decisivo, à medida que o Vietnã transita da fase de estabelecimento de mercado para a operação plena. “Esperamos fortalecer ainda mais nossa parceria com o Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas e expandir a cooperação entre os setores público e privado, a fim de contribuir para a construção de um mercado de carbono robusto, transparente e eficiente, promovendo a transição verde do Vietnã rumo a uma economia de baixas emissões”, disse a Sra. Leticia Guimarães. John Robert Cotton, Diretor do Programa de Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP) do UNOPS, afirmou que muito poucos países conseguiram fazer a transição da criação de um arcabouço legal para a operação de um mercado de carbono obrigatório no prazo alcançado pelo Vietnã. Ele também enfatizou que o mercado de carbono é particularmente importante para cumprir o compromisso do Vietnã com emissões líquidas zero. Você também pode gostar Segundo ele, essa jornada exige um enorme volume de capital de investimento que o orçamento estatal não pode fornecer por si só. O desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono ajudará a mobilizar recursos, incorporando os custos de emissão nos balanços das empresas e transformando a redução de emissões em uma decisão de investimento, em vez de apenas uma exigência legal. Em segundo lugar, a partir de 2029, quando o mecanismo de leilão de quotas começar a ser aplicado, o mercado gerará receitas para o orçamento do Estado, que poderão ser reinvestidas em atividades de redução de emissões na indústria. Além disso, por meio do Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris, o mercado abre oportunidades de acesso a capital internacional para projetos que antes tinham dificuldades em obter financiamento. Ele também compartilhou que, para desenvolver o mercado de carbono, o apoio dos parceiros de desenvolvimento desempenha um papel crucial. Esse apoio contribui para o fornecimento de recursos para pesquisa e análise, compartilhamento de experiências e conhecimentos de outros sistemas e para ajudar a superar dificuldades e obstáculos. “No entanto, é a determinação do governo que está impulsionando esse processo. artigo.texto: Introducing Vietnam's carbon market to the international community. TPO - Vietnam has just launched a carbon market information portal in Türkiye, aiming to publicly share important information about the policies, regulations, and operations of Vietnam's carbon market with the international community. Within the framework of the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), the Climate Change Department of the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment of Vietnam, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) organized the event “Promoting Vietnam’s Carbon Market: Transparency, Efficiency, and International Cooperation” . The highlight of the event was the launch of the Carbon Market Information Portal. This is a channel that publicly provides important information on policies, regulations, and market operations, helping businesses, investors, and stakeholders access information and participate in the emerging carbon market in Vietnam. In recent years, Vietnam has made significant progress in establishing a domestic carbon market, with the launch of the Carbon Exchange on June 29, 2026. During the 2025–2026 period, the Government approved a total pilot emission quota of approximately 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent, allocated to 110 facilities in the thermal power, iron and steel, and cement industries. The pilot phase of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) will last until the end of 2028, aiming for the official operation of the market from 2029. According to Mr. Bui Duc Hieu, Deputy Director of the Climate Change Department, Vietnam recognizes that the carbon market is not only a tool for managing emissions but also needs to create incentives for businesses to innovate technology, improve energy efficiency, and invest in emission reduction solutions. Since 2022, UNDP has supported the Climate Change Agency in developing policies, institutional frameworks, and roadmaps for implementing carbon markets, while also strengthening its capacity to participate in international cooperation mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. UNDP also supported the development of the National Registration System for Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Carbon Credits (VCRS) and its connection to the Hanoi Stock Exchange and the Vietnam Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation. You may also like Together with the new portal, these systems form a crucial digital infrastructure foundation for operating a transparent carbon market in Vietnam. Leticia Guimaraes, Head of Global Carbon Markets at UNDP, said that around the world , more and more countries are developing carbon markets as an important tool for cost-effective emission reduction and climate finance mobilization. Ms. Leticia Guimaraes assessed that Vietnam has made remarkable progress in developing its carbon market, gradually transforming its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 into concrete actions. Significantly, the pilot Emissions Trading System (ETS) currently includes 110 facilities in the thermal power, iron and steel, and cement industries, accounting for approximately 40% of the nation's total greenhouse gas emissions. Ms. Leticia Guimaraes believes that the next two to three years will be a decisive period as Vietnam transitions from market establishment to full operation. “We look forward to further strengthening our partnership with the Climate Change Department and expanding cooperation between the public and private sectors, in order to contribute to building a robust, transparent, and efficient carbon market, promoting Vietnam’s green transition towards a low-emission economy ,” said Ms. Leticia Guimaraes. John Robert Cotton, Director of the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) Programme at UNOPS, stated that very few countries have been able to transition from establishing a legal framework to operating a mandatory carbon market in the timeframe that Vietnam has achieved. He also emphasized that the carbon market is particularly important in fulfilling Vietnam's commitment to net-zero emissions. You may also like According to him, this journey requires a huge amount of investment capital that the state budget cannot provide on its own. Developing a carbon market will help mobilize resources by incorporating emission costs into businesses' balance sheets, transforming emission reduction into an investment decision instead of just a compliance requirement. Secondly, from 2029, when the quota auction mechanism begins to be applied, the market will generate revenue for the state budget, which can be reinvested in emission reduction activities in industry. Furthermore, through Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, the market opens up opportunities for accessing international capital for projects that previously struggled to raise funding. He also shared that, in order to develop the carbon market, the support of development partners plays a crucial role. This support contributes to providing resources for research and analysis, sharing experience and expertise from other systems, and helping to overcome difficulties and obstacles. “However, it is the government’s determination that is driving this process. The progress we have witnessed over the past four years is a testament to the vision and commitment of the Vietnamese government,” said John Robert Cotton. At the event, many also emphasized that close cooperation between the Vietnamese Government, development partners, and businesses will continue to play a crucial role in ensuring a carbon market. This will contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, attracting investment, and fulfilling Vietnam's commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050.

artigo.texto: Chris Meiter & Ed Evans from AMAG Technology and Eric Zei from Salient Systems examine why data center security gaps often stem from unfinished integration and unclear ownership, rather than outdated technology. Article Chapters Toggle Data centers are going up faster than almost any other facility type, and the security problem inside them resembles nothing else. A large colocation site moves tens of thousands of people through its doors in a year, working for hundreds of separate tenant companies, most of whom the operator does not employ. Community opposition and organized protests are trying to reshape where these buildings go and how their perimeters get designed. Drones are a concern, though not for what they can see: everything in a data center comes back to cooling, and material dropped into an intake causes an operational event without anyone crossing the fence. Even video retention, a policy question in most buildings, is a contractual obligation with real money attached. Salient Systems and AMAG Technology have worked on these buildings together since 2012. AMAG is among Salient’s closest technology partners, and the work we do together concentrates in exactly this segment: the large operators running multi-tenant sites at scale. So, when an operator tells one of us that the security system isn’t doing what they expected, we compare notes. Comparing notes works because the two halves are not as separate as they look. Access control is often treated as finished technology: badge, reader, door. Visibility is treated as something happening on the video and analytics side. But that mistakes maturity for being solved. A protocol can be decades old and entirely stable, yet still be poorly managed. It is also backwards. Analytics are only ever as good as the access data they compare themselves against. Access events arrive in the video system with the cardholder attached to the alarm, which is what allows an operator to see who badged and to pull the recorded video by clicking the event rather than hunting for a camera and a time. The traffic runs both ways: video can trigger a lockdown, and a credential flagged as stolen can raise an alert with the right camera already attached to it. Video used to be evidence you went back for after somebody reported an incident. Now it is meant to raise the alarm while the incident is still underway. That only works if the access side is alerting personnel to something worth raising. Tailgating is the clearest case. Access control records one valid swipe. Video, counting people, sees two bodies come through. Neither system flags anything alone, because the log says a valid credential was granted and video has no view on how many people should have passed. The alert exists only in the comparison. And in a data center, the second person is rarely an intruder. It is a colleague who did not badge, or a contractor’s second technician on one credential, walking past cages that belong to somebody else. That is what the two systems do when they work. Far more often, what we hear is that they don’t. The complaint is always the same sentence. What is causing it almost never is. In one building the recording servers are eleven years old and the software is four versions behind. That is a budget conversation, and there is no clever way around it. In the other, everything is current and everything works. Nothing was ever finished: the detection zones are drawn so wide that somebody switched the alarms off, the cameras and the doors carry different names in each system, and the clocks drifted apart two years ago without anyone noticing. That one is an afternoon of work. From the operator’s chair the two are indistinguishable. Ed Evans of AMAG Technology puts it at four out of five being the second kind, and suspects that estimate is generous. Neither got that way by accident, and the routes are different. The first route is money. Hardware debt accumulates because security sits behind other IT in the funding order, and a department whose failures stay invisible is easy to defer. Nobody runs a laptop for eleven years. A recording server that has been writing continuously for eleven years draws no comment at all. Version drift is quieter still. One operator can run a dozen sites on the same platform with eight different builds among them and never log it as a fault. That is why someone will watch a capability demonstrated at a trade show and insist their own system cannot do it. It can. Theirs is four versions back. The second route is easier to travel because nothing along it announces itself. A detection zone, a door name, a drifted clock: none of it registers as an incident on its own. Collectively they are the distance between the system as designed and the system as installed, and almost nobody measures that distance. “The system does what it’s told,” Ed says. “It’s just being told the wrong thing.” Colocation multiplies everything that has to be told correctly. “The big thing colocation has to deal with that single-tenant and hyperscale rarely do, is keeping tenants separated from each other, not just keeping outsiders out,” Ed adds. That one difference reaches into every part of the design. Segmentation has to go down to the cage and sometimes the cabinet. Every tenant runs its own authorized-personnel list, with its own churn. Audit evidence has to come out per tenant, PCI for one and HIPAA for the next. And a tailgate into the wrong cage is not an internal write-up. It is a contract problem with a paying customer. An unfinished system is not a technology failure. It is a failure of ownership, and a data center project is structured in a way that almost produces it. On paper, commissioning splits three ways: “Nobody is structurally incentivized to find the gaps,” Ed says. Verification falls to whoever volunteers, and frequently nobody does. artigo.texto: On November 12, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published a comprehensive Finance and Economics Discussion Series working paper documenting that while U.S. capital commitments for artificial intelligence data centers have surged past $1 trillion, aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted. For university research leaders, economics scholars, and facility directors, the empirical findings highlight severe upstream hardware inflation, substantial import leakage, and mounting compute procurement pressures across higher education. FEDS 2026-074: Quantifying the Capital Boom in Artificial Intelligence Authored by Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols, working paper FEDS 2026-074—titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence (DOI: 10.17016/FEDS.2026.074)—evaluates how generative AI infrastructure is rippling through national accounts. Crucially, this working paper investigates real macroeconomic variables, capital accumulation, and industry output, keeping its analysis distinct from the central bank’s semi-annual Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, which focused on debt liquidity and bank credit exposures. The paper documents a massive escalation in planned domestic data-center construction, which climbed from roughly $300 billion in 2024 to more than $1 trillion in announced pipelines by 2025. Applying the project forecasting methodology from Brandsaas et al. (2025), the authors estimate that baseline annual data-center investment will step up from $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027, exceeding 2.0% of U.S. GDP. Approximately one-third of this outlay funds physical structures, while two-thirds is absorbed by high-tech equipment including GPUs, TPUs, high-density memory, and server cooling systems. Data-Center Capex Projections, Import Leakage, and Component Inflation The pace of data-center capital deployment has generated distinct supply-chain pressures and macroeconomic offsets. Key benchmarks established in FEDS 2026-074 include: Crucially, Carollo and colleagues calculate an import share of roughly 50% for high-tech compute hardware, with components primarily sourced from East Asian fabrication and packaging corridors. Because imported equipment enters national accounts as a deduction, this substantial leakage moderates the direct domestic output multiplier. Concurrently, direct inputs like high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and specialized printed circuit boards experienced annualized price increases of nearly 8% through early 2026, reversing a multi-decade trend of technological price deflation. Surging electricity requirements also prompted a sharp rise in power-generation interconnection requests in late 2025. These local infrastructure dynamics align with NBER research by Alvarez et al. (2026), which shows that data centers generate brief construction bursts but minimal long-term local employment. The Solow Productivity Paradox in the Generative Era Despite heavy capital commitments, FEDS 2026-074 finds that generative AI has yielded negligible measurable impact on aggregate U.S. labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity (TFP). Addressing this gap on November 13, 2026, at the UC San Diego Economics Roundtable, Federal Reserve Board Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a keynote address titled New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy. Jefferson invoked Robert Solow’s famous 1987 paradox that ‘you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.’ Jefferson noted that early personal computer investment in the late 1980s required more than a decade of organizational adaptation before aggregate productivity accelerated. Econometric decomposition in FEDS 2026-074 indicates that recent post-2023 productivity pickups primarily reflect cyclical supply-chain normalization rather than AI diffusion. Furthermore, the authors review growth literature: Daron Acemoglu (2025) estimates cumulative TFP gains of only 0.7% over the next decade, while optimistic projections by Filippucci et al. (2025) reach 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points annually. Task-level studies by Jones and Tonetti (2026) and Demirer, Musolff, and Yang (2026) confirm that coding agents accelerate syntax generation, but software deployment remains tightly bounded by human review and integration testing. Federal Reserve Leadership Perspectives: Barr and Waller on Labor and Inequality Central bank governors expanded on these macroeconomic themes during November 2026 addresses. On November 12 at Yale University, Governor Michael S. Barr presented remarks on American Inequality and the Future of AI, analyzing findings from the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Barr warned that because AI infrastructure requires massive capital reserves, financial gains are heavily concentrated among top software firms and high-wealth equity holders, raising distributional risks if routine entry-level cognitive tasks face wage erosion. Conversely, Governor Christopher J. Waller emphasized labor resilience in his November 10 speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference on The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism. Waller noted that aggregate claims, vacancies, and payrolls show no sign of widespread displacement. This stability is corroborated by New York Fed research (Abel et al., 2025) and independent market analysis from TradingView, which report that only ~10% of workers use AI daily, with firms primarily augmenting existing roles rather than reducing headcounts. artigo.texto: How data centers lost in the midterm elections COLUMBUS, Ohio - Beyond political parties and individual candidates, there was a clear loser in the 2026 midterms: data centers. As these essential pieces of AI infrastructure have dropped in popularity, they’ve been met with staunch resistance at the ballot box. Data centers lost on the ballot in the midterms By the numbers: According to research by Rosebud Consulting, voters in cities across the nation approved 44 ballot measures restricting data centers this November. Nearly half of those ballot measures came out of cities in Ohio, one of the nation’s largest data center markets. Ohio has more than 250 data centers. That’s the fifth most in the nation. Voters in Kansas, Illinois, Wisconsin, Maine, New Jersey, Florida, California and Nevada also approved restrictive ballot measures. By contrast, a single community voted in favor of data centers on a ballot measure. That was in Harwood, North Dakota — a town of less than a thousand residents. Data centers proved unpopular Dig deeper: AI proponents took a shellacking in Ohio, where midterm voters approved 21 restrictions for data centers in cities across the state. And that’s no surprise for researchers at Ohio Northern University. "These election results reflect a well-established majority consensus across Ohio communities demanding greater local control and strict oversight." said Keith Durkin, a professor at Ohio Northern University. He’s also director of the university’s Institute for Civics and Public Policy. The college released a study in October that found widespread opposition to data centers. "Our statewide Northern Poll found that 55% of Ohio adults oppose data center construction in their communities, and 57% support legal restrictions and megawatt caps on hyperscale development." Durkin said. Big Tech growing pains appear to go beyond a rural and urban or political divide. "The underlying voter sentiment shows minimal geographical differences in the state of Ohio," Durkin said. "Concerns over escalating home electric bills and grid vulnerability resonate equally across urban centers, suburban developments, and rural farming communities. The demand for ratepayer protection and community zoning authority spans all geographic demographics." Ohio's Senate race: Data centers may have been a factor in Ohio’s Senate race. While Ohio has typically been a stronghold for Donald Trump — he carried the state in the last three presidential elections — this year, Ohio voters rejected his endorsed Senate candidate and instead sent Democrat Sherrod Brown to Washington D.C. Brown, who previously served in the Senate, labeled his competitor Republican Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers" in a campaign ad. In another, Brown’s campaign called Husted, who was the incumbent in the race, the "chief reason Ohio has so many data centers." Meanwhile, President Trump, who endorsed Husted, has vocally supported AI and data centers, saying communities that reject them are destined to become "backwards and poor." Brown ultimately won his seat with 50% of the vote. Husted trailed with 45.1%, according to the Associated Press. Anti-data center sucesses: Beyond Ohio, candidates looking to battle Big Tech performed well on election night. Gina Hinojsa, the Democrat and Texas Governor-elect who unseated Republican Greg Abbott, has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers. Likewise, in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who won a bitter Senate race, was also outspoken on data centers. Their wins help to validate survey results from Pew Research Center, which found that a large portion of Americans are feeling pessimistic about data centers. Six in 10 adults surveyed said they would not be comfortable with a new data center in their area. Another 58% said they disliked politicians who supported building data centers near their homes or communities. However, Dirkin, the professor from Ohio Northern University, cautioned against drawing a straight line between candidate success or failure and anti-AI sentiment. "While data center expansion and tax subsidies carry clear public unpopularity, it is difficult to draw a direct causal line to candidate losses," Dirkin said. "Multi-issue elections are complex, and our findings indicate that data center concerns do not operate in a vacuum—they are tied to a larger, overarching voter focus on overall economic affordability, household utility costs, and community tax policy." Are data center laws going to change? Big picture view: It’s unclear if the anti-data center sentiment that came through in the midterms will result in new laws governing AI’s continued buildout. Wall Street appeared fearful of a data center slowdown, leaning into a multi trillion-dollar post-election sell-off of AI stocks. At the same time, some in the Big Tech world are asking for clarity in future laws. "New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies," wrote OpenAI, the owner of ChatGPT, in a Nov. 5 statement. "Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared." The company also offered a new set of data center commitments, saying it will pay the full costs of electricity and infrastructure and introduce new environmental protection plans. The Source: This story was written using interviews with a Northern Ohio professor, Pew Research Center and Rosebud Consulting data, election night results and public statements made by candidates and OpenAI. It was reported from Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

artigo.texto: GCL Energy Technology Co., Ltd. (GCL-ET), the energy technology solutions arm of GCL Group, and QIJI Energy, CATL’s heavy-duty truck battery-swapping subsidiary, have commissioned an integrated renewable energy demonstration station in Ningde, Fujian province. The station combines a 94 kW wind-solar generation system with 930 kWh of energy storage and supports five-minute battery swapping and MW-scale supercharging. It is expected to consume 120 MWh of renewable electricity annually and cut carbon emissions by about 72 tonnes. According to the companies, the project represents China’s first deployment of perovskite tandem PV technology in a heavy-duty truck charging and battery-swapping load scenario. Connected to GCL-ET’s virtual power plant (VPP) platform, it uses AI algorithms to dynamically coordinate PV generation, energy storage, and charging and battery-swapping loads for grid response and electricity market participation. In July, GCL ET signed a framework agreement with the Shaoguan municipal government in Guangdong Province to develop a large-scale green computing hub (see China Solar PV News Snippets). The China Electricity Council (CEC) reported that enterprises within its statistical scope commissioned 87 new electrochemical energy storage stations in Q3 2026, adding 12.6 GW/39.36 GWh of capacity. New installations rose 172% YoY and 3% QoQ, with Inner Mongolia, Xinjiang, Hebei, Shanxi, and Shandong ranking as the top five provinces and regions by additions. By the end of the quarter, CEC’s statistics covered 2,363 operating electrochemical energy storage stations with a combined capacity of 143.53 GW/375.80 GWh. In August, CEC forecast that solar power would surpass coal-fired power in installed capacity during the third quarter of 2026 (see China Solar PV News Snippets). PV and lithium battery equipment manufacturer LEAD has delivered a full-line equipment solution to upgrade an existing TOPCon cell production line to back-contact (BC) technology for an undisclosed major PV customer. The solution uses an LPCVD + PE-Poly process compatible with existing TOPCon lines, enabling conversion into high-efficiency BC lines without constructing new factory buildings. LEAD said the project reuses wet-process, high-temperature, film-deposition, screen-printing, and firing and automation equipment, requiring only additional laser and etching equipment. According to the company, this achieves a 75% equipment reuse rate and cuts capital expenditure by more than half compared with building a new BC line. On the topic of TOPCon to BC line conversion, DAS Solar recently revealed that it plans to convert its 14 GW TOPCon cell production base in Xinzhou, Shanxi Province, to DBC technology (see China Solar PV News Snippets). China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs have extended the suspension of export controls covering lithium batteries, specified battery materials, and related manufacturing equipment and technologies from November 11, 2026, through January 10, 2027. The measures apply to rechargeable lithium-ion batteries with a gravimetric energy density of at least 300 Wh/kg, as well as specified LFP cathode materials, ternary cathode material precursors, lithium-rich manganese-based cathode materials, graphite anode materials, and related manufacturing equipment and technologies. Announced in October 2025, the controls were originally scheduled to take effect on November 8, 2025, but were suspended prior to implementation and have never entered into force. The latest notice states that the suspension will run until January 10, 2027, without specifying arrangements beyond that date. The Jiangxi provincial government has issued its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for developing a new energy system. The province targets total power generation capacity of more than 110 GW by 2030, including over 55 GW of new energy capacity – with an aspirational target of 60 GW – making new energy the province’s largest source of installed power capacity. The plan calls for adding more than 18 GW of wind, solar, and biomass capacity during 2026-2030 while maintaining a new energy utilization rate above 90%. By 2030, Jiangxi aims for new-type energy storage capacity to exceed 5 GW, pumped-storage capacity to reach 3.3 GW, VPPs to provide 3 GW of regulation capacity, and demand response capability to reach 2.9 GW, while raising generation- and storage-side regulation capability by more than 40%.
