artigo.texto: India's renewable energy ambitions have reached a stage where generating clean electricity is no longer the only challenge. The more difficult task is ensuring that electricity generated during sunny and windy hours remains available when households, industries and businesses need it. With solar and wind capacity expanding rapidly, India faces a fundamental question: how can intermittent renewable energy become a dependable source of round-the-clock electricity?The Union Cabinet's approval of a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme on November 4, 2026, represents a major intervention in addressing this challenge. The programme envisages developing 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between 2026–27 and 2030–31, involving an estimated investment of ₹97,600 crore.Of the proposed capacity, 60 GWh will come from pumped hydro storage projects, 30 GWh from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and 2 GWh from emerging storage technologies. The programme also introduces a minimum domestic content requirement of 40% for battery storage projects, reflecting the government's intention to strengthen indigenous manufacturing.The significance of this initiative extends beyond the installation of batteries and storage infrastructure. It represents an attempt to transform the operating architecture of India's electricity system, which has traditionally depended on coal-fired generation to provide reliable power when renewable energy production fluctuates.Solar power generation peaks during daylight hours, while electricity consumption frequently rises in the evening. Wind generation also varies according to weather conditions. Without sufficient storage, renewable electricity may be curtailed during periods of surplus generation, while conventional power plants must compensate when output declines.Battery storage can absorb surplus electricity and release it during peak demand. Pumped hydro storage performs a similar function by using electricity to move water to an elevated reservoir and subsequently releasing it through turbines.Together, these technologies can reduce renewable energy curtailment, improve grid flexibility and limit the need for additional coal-based balancing capacity. However, storage cannot eliminate coal dependence immediately, particularly during prolonged periods of low renewable generation.According to the Ministry of Power, India's grid-scale energy storage requirement is projected to reach 411 GWh by 2031–32. The newly approved programme is therefore an important addition, but it will meet only part of the country's anticipated requirement.A more complex challenge lies in India's dependence on China for battery cells, components and processing technologies. China dominates several critical stages of the global lithium-ion battery supply chain, particularly lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which are widely used for stationary energy storage because of their cost advantages and durability.According to a May 2026 analysis by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), China accounts for approximately 74% of global lithium refining, 80% of cobalt refining and 98% of LFP cathode active material production. India's domestic lithium refining capacity remains negligible, while its battery cell manufacturing industry is still developing.The same analysis estimated that India's advanced chemistry cell battery demand could increase from 28 GWh in 2025 to approximately 272 GWh by FY2030. Despite the government's ₹18,100 crore production-linked incentive programme, only 1.4 GWh of cell manufacturing capacity had been commissioned under the scheme by early 2026.This creates a strategic contradiction. India is investing heavily in renewable energy to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, but its transition could create another form of external dependence through imported batteries and processed minerals.Assembling battery packs domestically does not necessarily constitute technological self-reliance if the cells, cathodes, anodes, electrolytes and manufacturing equipment continue to come from China. Changing this situation requires coordinated intervention across the entire battery value chain.India must accelerate domestic cell manufacturing while developing facilities for processing lithium, nickel and other critical minerals. The Cabinet's simultaneous approval of a ₹2,814 crore capital-support scheme for critical mineral processing provides an opportunity to connect mineral refining with battery manufacturing.India should also expand long-term mineral supply partnerships with countries such as Australia, Argentina and Chile, encourage Indian companies to acquire overseas mineral assets, and develop recycling facilities capable of recovering valuable materials from used batteries.Equally important is investment in alternative battery technologies, including sodium-ion systems, which could reduce dependence on lithium for some stationary storage applications. Domestic research institutions and manufacturers need sustained support to commercialise these technologies at competitive costs.The Ministry of Heavy Industries has acknowledged that Chinese dominance in technology and mineral processing creates difficulties for Indian manufacturers, including restricted access to some refining technologies. Addressing these constraints will require technology development, international partnerships and a predictable domestic market.Financing presents another major challenge. Battery storage projects require substantial upfront investment, while revenues depend on electricity price differences, storage utilisation, contractual arrangements and the financial health of electricity distribution companies.The VGF scheme can improve project viability by reducing initial capital costs. artigo.texto: O reconhecimento dos esforços da Amazônia Legal para reduzir o desmatamento e a discussão de caminhos para ampliar o acesso dos estados ao mercado internacional de carbono marcaram a reunião entre representantes dos governos amazônicos e o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, nesta sexta-feira, 13, durante a COP31, em Antalya, na Turquia. O encontro ocorreu no Hub Amazônia, espaço do Consórcio Interestadual de Desenvolvimento Sustentável da Amazônia Legal, e contou com a participação do secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente do Acre, Leonardo Carvalho. Também participaram o secretário de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade do Pará, Raul Protázio; a secretária de Meio Ambiente de Mato Grosso, Mauren Lazzaretti; o secretário executivo de Meio Ambiente de Mato Grosso, Alex Sandro Marega; o secretário de Desenvolvimento Ambiental de Rondônia, Marco Lagos; o diretor-presidente da Tocantins Parcerias, Aleandro Lacerda; e a secretária executiva do Consórcio Interestadual da Amazônia Legal, Vanessa Duarte. A reunião teve como pauta a regulamentação dos Resultados de Mitigação Transferidos Internacionalmente (ITMOs), mecanismo previsto no Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris que permite a transferência internacional de resultados de redução ou remoção de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Os estados apresentaram preocupações em relação à minuta inicial da resolução do Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima (CIM), que prioriza, em sua primeira etapa, atividades de remoção de carbono e redução de emissões de metano, sem incluir inicialmente os programas jurisdicionais de REDD+. Esses programas, desenvolvidos pelos governos estaduais ao longo de mais de uma década, integram políticas públicas de conservação florestal, de redução do desmatamento, de fortalecimento da produção sustentável e de proteção dos direitos dos povos indígenas e das comunidades tradicionais. Durante o encontro, os representantes da Amazônia Legal destacaram que os resultados alcançados na conservação das florestas são fruto de investimentos contínuos em fiscalização, governança territorial e políticas socioambientais. Também ressaltaram a importância de mecanismos econômicos que reconheçam esses esforços e contribuam para financiar a manutenção da floresta em pé. O ministro João Paulo Capobianco reconheceu a contribuição dos estados amazônicos para as metas climáticas brasileiras e reafirmou a importância estratégica dos programas de REDD+ jurisdicional. Explicou que a definição inicial das atividades elegíveis considerou a necessidade de estruturar o mercado de forma gradual, com atenção à demanda internacional e à valorização dos créditos de carbono. Ao final da reunião, ficou estabelecido o compromisso de manter canais permanentes de diálogo entre o Ministério do Meio Ambiente e os estados da Amazônia Legal, com novas discussões técnicas a partir do encerramento da COP31. O processo deverá contribuir para a construção compartilhada da lista de atividades elegíveis aos ITMOs, após a publicação da resolução inicial do CIM. O secretário do Meio Ambiente do Acre, Leonardo Carvalho, avaliou que a reunião representou um avanço na articulação entre os estados e o governo federal, especialmente diante das oportunidades de financiamento climático que podem beneficiar diretamente as populações amazônicas. “Foi uma reunião muito importante dos secretários de Meio Ambiente com o ministro Capobianco para tratar dos ITMOs, um assunto técnico, mas que pode permitir um acréscimo de valor aos créditos de carbono dos programas jurisdicionais de REDD+ da Amazônia, ampliando o acesso a mercados cada vez mais exigentes. A ideia foi mostrar ao Ministério que os estados vêm trabalhando há muitos anos nessa agenda e que esses esforços precisam ser reconhecidos”, destacou. O secretário ressaltou que a continuidade do diálogo permitirá avançar na construção de soluções que considerem as características dos programas estaduais e a necessidade de ampliar os benefícios da conservação. “Saímos com um bom encaminhamento. O governo federal vai construir conosco, por meio do Consórcio da Amazônia Legal, dos secretários de Meio Ambiente e das equipes técnicas dos estados, uma agenda propositiva para que os programas jurisdicionais de REDD+ sejam considerados prioritários. Isso lança uma mensagem importante ao mercado, para que nossos créditos sejam valorizados e possamos alcançar melhores condições de comercialização, com recursos que, no futuro, cheguem às comunidades e ajudem a conservar nossas florestas”, afirmou Leonardo. Durante a reunião, o ministro João Paulo Capobianco explicou que a definição das primeiras cotas de ITMOs buscou considerar a capacidade de absorção dos créditos pelo mercado e evitar efeitos que possam comprometer sua valorização. Segundo ele, a cautela inicial não representa uma desvalorização dos programas jurisdicionais de REDD+, mas a necessidade de avaliar mecanismos econômicos capazes de assegurar melhores condições de comercialização. “A decisão está tomada. Nós estamos trabalhando para construir um mecanismo financeiro e econômico em paralelo aos ITMOs, para que possamos fazer isso”, explicou o ministro, ao apresentar alternativas de financiamento complementar que poderiam ampliar o valor recebido pelos estados. Capobianco também manifestou disposição para aprofundar as discussões com os governos amazônicos e suas equipes técnicas, reconhecendo a importância de uma agenda específica para os programas jurisdicionais. Entre os encaminhamentos, está o compromisso de elaborar em conjunto a lista de atividades elegíveis às transferências internacionais e de aprofundar o debate sobre a segurança jurídica e o reconhecimento institucional dos sistemas estaduais de REDD+. artigo.texto: RWE starts construction of its first battery in Italy Essen/Rome, 10 November 2026 RWE has started construction of its first Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Italy. The 62,5-megawatts (MW) Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for 4 hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262,5 megawatt hours (MWh). Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. ”We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for 4 hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. Battery storage at RWE As a driver of the energy transition, RWE develops, builds and operates battery storage systems in the US, Europe and Australia. Globally, RWE currently operates battery storage systems with a total capacity of around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) and 3 GW are under construction. As an integral part of its growth strategy, RWE plans to significantly expand its battery storage capacities worldwide. RWE Renewables Italia – strong presence in Italy’s renewables market RWE is a key player in the Italian renewables market. The company takes an integrated project approach that incorporates the development, construction and operation as well as the marketing of wind farms and solar plants. With 18 onshore wind farms, one photovoltaic plant and three agrivoltaic plants in operation, RWE currently manages a total installed capacity of approximately 670 MW in Italy, enough to supply green electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households. In addition, RWE currently has around 200 MW of further wind and solar capacity under construction in Italy. artigo.texto: Sutton is a tiny, scenic town in the Blackstone Valley. Its recorded history, which dates back to the early 18th century, includes no major military clashes, no uprisings, no memorable protests. Leave it to Robert Kraft to rewrite that history in just a couple of days. The New England Patriots owner and inscrutable social activist has announced plans to build a ginormous data center in Sutton. And it’s already clear that a lot of Sutton wants no part of it. Residents packed a public meeting at the Town Hall earlier this week to say they hate the idea of a $16 billion data center complex that would basically take over the town. Kraft already owns the land. His cardboard box company, Unified Global Packaging, holds a huge parcel that would, if this crazy plan happens, eventually house 10 buildings and suck up enough electricity to power a decent-sized city. In fact, it would be the fourth-largest data center in the country. I’m sure Bob Kraft has many kinds of experts on his vast payroll. But I wonder if any of them follow politics, or had access to media sources after last week’s election. Because they could have told him that a wide swath of voters across the country clearly expressed their hatred of data centers. Voters from Maine to California voted to ban just the kind of operation Kraft is now seeking to build. They don’t seem to be any more popular in Massachusetts: Just last month, Westfield shot down a data center that was a fraction of the size Kraft is proposing for Sutton. Reading the room on this doesn’t seem all that hard. “Data centers are the third rail of American politics,” said political analyst Mary Anne Marsh. “Getting this approved could be harder than getting the Patriots to the Super Bowl.” This is not the first time Kraft has been, shall we say, less than a wizard at reading public sentiment. A quarter-century ago, Kraft whiffed badly on two attempts to build a new football stadium in the city. The first location was near what we now call “Mass. and Cass”; the other was in South Boston. Both plans were resoundingly rejected by residents and local politicians. They stood firm even after Kraft threatened to move the Patriots to Hartford in a truly ludicrous attempt at a power play. More recently, he has tangled with the city of Everett (and Boston, as well) over his plans to build a soccer stadium. And, lest we forget last summer, Foxborough successfully went to war with Kraft over some $8 million in payments for security for the World Cup. The Kraft Group has resorted to a time-honored strategy to push their Sutton proposal through: cold, hard cash. By one reliable estimate, the Kraft Group would be paying $27.8 million in property taxes by 2035. That’s a windfall for a community with an annual operating budget of just $40 million. But Mr. Kraft’s forthcoming largesse wasn’t enough to deter the folks at the meeting Tuesday night. Though the public comment period was limited to 15 minutes, the Globe reported that each of the six people who got to speak opposed the data center. It’s easy to make fun of Kraft’s virtually unbroken record of misreading the political will of the hoi polloi. But the opposition to this, I believe, goes further than your everyday NIMBY political fighting. People have grown increasingly skeptical of the sweeping claims that AI is on the verge of bringing all sorts of great things to our lives. From workers quietly revolting to college graduates literally turning their backs on tech titans, the doubt is evident. And people are really, really tired of being told that the ascent of AI is an inevitability that we are foolish to think we can stop. Voters are tired of the “tax incentives,” the lobbyists for billionaire business interests, the insistence that public education needs to be reshaped now to accommodate a future nobody asked for. In the already-here battle between the billionaires and the rest of us, people have had enough of being told that decisions about their communities are no longer theirs to make. Billionaire Bob Kraft is on the wrong side of a political tsunami. And he seems to be the only person who doesn’t know it. Adrian Walker is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at adrian.walker@globe.com. Follow him @Adrian_Walker.

artigo.texto: - Sublime Systems and tech giant Meta have signed a multi-year supply agreement granting Meta priority physical access to Sublime Cement for future US data center construction. - The contract includes the purchase of third-party verified environmental attribute certificates (EACs) tied to at least 180,000 tons of Sublime Cement production. - Sublime’s technology eliminates kiln emissions and supports co-location retrofits at aging domestic cement facilities to reduce US import reliance. US low-carbon cement manufacturer Sublime Systems has entered into a multi-year supply agreement with Meta, securing priority physical access to Sublime Cement for Meta’s upcoming data center construction pipeline alongside environmental attribute certificates (EACs) tied to at least 180,000 tons of production. By committing to multi-year, fixed-volume offtake terms, Meta is providing the long-term revenue certainty required to finance and construct Sublime’s first commercial-scale US manufacturing facilities. The agreement aligns with the Book and Claim Framework for Cement and Concrete developed earlier in 2026 by RMI and the Center for Green Market Activation, allowing corporate buyers to separate and claim verified embodied carbon reductions from physical material delivery. Electrochemical Manufacturing and Domestic Supply Chain Integration Sublime Systems replaces conventional fossil-fuel-fired rotary kilns with an ambient-temperature electrochemical process that converts calcium-bearing minerals into reactive cement without process or combustion CO2 emissions. Third-party accredited laboratories have validated that Sublime Cement complies with ASTM standards while matching or exceeding the early strength and durability of traditional Portland cement. Engineering studies completed by Sublime in 2026 also confirmed that its electrochemical modules can be integrated via a co-location model into existing, underutilized US cement plants. Relevant: Microsoft And Sublime Systems Sign Deal To Scale Clean Cement With the average US cement facility reaching 36 years of age and domestic imports accounting for 22% of national consumption, retrofitting legacy infrastructure offers a pathway to expand domestic supply capacity while decarbonizing hard-to-abate construction supply chains. Meta Head of Net Zero Strategy Devon Lake noted that embodied carbon in cement represents one of the most challenging components of hyperscale infrastructure footprints, emphasizing that multi-year buyer commitments are critical to bringing next-generation industrial materials to commercial scale. artigo.texto: A Turquia, país que sedia a COP31, em Antália, recebeu do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB) a aprovação de US$ 1,6 bilhão para acelerar sua política climática. O financiamento foi aprovado em 22 de outubro de 2026, semanas antes da conferência, segundo a página oficial do projeto no banco. O AIIB é um banco multilateral criado por iniciativa da China, com sede em Pequim, que financia infraestrutura na Ásia e em outras regiões. Como funciona o dinheiro O pacote tem duas partes de US$ 800 milhões cada. A primeira é um financiamento atrelado a políticas climáticas, e a segunda vem de um fundo do banco para energia, segurança alimentar e resiliência econômica. Nos dois casos, o dinheiro só sai se a Turquia cumprir 12 medidas acertadas antes, com metas acompanhadas por indicadores. O prazo previsto para o fim do empréstimo é dezembro de 2028. Os três eixos - Mercado de carbono e finanças verdes: pôr em funcionamento o sistema turco de comércio de emissões e criar regras para as finanças verdes; - Descarbonização: reduzir emissões em energia, indústria e transporte, com melhor monitoramento; - Adaptação: governança climática local, segurança hídrica, sumidouros de carbono e riscos do clima para a saúde nas 81 províncias do país. Por que a Turquia precisa Segundo o AIIB, a Turquia é o 17º maior emissor de gases de efeito estufa do mundo. O banco cita duas pressões sobre o país: o imposto de carbono na fronteira da União Europeia, que vai encarecer exportações de produtos com muitas emissões, e o custo maior da energia importada com a situação no Oriente Médio. O programa apoia a nova meta climática turca e a Lei do Clima do país, que o banco descreve como o marco legal climático mais substancial da Turquia até hoje. A anfitriã sob os holofotes Sediar uma COP coloca o país anfitrião sob escrutínio. A Turquia levou à conferência prioridades como eletrificação e redução de resíduos, mas ainda depende bastante de carvão e gás. O financiamento do AIIB é um dos instrumentos com que o país tenta mostrar avanço na própria casa. O paralelo com o Brasil O Brasil também tem um sistema de comércio de emissões aprovado por lei e em fase de regulamentação. Na COP31, o BNDES anunciou fundos que podem mobilizar R$ 39 bilhões para transição energética, com apoio do Fundo Verde para o Clima da ONU. Acompanhe a cobertura diária na página especial da COP 31. Perguntas frequentes Quanto a Turquia recebeu do AIIB? US$ 1,6 bilhão, em duas parcelas de US$ 800 milhões, segundo o banco. O que é o AIIB? O Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura, banco multilateral com sede em Pequim. Com informações do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Gostou desta reportagem? artigo.texto: SubTel Forum Issue 151 – Data Centers & New Technology OUT NOW! SubTel Forum Press Release November 16, 2026 Sterling, Virginia – Submarine Telecoms Forum, Inc. announces Issue 151 of Submarine Telecoms Forum Magazine, a special 25th anniversary edition exploring Data Centers & New Technology. AI and cloud services depend on physical networks. This edition examines the cables, landing stations, data centers and interconnected infrastructure that support those services, along with the security, planning and operational challenges facing the people who build and maintain them. What’s Inside Issue 151 The November edition explores how data center growth is changing the requirements for subsea connectivity. Contributors examine Loudoun’s next chapter, the role of shorter unrepeatered systems and the influence of cable route diversity on where cloud and AI infrastructure is built. Security and resilience run throughout the issue, from submarine cable protection to the connection between a landing station and a data center. Other features consider repair readiness, future Atlantic routing constraints, integration across network domains and the work still needed to connect African schools. Feature Articles - The Next Chapter of Loudoun’s Data Center Alley: Applying the Lessons of Scale and Experience by Buddy Rizer - Understanding the Security Layers in Submarine Cables by Sharat Sinha - Short Spans, Big Shifts: Unrepeatered Cable, Data Centers and the New Map of Subsea Projects by Christian T. Priess - The Internet Runs Through Cables We Rarely Think About by Kiran S. Pillai - No Cable, No Cloud, No AI: Why Subsea Networks Decide Where Data Centers Are Built by Natalia López Céspedes - The Shore End Is the Weak End: Securing the Cable-to-Data-Center Seam in the AI Era by José Silva Amaro - Painful Connectivity Cuts: Why Readiness Must Begin Before the Race to Repair by Olivier Côté and Gwenn Amice - The Coming Challenge of Deep-Water Cable Congestion: Using Automated Route Engineering to Forecast Future Routing Constraints in the Atlantic by Adrian Jelffs and Nick Harrington - The End of the Single-Domain Network by Bob Brumley and Alex Vaxmonsky - We Invested Billions in Subsea Cables, Yet Children Are Still Waiting: What Will It Take to Connect Africa’s Future Generation? by Aleksandra Chmielewska, Ben Roberts and Naroa Zurutuza Looking Ahead to PTC’27 A conversation with PTC CEO Brian Moon explores the conference’s relevance to the subsea community. The edition also includes an agenda preview and a guide to attending PTC’27, connecting the issue’s technology theme with the discussions shaping digital infrastructure. Celebrating 25 Years SubTel Forum looks back at the publication’s beginnings in November 2001 and the community that has grown around it. Anniversary features recognize the authors and company sponsors whose contributions have supported its work over a quarter-century. Regular Departments Cable map updates, analytics, Sustainable Subsea and cableship coverage sit alongside Permitting Pathways, Fault Lines, Legal & Regulatory Matters, Back Reflection and Advertiser’s Corner. Redesigned News Now and On the Move pages bring a refreshed presentation to industry developments and personnel news. Special Thanks to Our Issue 151 Advertisers We thank the advertisers and partners supporting this edition: Their support helps keep the magazine freely available to readers across the submarine telecommunications community. About Submarine Telecoms Forum, Inc. Submarine Telecoms Forum publishes news, analysis and reference resources for the submarine telecommunications industry. Its magazine, Almanac, Industry Report, maps and online tools help readers follow projects, explore industry developments and connect technical, commercial and policy perspectives. artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - CATL's plan includes 5,000 urban stations and 1,000 highway stations, covering 297 cities in China. - Nio currently has 4,254 battery swap stations, including 1,081 along highways. CATL (HKEX: 3750) plans to expand its passenger car battery swap network to 6,000 stations in 2027, potentially overtaking Nio Inc (NYSE: NIO) to become China's largest battery swap network operator. The power battery maker disclosed the plan in a statement on Friday, targeting coverage of 297 cities in China through its Choco swap network in 2027. Nio had 4,254 battery swap stations in China as of November 13, including 1,081 along highways, according to real-time data published by Nio Power. If CATL meets its 6,000-station target and Nio maintains its goal of adding about 1,000 stations annually, as it has in recent years, CATL's passenger car battery swap station count could surpass Nio's in 2027. That comparison depends on both companies' actual construction progress. Nio has maintained its target of adding more than 1,000 battery swap stations this year, while it added 679 in 2024 and 681 in 2025, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. CATL's latest plan includes 5,000 urban battery swap stations, designed to put battery swapping within a 10-minute reach in core urban areas, alongside 1,000 highway stations. The highway stations will form a network spanning 11 north-south and 9 east-west routes. The overall network will cover all prefecture-level cities and directly administered municipalities in China except Sansha, the company said. CATL's battery swap network has been expanding rapidly. The company had built 1,020 Choco swap stations by the end of 2025, reaching 2,000 in July this year and 2,520 by September 29. The battery giant previously announced plans to have more than 3,000 passenger car battery swap stations in China by the end of this year. The new 6,000-station target would bring CATL's network to roughly twice its year-end target level in 2027, as the company also expands its lineup of compatible vehicles. Beijing Automotive Group, or BAIC Group, signed an agreement with CATL in October to deepen their battery swap cooperation, with plans to connect models from multiple brands to the Choco swap network and open its dealer network to support station construction. The partners aim to build a battery swap ecosystem serving 1 million vehicles, though they have not announced a timeline for reaching that scale. BAIC's Arcfox brand today launched a battery swap version of the Beta T1, which uses CATL's Choco swap batteries and supports 99-second battery swaps, adding a mass-market model to the network. At the same Arcfox launch event, CATL also introduced its Choco battery management service, integrating battery health checks, early warnings and repair and replacement services into its battery swap platform. The system supports 53 on-board checks and performs another 13 in-depth checks during battery swaps, covering indicators including insulation status, thermal runaway risks and voltage differences, according to CATL. The company pledged lifetime monitoring and warranty coverage, as well as free repairs and replacements, for all Choco batteries while they remain in the network. The network expansion also aligns with CATL's push to promote sodium-ion batteries. CATL chairman Robin Zeng said this week that their range is sufficient for everyday urban driving and that more battery swap stations could help ease concerns about long-distance travel.

artigo.texto: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town? In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs. Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country. The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities. A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2,000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like. For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump. Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers, a land development firm, for a 100,000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems. For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $16.2 million clean energy plan. What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system. Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. “I think things are possible,” he said. “We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.” Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. “Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. “There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added. A cheap, quiet option for cooling data centers A year ago, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, became the first local government in the country to sign a community benefits agreement with a data center project, according to researchers at the World Resources Institute. The agreements have long been used for other types of developments, from manufacturing plants to solar farms, said Danielle Riedl, research associate at the nonprofit. “But now, of course, the conversation — seemingly everywhere — is focused on data center development,” she said. Still, the agreements are no silver bullets. “You really want to see CBAs as one tool, together with zoning policies, development agreements, and other accountability mechanisms.” In Halifax County, Quiet has pledged to mitigate some common data center complaints. At a public meeting this summer, the company said the 88-megawatt facility will plug into the Dominion Energy grid on its own dime and pay for all the electricity it needs, according to the local news outlet RRSpin. It will run backup generators for no more than 30 minutes a month, on average, unless there is an outage. But the company also has to alleviate the immense heat generated by racks of computers inside the facility. And while Quiet has pledged to use closed-loop cooling — a less-water-intensive process than sending waste heat to cooling towers, where water then evaporates — the technology is expensive and noisy. That’s where the thermal energy network comes in. The system is essentially a network of ground-source heat pumps. They’re analogous to air-source heat pumps, but move heat between the buildings and the earth rather than the outside air, thanks to a water-based solution that flows through a system of buried pipes. Some data centers in Europe are already plugged into such systems as a way to release excess heat. The same technology could be used in Enfield, providing cooling without the noise and at less cost, said Eric Bosworth, a pioneer on utility-run thermal energy networks who runs his own consultancy called Thermal Energy Insights. “It gives a layer of resiliency, and it’s going to save them money on cooling, too,” Bosworth said, referring to Quiet. “Every [unit] of heat that they send to the network is going to be cheaper than putting it up through their chillers.” The nonprofit Enfield Energy Futures won a seed grant earlier this year to design the thermal energy network. But receiving funding from Quiet for the geothermal project — and the entire clean energy plan — would be game-changing. artigo.texto: Os temores de que a expansão dos data centers esteja perdendo força são exagerados, segundo executivos de concessionárias de energia e investidores do setor ouvidos pela CNBC na conferência anual do Edison Electric Institute, no Arizona. Todos os gestores de elétricas com quem a emissora conversou no evento afirmaram não ver sinal de desaceleração nas estimativas internas de crescimento do consumo de eletricidade. O pano de fundo é político. No Texas, estado decisivo para o setor, a governadora eleita Gina Hinojosa e o senador eleito James Talarico fizeram campanha prometendo enfrentar o que consideram problemas de custo acessível associados aos data centers. Hinojosa disse recentemente que pode tentar congelar as tarifas de energia, segundo a CNBC. A emissora ressalva que a instalação desses centros é sobretudo uma questão estadual e que o governador texano tem menos poder direto do que em outros estados. A autorização passa por duas agências: a PUCT, que regula eletricidade, telecomunicações e água e cujo presidente, Thomas Gleeson, também integra o conselho da ERCOT e tem mandato até setembro de 2029; e a TCEQ, comandada por Brooke Paup, indicada pelo governador Greg Abbott e com mandato até o próximo ano, responsável por licenças ambientais, inclusive de instalações que operam fora da rede elétrica. Abbott, aliás, já impôs de forma discreta uma pausa na concessão de licenças para data centers, em vigor há algumas semanas, de acordo com a CNBC. A avaliação da emissora é que, a menos que esses nomes deixem os cargos, o ambiente regulatório tende a mudar pouco. A reportagem aponta que, se os projetos forem barrados no Texas, eles devem migrar para estados vizinhos. A CNBC relata que o governador da Louisiana, Jeff Landry, e sua equipe já telefonam para empresas oferecendo o estado como destino, movimento semelhante ao de Oklahoma. Ambos são ricos em gás natural e dispostos a receber os investimentos dos data centers. A própria CNBC faz uma ressalva: não são todos os data centers planejados que serão construídos. Existem planos em excesso, parte deles engavetada antes das eleições e outra parte que pode ser cancelada, por pressão pública ou outros motivos. Também não está claro se todo o poder de computação planejado será necessário. Goldman Sachs vê risco modesto Em nota divulgada no fim da semana, o Goldman Sachs afirmou que o resultado das eleições de meio de mandato traz apenas riscos modestos ao investimento em inteligência artificial, por ora. O banco espera que novos governadores democratas em estados que respondem por mais de um terço da capacidade planejada de data centers nos EUA imponham moratórias, que devem atingir sobretudo projetos ainda sem licença, preservando a maior parte da construção prevista para 2027. Moratórias mais rígidas ou duradouras do que o esperado, pondera a instituição, representam risco de baixa. O Goldman projeta que os gastos com construção de data centers seguirão fortes no próximo ano e estima o investimento em hardware de IA em cerca de US$ 1,4 trilhão até o fim do próximo ano. A CNBC lembra que os data centers são apenas um dos vetores da demanda por eletricidade, ao lado de carros elétricos, da repatriação de fábricas e da eletrificação generalizada do consumo. Os executivos Calvin Butler, da Exelon, e Drew Marsh, da Entergy, além de Drew Maloney, à frente do Edison Electric Institute, disseram à CNBC não ver nenhum arrefecimento.

artigo.texto: AI data centers in space aren't taking off anytime soon, according to Amazon cloud chief Matt Garman. On an episode of the Sources Podcast released Tuesday, Garman cast doubt on the near-term prospect of orbital data centers, saying they are "highly unlikely to be economically feasible or practical in the next decade or two." Space-based data centers "sounds good," Garman said, because they could tap free energy in orbit, but explained rocket launches into space are still "relatively infrequent and expensive." "We as a world don't do one launch a day today," said Garman, the CEO of Amazon Web Services, adding, "We're landing in a data center today one GPU every 14 seconds." The idea of orbital data centers has been championed by Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, as a potential solution to AI's soaring energy demands. Earlier this year, SpaceX said it aims to build a "constellation of a million satellites that operate as orbital data centers" and that it had begun hiring engineers to make the vision a reality. In January, Musk said that within three years "at the latest" space could be the cheapest place to put data centers. Amazon and Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos is also among the tech billionaires who have embraced the idea of space-based data centers to scale AI. In a CNBC interview in May, Bezos called data centers in space "very realistic," though he said the timeline could take longer than some expect. "Some of the timelines we hear are very short," Bezos said. "People would talk about two or three years. That's probably a little ambitious." On the Sources Podcast, Garman said space-based facilities would face a major engineering challenge in managing heat. "Dissipating heat in space is actually quite hard," Garman told podcast host Alex Heath. "It's just a really hard environment. There's radiation everywhere, so you have to build things." Garman said it would be "way more" expensive to build servers in space, but the feat is not impossible. "These are all technically solvable problems," he said. "It's just going to take a while." Garman also expressed skepticism about underwater data centers. "Oceans, there's some of those same problems," he said. "I find oceans to be also probably impractical." Deserts, however, seemed to strike Garman as a more plausible frontier. "I think deserts of those three that you mentioned are by far the most likely," Garman told Heath. "You have relatively good environmental areas. You actually have heat sinks. You have solar areas that you could do it." Though Garman argued building data centers far from communities would mean towns miss out on the increased tax base and high-paying jobs data centers can bring. During the interview, Garman pushed back on concerns about data centers' water use, saying Amazon's largest facilities use less water than 40 US households.

artigo.texto: O evento ocorreu durante o evento “Promovendo o Mercado de Carbono do Vietnã: Transparência, Eficiência e Cooperação Internacional”, organizado em conjunto pelo Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas ( Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente ), o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) e o Escritório das Nações Unidas de Serviços para Projetos (UNOPS), por meio da Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP), no Pavilhão do Vietnã. O ponto alto do evento foi o lançamento do Portal de Informações sobre o Mercado de Carbono, desenvolvido com o apoio do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento e em colaboração com o Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas. O portal disponibiliza publicamente informações cruciais sobre políticas, regulamentações e operações de mercado, auxiliando empresas, investidores e demais partes interessadas a acessar informações e participar do mercado de carbono emergente do Vietnã. Em seu discurso no evento, o Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, afirmou que o mercado de carbono não é apenas uma ferramenta para gerenciar emissões, mas também precisa criar incentivos para que as empresas inovem em tecnologia, melhorem a eficiência energética e invistam em soluções para a redução de emissões. O Vietnã fez progressos significativos no estabelecimento de um mercado de carbono doméstico, com o lançamento da Bolsa de Carbono em 29 de junho de 2026. Durante o período de 2025-2026, o Governo aprovou uma cota piloto de emissões de aproximadamente 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente, alocada a 110 instalações nos setores de energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento. A fase piloto do sistema de negociação de cotas de emissões de gases de efeito estufa se estenderá até o final de 2028, com o objetivo de iniciar as operações oficiais do mercado em 2029. Desde 2022, o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) tem apoiado o Vietnã no desenvolvimento de políticas, estruturas institucionais e roteiros para a implementação de um mercado de carbono e no fortalecimento de sua capacidade de participar de mecanismos de cooperação internacional, conforme o Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris. O PNUD também apoiou o desenvolvimento de um sistema nacional de registro de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono, conectando-o à Bolsa de Valores de Hanói e à Corporação de Custódia e Liquidação de Valores Mobiliários do Vietnã. Entretanto, o UNOPS/ETP prestou apoio técnico no desenvolvimento de sistemas de negociação de quotas de emissão, na alocação de quotas, na operação das bolsas de valores e na cooperação internacional. As atividades de apoio incluíram a elaboração de 20 relatórios técnicos, o trabalho com 535 empresas e a formação de aproximadamente 600 pessoas. No evento, os participantes se concentraram em discutir os requisitos para a transição do estabelecimento do mercado para a operação prática, especialmente o fortalecimento do sistema de medição, relato e avaliação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa; a melhoria dos mecanismos de gestão e monitoramento; o aumento da capacidade empresarial; e a garantia da integridade ambiental dos créditos de carbono. Com 2.441 instalações sujeitas a inventários de gases de efeito estufa sob as regulamentações atualizadas do Vietnã, a qualidade dos dados e a capacidade técnica foram identificadas como fatores cruciais para o funcionamento eficaz do mercado. Os participantes também trocaram experiências internacionais, discutiram oportunidades de cooperação e mobilizaram recursos para o financiamento climático, contribuindo para a meta do Vietnã de emissões líquidas zero até 2050.

artigo.texto: The Anutin government last Thursday discussed with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to expand its data centers in Thailand, according to local publication Banmuang. The Thai government also outlined plans for a data center one-stop service, faster investment approvals, clean energy procurement and workforce development. This came following Thailand’s tightening of data center rules to chart a sustainable growth path for its booming data center industry. To support the growth of data centers, AWS affirmed its commitment to clean energy, including direct PPA and air cooling technology. The tech giant has previously pledged to invest more than US$ 5 billion over 15 years in Thailand. The first phase of the data center project worth more than 24,800 million baht and the AWS Asia Pacific (Thailand) Region have been previously launched. At the same time, AWS continues to develop the skills of the Thai digital workforce through partnerships with universities and educational institutions. The proposed Data Center One Stop Service seeks to promote the Board of Investment’s Thailand Fast Pass Service measures while at the same time reducing the approval and permitting processes in order to create a conducive environment for investment. Besides Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnwirakul, executives of the Board of Investment (BOI) and the Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC) were also present at the discussion.

artigo.texto: 16 November 2026 Thailand Carbon Markets Club Joins Carbon Market Partners in ASEAN to Renew Memorandum of Collaboration at COP31 in Turkey On November 12, 2026, the signatories to the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), comprising Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), the Malaysia Carbon Market Association (MCMA), the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), the Indonesia Carbon Trade Association (IDCTA), and the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets (AACM), signed a renewal of their Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) for a further two years at COP31 in Türkiye. The renewal reaffirmed their shared commitment to regional cooperation and to developing high-integrity, interoperable carbon markets across ASEAN. As part of the renewal, Aboitiz Foundation, Inc. from the Philippines formally joined the ACCF and signed the MoC as an observer. Its participation broadens regional representation in the ACCF and reflects growing interest among ASEAN member states in linking national carbon market development with regional coordination. The renewal also marks progress in aligning approaches on the demand side. AACM and CMC joined IDCTA, SSFA, and MCMA in supporting the Shared Principles under the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a government-led initiative co-chaired by Kenya, Singapore, and the United Kingdom. Launched in November 2025 at the COP30 Business and Finance Forum, the Shared Principles set out six pillars for the credible corporate use of carbon credits alongside deep decarbonization. With all five signatories now supporting the Shared Principles, the ACCF will explore ways to contribute to and advise global initiatives, including those led by the Coalition, so that carbon market development reflects ASEAN’s circumstances. Under SSFA’s chairmanship, which began in the second half of 2026, the ACCF established five priorities for its 2026–2028 strategy. - Bring the ACCF’s work into formal ASEAN processes. - Broaden the signatory base to ensure wider and more balanced regional representation. - Bring ASEAN carbon markets into closer alignment with global standards. - Coordinate with the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and contribute ASEAN perspectives to its work. - Establish an ASEAN Community of Practice (CoP) as a structured platform for sharing knowledge and consulting on longer-term ACCF projects. The ACCF’s work covers three main areas. - Supply and demand - Develop interim guidance for companies on using high-integrity carbon credits to support demand. Build capacity among financiers through a preliminary due diligence framework for assessing key criteria for carbon project financing. - Market infrastructure - Examine the legal nature and status of verified carbon credits and explore ways to reduce cross-border barriers, better align market rules, and enable the use of credits interchangeably across ASEAN carbon markets. - Capacity building - Work with international partners to provide technical and advisory support for carbon project financing and bring the ACCF’s work to ASEAN forums. Since its establishment at COP29 in November 2024, with MCMA serving as chair for the first 18 months, the ACCF has gained wider regional recognition. It was acknowledged in the Joint Media Statement of the 57th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and the ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP30. It was also cited in the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum’s Guidance for an ASEAN Voluntary Carbon Market. Over the past year, the ACCF has supported national and independent carbon standards aligned with benchmarks set by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), helping strengthen the integrity and market acceptance of ASEAN carbon credits. Under its renewed strategy, the ACCF will prioritize putting its work plans into practice alongside policy alignment and capacity building. These efforts aim to strengthen confidence in ASEAN-origin carbon credits, facilitate cross-border cooperation, and support the region’s climate objectives. Mrs. Gloyta Nathalang, Senior Executive Vice President, Sustainability Management and Corporate Communications, Bangchak Corporation Public Company Limited, and Chair of Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), said, “ASEAN’s strength lies in its diversity. Cooperation between governments and businesses can build on the region’s progress in developing carbon markets, strengthening credit quality and interoperability while respecting national priorities. CMC contributes by supporting government efforts to connect markets across the region, engaging businesses, sharing knowledge, and bringing the practical experience of project developers and buyers to the ACCF. Through these efforts, we hope to help channel financing toward high-quality projects that deliver measurable emissions reductions and benefits for local communities.” Ms. Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF Co-Chair, Co-Lead of SSFA’s Carbon Markets Workstream, and CEO of Climate Impact X, said, “This renewal marks the next phase for the ACCF. As chair, SSFA will work closely with the Singapore government, which will assume the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, to complement its market-building efforts from the private sector. artigo.texto: Arrests and scuffles with police. Shouts of “shame.” Litigation, petitions and public comment sessions stretching past midnight. This is how Coloradans are reacting to the arrival of large-scale data centers in the Centennial State. Smaller data centers have operated in Colorado for years, tucked into unassuming office parks and downtown skyscrapers. But a new era of hyperscale data centers made for the age of artificial intelligence has begun in Colorado and — despite near-universal pushback in the communities where they are planned — more developments are underway as governments and regulators struggle to keep up. “This has moved so fast, the data center demand is so incredibly strong and powerful that it’s really caught local governments like us off-guard,” Aurora mayor Mike Coffman said. “There’s a feeling of vulnerability right now. It came so fast, so hard, it’s forced me to push back – and I’m pretty pro-business.” Four large data centers are in the planning phases or under construction in Colorado, several of which are competing to become the state’s largest. Combined, their max power needs could equal those of more than 819,000 homes — or 16 times the amount of power used by Denver International Airport. The development comes despite a patchwork of regulations, moratoriums and local opposition that has slowed — though not stopped — industry growth. In Aurora, plans for a 500-megawatt facility next to a neighborhood are moving forward, despite the mayor’s pledge to stop it at all costs. If built, the facility’s power needs could outstrip the city’s entire residential use. In Weld County, a successful petition drive sought to stop an artificial intelligence data center planned there, but it’s unclear whether a ballot measure could halt the project. In Colorado Springs, the City Council voted to put off a vote on a data center until the spring, but the developer said he plans to continue working on the project in the interim. If built, the data center would be the largest power user in the city, by far. There is no standard definition of “hyperscale” data centers, but the term is generally used to describe large facilities that use lots of power and often the computing power needed for artificial intelligence. The Colorado utility regulators writing new rules for large electrical loads (like data centers) are looking at facilities that draw at least 50 megawatts, though they are considering lowering that threshold to 20 megawatts for new customers. A megawatt of power can power approximately 1,100 homes, according to Xcel Energy. Local governments remain the primary regulators of data centers big and small in Colorado. The state lacks broad regulation of the industry, prompting city councils and county commissions of a variety of political persuasions to pass their own rules or enact moratoriums. Larimer County is seeking public comment on a proposed ban on hyperscale data centers, defined as any facility that would draw more than 30 megawatts of power. Brighton in late October enacted a moratorium weeks after residents learned of a 2.5 million-square-foot data center proposed for the Adams County town. The company later withdrew its application. Denver, Arvada, Commerce City, Pagosa Springs, Boulder County and Jefferson County are some of the more than one dozen local governments that enacted a temporary moratorium on data center development. The topic has drawn the attention of governor-elect Phil Weiser, who said at an event in October that his first legislative priority would be a bill to “put guardrails on data centers,” though he did not support an all-out ban. “Communities need to be listened to,” he said. “These data centers shouldn’t be shoved down the throat of communities.” Opposition to data centers is not always about the specifics of a project, said Jason Green, whose company Raeden is building a 50-megawatt facility in Colorado Springs. Instead, developers feel like they are defending against the broad swell of growing hostility against the industry — and the artificial intelligence technology it fuels — as a whole. “There isn’t a data center project in the U.S. that in some form isn’t caught up in the referendum of data centers,” said Green, who has worked in the data center industry for more than 25 years. That broader conversation is also playing out in discussions about potential statewide legislation regulating the industry, said state Sen. Cathy Kipp, who sponsored a failed bill in the last legislative session to regulate data centers. The issue is not about left or right politics, she said, but about regular people bearing the costs to their quality of life from projects that make huge amounts of profit for wealthy companies. “People see these very wealthy companies coming in, building whatever they want, taking our precious resources and people are saying, ‘Why should we support this?'” she said. “It’s no longer left or right, it’s up and down.” Data center capital of the state? When Amy Wiles bought her home in Aurora in 2020, the realtor told her that the open fields abutting her neighborhood would eventually become a small, walkable cluster of shops and restaurants on the eastern edge of Colorado’s third-largest city. Wiles never got her neighborhood coffee shop. Instead, the land became home to the state’s largest data center. And Wiles, now a city councilmember, has found herself deeply embroiled in the debate about how local communities should regulate the booming, unpopular industry. The ward she represents sprawls across the city’s northeast corner and has a lot of attributes data center developers value: large parcels of undeveloped land, relatively easy access to power and water resources, proximity to an urban core and — an increasing rarity on the Front Range — a lack of a moratorium against data center development. artigo.texto: COP31 opened in Antalya this week with expectations low and a familiar argument about money. That diplomatic theatre matters less to New Zealand business than what has happened in our own carbon market over the past 12 months. The cost allocation the conference keeps circling has already landed here, and the result has been more policy fog, not less. The conference has already lowered the bar The backdrop is grim. October 2026 was the warmest on record, and UNEP says emissions must fall 18% by 2030 against 2025 levels, while current national plans deliver just 5-8%. Fossil fuel phase-out is not formally on the agenda. New Zealand collected a Fossil of the Day award on opening day, its fifth in six years, partly over a complaint tied to the EU free trade agreement. Australia’s Chris Bowen, COP31 President of Negotiations, framed the core problem as finance, telling delegates that too many countries “can’t access the finance at the speed, scale and terms required” to deliver their plans. In other words, the era of pledges is giving way to the era of invoices. Wellington has seen its invoice and declined it New Zealand got its bill in June. Treasury put the cost of closing the country’s 84 million-tonne Paris gap through offshore mitigation at $4.4 to $5 billion. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s response was blunt: “we ain’t shutting down farms and we certainly aren’t sending billions of dollars offshore.” There is a defensible fiscal case against wiring $5 billion overseas for credits of variable quality. But the liability did not appear from nowhere. Treasury’s 2023 climate fiscal assessment flagged the offshore mitigation risk years ago, and successive governments let it grow. Walking away from a target is a choice with consequences, and one of them is trade. In 2025, University of Waikato’s Nathan Cooper warned that loosening targets risked undermining the EU FTA’s requirement for mutually supportive trade and climate policy. Exporters selling into Europe should treat that as a live risk, not an academic one. The ETS took the hit first The domestic damage started in November 2025, when Simon Watts, climate change minister at the time, announced the ETS would be uncoupled from international pledges. The carbon price fell from about $50 to as low as $33 almost overnight. The Conversation, writing in 2025, recorded an 18% drop by the end of that day and called it a soft renege. It got worse. A subsequent quarterly auction failed to sell a single unit, and the government considered cancelling auctions outright while officials warned more surprises would deepen buyer uncertainty. Ministers eventually left volumes largely unchanged to 2030. For foresters, emitters and anyone holding NZUs on the balance sheet, that is a year of mark-to-market pain caused by the rule-maker, not the market. The shortage nobody is pricing Here is the part business should watch. In April 2026, the Climate Change Commission described the market as being in a fragile state with low and volatile prices. It found the unit surplus shrinking faster than expected, warned of a possible shortfall as early as 2028, and projected that industrial free allocation will hit the overall cap by 2035, leaving nothing to auction. That is a classic setup for a price spike after a price crash. Firms that read today’s soft NZU price as the new normal could be badly caught out when supply tightens. The Commission’s July monitoring report adds pressure. The second emissions budget can still be met, but by a thin 3.6 MtCO2e margin, with more than half the planned reductions at significant risk. The 2030 methane target is projected to be missed, and the Commission warns that without action in the next one to two years, both that target and the third budget become no longer feasible, with delay raising costs for households and the economy. Less disclosure, more scrutiny Meanwhile, the compliance burden moved the other way. In 2025 the External Reporting Board lifted the mandatory climate disclosure threshold for listed issuers from $60 million to $1 billion. That is welcome relief for mid-sized listed companies drowning in reporting costs. But it lands just as international buyers and trade partners are paying closer attention to New Zealand’s credibility, so many exporters will find their customers asking the questions regulators no longer do. What firms should plan for Nothing decisive will come out of Antalya for New Zealand business. The decisions that matter are domestic, and they are coming fast. A tightening cap, a shrinking surplus and a government that has said no to offshore spending point to one outcome: the cost of emissions shifts back onto the domestic market from 2028. The smart move is to stop budgeting on a $33-ish carbon price, stress-test exposure to a shortage-driven rebound, and press Wellington for stable settings that survive the next election. Business can live with a high carbon price. What it cannot plan around is another year of rules rewritten overnight. artigo.texto: Battery storage: avoid auto sector mistakes The Express Tribune • • 1 min read The Express Tribune published an argument on November 15 that Pakistan should approach battery-storage investment cautiously, rather than repeat the protected assembly model seen in automobiles and mobile phones. The article says producing battery cells requires significant capital, specialised skills and technology, and notes that China held more than 80% of global manufacturing capacity and cell production in 2025. It proposes starting with assembly using imported cells while building local capabilities, but cautions that falling prices, changing technology and the National Tariff Policy 2025-30 could undermine reliance on tariff protection. It argues that investment should be judged by domestic value addition, technology transfer, productivity and eventual exports. artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms LS ELECTRIC to Supply Switchgear for US AI Data Center Expansion Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Key PointsLS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data… View more - LS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data center customer. - Repeat awards hinge on meeting hyperscale delivery schedules across its Korea and US production sites. - LS ELECTRIC is also developing DC distribution systems at its Cheonan facility for future AI data centers. LS ELECTRIC announced on November 16, 2026, that it had signed a power-system supply contract worth approximately $93.83 million (KRW 130 billion) for a global big-tech company’s U.S. hyperscale AI data center project. The contract covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear and low-voltage switchgear, which will be supplied sequentially for the data center’s power network. The high-voltage equipment distributes incoming electricity to individual facilities and protects equipment when power abnormalities occur. LS ELECTRIC participated in the customer’s large local data-center project from its initial construction phase. The new contract continues its high-voltage switchgear awards into the expansion phase, making it a follow-on order from an existing customer and directly connecting the supplier’s role to the project’s continued buildout. Delivery Capacity Underpins the Expansion Order LS ELECTRIC identifies time to power—the interval before a data center receives electricity and can begin operating—as a central competitive concern in AI infrastructure. It attributes its repeat awards to meeting the customer’s quality requirements and hyperscale delivery schedules from the project’s early stages. Its named production bases are the Cheongju smart factory in South Korea, LS ELECTRIC Utah and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. The company presents that footprint as the foundation of its delivery competitiveness. For this expansion order, the delivery requirement has a concrete operational dimension: the equipment contract depends on industrial capacity and scheduling as well as product specifications. Recent Contracts Span the Power System A separate October 2026 announcement disclosed a KRW 168.9 billion ($125.23 million) long-term agreement with another U.S. big-tech company covering 2027–2028. The announced amount represents products scheduled for delivery in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business remains subject to further discussions. That agreement covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear. Possible additional supplies of low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers and ring main units remain under discussion, creating a potential broader equipment package around the committed deliveries. LS ELECTRIC announced on October 1, 2026 a KRW 181.2 billion ($133.41 million) contract for 345 kV extra-high-voltage transformers. Deliveries are scheduled in phases to nine substations through 2030 for a North American hyperscale AI data center project. Read together, the company’s records describe work across both data-center distribution equipment and the higher-voltage infrastructure required to power large AI projects. AC Business and DC Development Beyond conventional alternating-current (AC) distribution, LS ELECTRIC is pursuing next-generation direct-current (DC) systems for AI data centers. It describes its Cheonan DC Factory as the first manufacturing site to commercialize DC distribution. Solid-state transformers, solid-state circuit breakers and energy-storage systems are used there to test next-generation grids and data-center environments. The contract highlights the commercial connection between power delivery and AI compute: new capacity cannot be energized until electrical equipment is in place. LS ELECTRIC’s repeat role ties its switchgear business to that schedule, while the Cheonan test site provides a route into future DC designs as hyperscale projects expand and their power architecture evolves.

New Storage Projects Lift Revenue Ormat combines geothermal power generation with an expanding battery-storage business. Geothermal plants can supply electricity around the clock, making them useful to customers seeking dependable renewable power. Batteries add a different source of revenue by shifting electricity between periods of low and high demand. Our discussion of Ormat's stable cash flows and growing storage business examines how that combination supports its development plans. Segment revenue increased 145% year over year to $49.9 million as new facilities entered service and market conditions supported existing assets. Net income attributable to shareholders rose 32% to $31.9 million. The results demonstrate how incremental storage capacity can contribute to earnings, although favorable wholesale electricity prices also helped the comparison. Ormat's planned 100-megawatt Denali battery has a 20-year tolling agreement that gives the customer access to capacity and provides greater revenue visibility for Ormat. Projects earning more of their income from wholesale markets face a different risk profile because charging and discharging margins fluctuate. The balance between contracted payments and market revenue will influence how predictable the storage business becomes as it grows. artigo.texto: St. Cloud is latest Minnesota city to consider new rules for data centers Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read St. Cloud officials will hear from residents Monday night about possible new restrictions for data centers. St. Cloud hasn't yet received any proposals from developers who want to build a large data center, as other Minnesota communities have, but the City Council is considering adopting an ordinance so it's prepared for any future requests. The proposed rules would separate smaller data centers from hyperscale facilities — those with at least 2,000 computer servers housed in buildings larger than 10,000 square feet, or that use at least 50 megawatts of electricity. Under the ordinance, hyperscale data centers could only be located in the city's industrial district, at least a quarter mile from residential areas, and would require a conditional use permit. They must be connected to the city’s water system. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Data center developers also would have to study noise, vibration, environmental and community impacts. They would also be required to incorporate sustainability measures, including water conservation and renewable energy. After Monday’s public hearing, the council could vote on the ordinance or postpone action. Why Minnesota is attracting data centers Tech companies are eyeing Minnesota for data centers because of its relatively cool climate and available land, water and electricity. More than a dozen large projects have been proposed around the state. Meta is already building a hyperscale data center in Rosemount. Google plans to build massive data center campuses in Hermantown and Pine Island, although environmental groups are fighting those projects in court. Many Minnesotans have raised concerns about the impacts of a mega-sized facilities, including noise and light pollution, water and energy use. Proponents say they will bring construction jobs, property tax revenue and other economic benefits. Some of St. Cloud’s neighboring cities, including Waite Park and St. Joseph, have passed one-year moratoriums on new data centers. Others, including Sartell, have adopted similar regulations. Monticello, a city about 25 miles southeast of St. Cloud, adopted a data center ordinance in April. Its City Council will consider at a Nov. 30 meeting whether to allow a hyperscale project to move forward. In Minneapolis, a temporary moratorium that blocks most new data centers, with some exceptions downtown, expires Nov. 21. On Thursday, the Minneapolis City Council narrowly approved new data center regulations on a 7-6 vote, including a controversial proposal to require council approval of any new data center. The Minneapolis City Council plans to reconvene Nov. 20 to address a possible veto — one day before the moratorium ends.

artigo.texto: ANOTHER TOWN may be taking the first steps toward its own comprehensive data center bylaw amid a wider trend of towns adopting effective prohibitions on large-scale data center facilities. The Tewksbury Select Board has an item on its agenda Tuesday for a discussion on a data center bylaw with little information beyond that. The agenda item comes after residents spoke during recent Select Board meetings about the desire to implement Tewksbury’s own moratorium on data centers. When resident Sandra Poole spoke during the Nov. 4 Select Board meeting, she noted that she had drafted a data center moratorium policy herself. She expressed concern that the town could find itself in a similar situation to the Hillman Street battery storage site proposal, which drew backlash from surrounding residents and ultimately fell through earlier this year after the company withdrew its application. Board members Eric Ryder and Mark Kratman both noted that they had wanted to make it through the special Town Meeting last month before taking this issue up, and suggested that the conversation starting now would allow a bylaw proposal to make it to the annual Town Meeting next spring. “I have looked at what some of our surrounding communities have done, and it is something I intend on discussing with the town manager and other board members as well to get their inputs,” Ryder said during the Nov. 4 meeting. It will take some time before we can say what form a data center ban or moratorium would take in Tewksbury, if there is a big enough desire for such a thing at all, but if the town follows the same route as other nearby communities it could be one less option for a location for large scale data centers. In its fall Town Meeting last month, Chelmsford Town Meeting representatives voted to impose a total ban on medium- and large-scale data centers, leaving room for smaller data centers already commonly in use. This Saturday, Wilmington’s special Town Meeting will consider a similar prohibition. Data centers have been around in some form since the widespread adoption of the internet, but as the demand increases for larger facilities increases in our still young artificial intelligence era, so too do the concerns about the resource draw required by these facilities, and the effects they may have on the surrounding area via pollution or persistent noise. Notably, Tewksbury already has a definition for data center in its bylaws, but it is very much behind on the times. In Tewksbury’s zoning bylaws, a data center is defined as “A physical location that stores computing machines and their related hardware equipment. It contains the computing infrastructure that IT systems require, such as servers, data storage drives, and network equipment. It is the physical facility that stores a company’s digital data.” There is no mention there of the physical footprint of the facility, its water use, energy requirements, or any of the things people have been expressing concern over when it comes to data centers in the age of AI. If there is a desire to prohibit large data centers in Tewksbury, or any community without explicit policies toward them in 2026, those factors will be the likely place to start. — Peter Currier Will another one bite the dust? Instead of losing any say in the matter, Wilmington is going through the “paper compliance” strategy, where a zoning overlay is created in areas where there is not likely to be any new multifamily housing built in the near future. The slow capitulation of the noncompliant communities also comes after voters in Massachusetts very narrowly rejected a ballot measure to allow single-family homes to be built on lots as small as 5,000 square feet.
