artigo.texto: Malásia vai monitorar conta de luz de data centers para caçar contrabando de chips de IA da Nvidia Nova legislação quer usar picos anômalos de consumo elétrico e inventário obrigatório para flagrar servidores clandestinos com GPUs sob embargo. O governo da Malásia está preparando uma ofensiva regulatória sem precedentes para frear esquemas internacionais de contrabando de semicondutores. O país asiático planeja aprovar uma nova legislação que utilizará o monitoramento detalhado do consumo de energia elétrica em data centers para identificar e rastrear aceleradores gráficos de inteligência artificial da Nvidia que entram ilegalmente ou são desviados para mercados sancionados pelos Estados Unidos, como a China. Nos últimos dois anos, a Malásia tornou-se o principal polo de expansão de infraestrutura em nuvem do Sudeste Asiático, atraindo investimentos bilionários em polos tecnológicos como o estado de Johor. Contudo, esse crescimento meteórico também abriu brechas para operações de fachada, onde empresas fantasmas importavam hardware avançado sob o pretexto de hospedar servidores locais, apenas para posteriormente reexportar os chips de forma clandestina. Declaração obrigatória de chips e telemetria elétrica Pela nova proposta legislativa articulada pelo Ministério Digital e pelas autoridades de comércio exterior malaias, todos os proprietários e operadores de data centers sediados no país serão obrigados por lei a: - Inventário rigoroso de hardware: Declarar a contagem exata, número de série e modelo específico de cada chip acelerador (GPU) importado e instalado em suas instalações. - Transparência de clientes e hyperscalers: Fornecer a identidade dos verdadeiros beneficiários e empresas proprietárias das cargas de trabalho alocadas nos racks. - Relatórios contínuos de consumo de energia: Compartilhar dados detalhados de demanda elétrica em tempo real com a concessionária nacional de energia, a Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB). O princípio básico das autoridades é cruzar o perfil de consumo elétrico registrado nas subestações com a potência térmica declarada (TDP – Thermal Design Power) dos chips instalados. Se um galpão alegar operar apenas placas de servidores modestas, mas exibir picos contínuos de centenas de quilowatts compatíveis com fazendas de superchips Nvidia Blackwell ou Hopper, fiscais poderão deflagrar operações de busca e apreensão no local. Fim da “demanda fantasma” e multas dez vezes maiores A regulamentação também ataca outro problema crítico que ameaçava desestabilizar a rede elétrica do país: a especulação energética por parte de fundos de investimento em tecnologia. Muitos desenvolvedores de data centers vinham reservando gigantescos blocos de megawatts com anos de antecedência, criando uma “demanda fantasma” que travava a expansão de indústrias locais e residências. Para acabar com essa reserva especulativa, a nova regra forçará os operadores a pagarem pela capacidade reservada na rede independentemente de ela estar sendo utilizada ou não. Além disso, a taxa de penalidade para empreendimentos cujo pico real de consumo fique muito abaixo do volume contratado (Connected Load Charge – CLC) foi multiplicada por mais de dez vezes, saltando de RM 8,50 para RM 89,64 por quilowatt. Limitações técnicas: a variação de TDP na prática Apesar da ambição do projeto, especialistas em engenharia de computação alertam para gargalos técnicos relevantes. Na prática, o consumo elétrico de um servidor de IA não é uma linha reta constante: “O cálculo de potência térmica projetada (TDP) em folhas de especificações raramente reflete a realidade operacional. Dependendo da densidade dos modelos, se o sistema está executando inferência leve ou treinamento distribuído com FP8 ou FP16, a demanda energética de uma GPU pode flutuar de 30% a 100% de sua capacidade máxima em questão de segundos”, apontam analistas do setor de infraestrutura. Sem vistorias físicas periódicas e auditorias diretas nos racks para inspecionar os números de série soldados nos silícios, estimativas puramente baseadas na conta de luz podem gerar falsos positivos ou permitir que contrabandistas refinem suas técnicas de dispersão de carga para driblar os limites de monitoramento. Ainda assim, a movimentação da Malásia envia um recado explícito a Washington e ao mercado global de tecnologia: o país não aceitará se transformar em um entreposto clandestino para desvios de tecnologia militar e comercial em meio à guerra fria dos semicondutores.

artigo.texto: San Francisco lawmakers will have a busy, varied agenda this week as they consider legislation on issues ranging from hotel workers’ ability to sue their employers over health issues to restrictions on data centers, along with hearings on traffic safety and revitalizing Market Street. Meanwhile, commissions review surveillance policy and the state of cleanup at the former Hunters Point shipyard. El Niño, data centers, and traffic safety One of the first events on this week’s calendar is a Monday meeting of the city’s Disaster Council, chaired by Mayor Daniel Lurie and Department of Emergency Management Executive Director Mary Ellen Carroll, to review preparations for anticipated extreme weather events associated with El Niño. The meeting comes as officials consider the potential for heavier rainfall, flooding, and other weather-related disruptions from the climate pattern, and Lurie’s declaration of a city emergency last month, to expedite department response. The council includes the heads of the Police and Fire departments, Public Health, Public Works, the Port, the Municipal Transportation Agency and other city departments. A presentation for the meeting obtained by The Voice outlines the roles of different departments to coordinate preparedness, protect the city’s waterfront, drainage systems, transport, and public spaces from flooding, and generally “mitigate what we can and prepare to respond to impacts we cannot prevent.” Later that day, the Supervisors’ Land Use Committee considers items related to the interim moratorium on data centers, including a move to extend the freeze for another 10 months. The debate comes amid growing scrutiny of the potential environmental and land-use consequences of data centers, including their substantial electricity and water requirements. The committee will likely refer the extension and other items to the full board for approval on Tuesday; as an extension of emergency legislation, it will require nine votes for passage. The committee will also reopen a hearing convened by Board President Rafael Mandelman, along with colleagues Stephen Sherrill and Danny Sauter, on traffic enforcement and street safety. The hearing was originally convened in 2022, when it revealed significant deficits in enforcement, including a 97 percent decline in citations between 2014 and 2022, with less than half issued for the five violations most commonly associated with serious collisions. Subsequent meetings have found little improvement, and a 2025 Civil Grand Jury report found that police failed to prioritize traffic safety and had inadequate staffing. Health Commission reviews Hunters Point cleanup Also on Monday, the Health Commission will hear a presentation from the Department of Public Health on the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. The presentation, by Health Officer Susan Philip and other department officials, will cover remediation and restoration updates, health promotion in Bayview-Hunters Point, community outreach and regulatory oversight. The presentation includes updates on the July 2026 vegetation fire at the shipyard’s Parcel E-2 landfill, which burned an estimated two to three acres and damaged monitoring equipment and stormwater controls. The Navy subsequently repaired the damaged systems, while state regulators and the Health Department monitored the response. Full board: Strengthening the Healthy Buildings Ordinance Set for approval on first reading at Tuesday’s Board of Supervisors meeting is a Covid-era ordinance requiring hotels to follow specified cleaning and disease-prevention practices, including frequent cleaning of high-contact common areas. A proposed amendment would allow hotel employees and their unions to sue hotels for civil penalties and other remedies. The bill is sponsored by District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen, with Mandelman and colleagues Connie Chan, Shamann Walton and Jackie Fielder as cosponsors. After being held on ice at the Rules Committee since April, it was revived with amendments earlier this month. In a Nov. 14 oped in the Chronicle, Lynn S. Mohrfeld, president and CEO of the California Hotel and Lodging Association, criticized the proposal as expanding outdated pandemic-era requirements. The group has also placed ads on social media to coincide with the vote. Budget Committee: Can relocating courts jumpstart Mid-Market? On Wednesday, the supervisors’ Budget and Finance Committee will consider a bill sponsored by District 6 member Matt Dorsey and almost all his colleagues to enable “Sober Spaces” by increasing availability of public facilities such as community rooms to recovery groups at no cost, along with a fund to support such meetings when hosted by private nonprofit-owned facilities. Dorsey will also preside over a hearing on how to use city-owned assets to help revitalize Market Street. One presentation associated with the hearing explores the leveraging of courthouses for economic impact, and Dorsey has floated the idea of moving the Hall of Justice and related offices to the struggling Mid- Market area. Police Commission: Surveillance cameras Meanwhile the Police Commission will hear a briefing on on its live monitoring of surveillance cameras owned by private entities and other non-city organizations. Current city laws allow officers to access private camera feeds in emergencies involving imminent danger, certain significant public-safety events and active criminal investigations, with restrictions. They were enacted after a controversy in 2020 over the practice during the George Floyd protests. The department’s presentation reports that all requests for live monitoring from the third quarter of 2023 through the first half of 2026 were approved. During the first six months of this year, SFPD made 11 requests, involving 40 hours and 58 minutes of monitoring, and reported 10 arrests. artigo.texto: - With global data center electricity consumption projected to hit 2,354 TWh by 2035 (7.4% of global demand), operators are increasingly pairing natural gas generation with carbon capture to deliver fast, reliable, low-carbon baseload power. - Leaders from Baker Hughes and SINTEF stressed that hyperscalers must integrate CCUS into initial facility designs, standardizing turbine capture and co-locating near shared transport and storage hubs to avoid stranded assets. - Reaching gigaton-scale carbon management requires shifting from government subsidies to predictable, long-term revenue models, combining stable policy frameworks with institutional finance and corporate off-take demand. As artificial intelligence triggers an unprecedented surge in global electricity demand, carbon capture and storage (CCS) is rapidly emerging as a critical solution to keep data centers from derailing climate targets, provided the industry can crack the code on bankable financing and shared infrastructure. According to Bloomberg projections cited during a dedicated COP31 panel on decarbonizing data centers, global data center electricity consumption could reach 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, roughly 7.4% of global power generation. Because AI facilities require uninterrupted, round-the-clock baseload power while experiencing sharp computational load swings, many operators are turning to dedicated natural gas generation to achieve rapid “speed to power.” Speaking on the panel, Ilaria Perena, Global Sales Director for Climate Technology Solutions at Baker Hughes, noted that integrating CCUS from the outset, rather than treating it as an afterthought, is essential for hyperscalers seeking rapid, low-carbon deployment. Baker Hughes is already supporting a 1-gigawatt data center power project designed for CCUS integration, pairing turbine exhaust capture with facility cooling and digital reservoir monitoring. However, Mona Mølnvik, Vice President of Research at Norway’s SINTEF Energy Research and Director of GigaCCS, cautioned that capturing diluted CO2 (around 4% concentration) from gas turbines requires standardized, repeatable designs rather than bespoke one-offs. Crucially, she warned that developers cannot site data centers without planning the full carbon capture, transport and storage chain, urging operators to co-locate near industrial CCUS hubs rather than risking stranded assets. Unlocking the Capital to Scale That warning echoed a back-to-back COP31 discussion on financing global carbon management, where industry and financial leaders emphasized that proven technology is no longer the bottleneck – bankable business models are. Moderating the session, Jared Daniels, CEO of the Global CCS Institute, noted that while 113 commercial CCS facilities are operating globally (with capacity set to surpass 100 million tons per year once projects under construction come online), scaling toward gigatons requires market-driven capital. “Capital needs confidence,” Daniels said. “There needs to be confidence in the entire value chain that you’re going to get an appropriate return on that capital investment.” Relevant: Google Announces $17B Wyoming Data Center With Carbon Capture Panelists pointed to emerging templates proving that carbon infrastructure can attract institutional finance. Olivia Powis, CEO of the Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA), highlighted how UK revenue-support mechanisms unlocked £10 billion in non-recourse debt and drew major infrastructure equity into the HyNet cluster. Meanwhile, Tim Ashby, Global Head of Sustainability Strategy at HSBC, stressed that moving from “first-of-a-kind” to “nth-of-a-kind” projects depends on predictable, long-term revenue contracts, whether backed by stable carbon pricing, tax credits like US 45Q, or corporate off-take demand from sectors like AI and cloud computing. artigo.texto: Armazenamento de energia entrará no sistema elétrico como mais uma garantia da energia produzida por várias fontes de geração. Armazenamento de energia não significa depender de uma única tecnologia, mas um portfólio de soluções com diferentes características. Clique aqui e escute a matéria Ao participar do painel Armazenamento de Energia-UHR, na Coniben 2026, a presidente da Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica – ABRAGE, Marisete Pereira, destacou a importância da utilização das diversas fontes de energia para dar robustez ao sistema elétrico brasileiro, afirmando que armazenar o excedente e entregá-lo em outro horário melhora o aproveitamento dos recursos existentes e é estratégico. Usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis podem oferecer armazenamento de longa duração, flexibilidade e segurança ao sistema, complementando baterias e permitindo melhor integração das fontes renováveis variáveis, disse Marisete Pereira, que apresentou o armazenamento de energia como recurso indispensável para a evolução do sistema elétrico brasileiro. Ela disse que a expansão acelerada das fontes eólica e solar fortalece a descarbonização, mas também aumenta a variabilidade da geração e a necessidade de tecnologias capazes de fornecer flexibilidade, potência e segurança operacional. Ela representa uma entidade que reúne 25 empresas responsáveis por cerca de 90% da geração hidrelétrica brasileira e, na Coniben, explicou que o armazenamento pode contribuir para reduzir os cortes de geração que afetam empreendimentos renováveis. Os sócios da ABRAGE são investidores de longo prazo que possuem experiência, conhecimento técnico e disposição para ampliar investimentos, desde que existam planejamento, segurança jurídica e mecanismos adequados de remuneração. Segundo ela, o Brasil é reconhecido internacionalmente por sua matriz elétrica limpa e renovável, mas os investimentos em grandes hidrelétricas estão praticamente estagnados desde a entrada das últimas unidades relevantes. Enquanto outros países continuam expandindo a geração e o armazenamento hidráulico, o potencial brasileiro permanece parcialmente inexplorado. E no mundo, destacou a executiva que as usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis representam a maior parcela da capacidade de armazenamento de energia em larga escala. A tecnologia utiliza energia disponível para bombear água a um reservatório superior e, posteriormente, devolve essa água para gerar eletricidade quando o sistema necessita.Marisete Pereira reconheceu que baterias e usinas reversíveis não devem ser tratadas como concorrentes diretas. São soluções complementares, com características diferentes. “As baterias respondem rapidamente e normalmente operam durante quatro a seis horas. O armazenamento hidráulico pode atender períodos superiores a oito horas e, dependendo da configuração, manter energia disponível por dias ou semanas”, disse. Segundo ela, o movimento internacional demonstra que sistemas com participação crescente de fontes variáveis estão procurando armazenamento de maior duração para preservar confiabilidade e reduzir desperdícios. E disse que o Brasil possui vantagens relevantes: extensa experiência em hidrelétrica, sistema de transmissão de dimensão continental, empreendimentos distribuídos por diferentes regiões e profissionais qualificados. “Não aproveitar essa base significaria abrir mão de um recurso estratégico já dominado pelo setor nacional”, concluiu. As usinas reversíveis podem fornecer flexibilidade, confiabilidade, potência e serviços ao sistema. Também ajudam a integrar renováveis e a preservar a participação das hidrelétricas como elemento de equilíbrio da matriz brasileira. Para Marisete Pereira, o próximo desafio é transformar essas bases em investimentos concretos. Para isso, o setor precisa de regras claras, previsibilidade, segurança jurídica e modelos de contratação e remuneração que reconheçam os serviços prestados. Para ela, o país deve combinar tecnologias e aproveitar suas vantagens naturais. Baterias terão papel relevante, mas o Brasil não deve abandonar o potencial das usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis. Armazenamento não significa única tecnologia Para o presidente da ABSAE, Markus Vlasits, o armazenamento já é um mercado em operação no Brasil e deve avançar por meio de um portfólio tecnológico, com leilões recorrentes, recursos distribuídos, sinais económicos adequados e políticas estruturantes. Ele apresentou o armazenamento de energia como um setor que no Brasil deixou de ser apenas uma promessa tecnológica. Ele lidera uma entidade que reúne aproximadamente 90 associados de geração, transmissão, distribuição, financiamento, fabricação e serviços, refletindo o caráter multissetorial e multidisciplinar dessa atividade. E destacou que armazenamento não significa uma única tecnologia, mas um portfólio de soluções com diferentes características, escalas, durações e aplicações. Usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis, baterias eletroquímicas e recursos instalados junto aos consumidores podem prestar serviços complementares ao sistema. Markus Vlasits reconheceu os avanços recentes do poder público ao tratar da questão do armazenamento e destacou que planejamento, regulação e políticas energéticas começaram a incorporar o armazenamento, resultado da atuação conjunta de ministérios, agências, operador do sistema, empresas de pesquisa, associações e agentes privados. Hoje, o Brasil possui aproximadamente um gigawatt-hora de sistemas em operação, além de um mercado em expansão no segmento comercial e industrial. Mas todos os meses, novos projetos atrás do medidor entram em funcionamento, acumulando experiência e maturidade tecnológica. Para ele, o armazenamento responde a um duplo desafio do setor elétrico: falta de potência nos horários de ponta e excesso de oferta durante determinadas horas do dia. “As baterias podem absorver energia quando há abundância e entregá-la nos momentos de maior necessidade, reduzindo desperdícios e ajudando a integrar fontes v

ABM Industries (NYSE:ABM) is expanding its exposure to semiconductor facilities, data centers and microgrids as the facility services company faces pricing pressure in parts of its commercial real estate business. Chief Financial Officer David Orr said at Baird's Global Industrial Conference that the three growth areas account for about 11% of ABM's sales, up from roughly 7% last year. Collectively, they have grown at a very high double-digit rate this year, helped by both organic growth and the acquisition of semiconductor services provider WGNSTAR, he said. → Golden Dome's $185 Billion Question: Who Actually Gets Paid? Orr described ABM as a $9 billion company with services spanning janitorial work, parking, building engineering and technical services across commercial properties, airports, manufacturing facilities and schools. Growth pipeline and customer concentration Microgrid and semiconductor services have each grown organically at more than 20%, while data center services have grown at about 10%, Orr said. He added that the data center rate could increase as the company's pipeline expands. → Game On: The Hidden Value in Take-Two's Stock Vice President of Investor Relations Paul Goldberg said ABM has a qualified pipeline of about $1.5 billion across microgrids and data centers. The company hopes to convert those opportunities into contracts and revenue, he said. Orr said most current microgrid and data center revenue comes from five to seven major clients, while the pipeline spans 25 new clients. Converting those opportunities could broaden the customer base and reduce concentration risk, he said. → A 10-Stock Strategy That Balances AI Growth With Cash Flow ABM's data center work includes specialized cleaning and uninterruptible power systems through its Quality Uptime Services business. Its RavenVolt business provides microgrid equipment and services, including battery storage and backup power. Orr also discussed a joint venture's first task order under an Army Corps of Engineers program, announced in September. The roughly $20 million project involves battery storage and generator work at a New Mexico base and is expected to generate revenue in fiscal 2027. Orr said approximately $2 billion could be awarded under the program over 10 years, with ABM's joint venture competing for future work. He stressed that the company must execute on the initial project and win subsequent bids. Pressure in office services, improvement in aviation ABM's Business & Industry segment, which largely serves commercial real estate, is facing intense price competition on the West Coast, particularly in Northern California, Orr said. The company has been selective about taking lower-priced work and has declined some opportunities offering little or no margin. The segment is also contending with the revenue effect of exiting a Transport for London contract. Orr said ABM chose not to retain the work at margins it considered unacceptable. He sees a scenario in which Business & Industry returns to positive growth in the second half of fiscal 2027. In aviation, Orr said operating profit margin has improved from about 2% to nearly 6% over six years. He attributed the improvement partly to attention to underperforming contracts and a shift toward airport customers, whose contracts tend to be longer and more profitable than airline work. Airports now represent about 60% of the aviation portfolio, compared with airlines accounting for roughly 60% five years ago, he said. Orr added that ABM had not seen a significant recent drop in airline-related volumes. Cash flow, debt and labor priorities Orr said he would be disappointed if cash flow did not grow next year, while declining to provide specifics because the company was in a blackout period. He said reducing leverage is a priority, with ABM looking to move toward 2.5 times leverage in fiscal 2027. He also expects the company to continue its roughly 60-year record of annual dividend increases and offset dilution from share-based compensation. Beyond those priorities, ABM would weigh acquisitions against additional share repurchases, he said. Labor availability has largely returned to normal in ABM's core business, according to Orr, but skilled technicians remain a constraint in semiconductor and data center work. Goldberg said the company has opened training centers in Idaho and Austin, Texas, to help address that need. ABM is also testing floor-scrubbing robots, with a few hundred deployed nationally. Orr called their current impact a "rounding error" but said robotics could become more meaningful over the next several years. Its offerings include janitorial and custodial services, facility engineering and maintenance

artigo.texto: Proposta já está pronta no Ministério da Fazenda e, se aprovada pelo presidente, deve virar medida provisória no início de 2027. Um órgão com cerca de 150 funcionários e um colegiado de cinco diretores, com mandatos, pode passar a comandar o mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil. A proposta de criação de uma autarquia especial está pronta no governo federal e aguarda a decisão do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, segundo a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Cristina Reis, em entrevista ao UOL publicada em 10 de novembro de 2026. A expectativa é que o tema seja levado ao presidente ainda neste ano. Havendo aval, será editada uma medida provisória para criar a estrutura. Uma solução “engatilhada” para depois da COP31 Cristina Reis afirmou que o desenho do novo órgão já está concluído e que o debate deve ganhar força após a conferência do clima. A proposta está pronta. A gente está com uma solução engatilhada. Nessa volta da COP31, essa discussão vai ser mais aprofundada. Apesar disso, a secretária admite que o calendário é incerto. A proposta ainda depende de discussões dentro do governo e da palavra final da Presidência. “Tem muitas discussões a serem feitas, então é mais provável que fique para o começo do ano que vem”, disse. Como seria o novo órgão A autarquia teria um colegiado de cinco diretores, incluindo um diretor-presidente, todos com mandatos definidos. O quadro de pessoal seria de aproximadamente 150 funcionários. O órgão ficaria vinculado ao Ministério da Fazenda e teria estrutura própria para conduzir a regulamentação e a operação do mercado. Ele substituiria a Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, criada para conduzir a primeira fase de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), nome formal do mercado regulado de carbono no país. Até que a autarquia esteja efetivamente constituída, com pessoal contratado e estrutura montada, a Secretaria Extraordinária continuaria em funcionamento. A transição, portanto, evita um vazio de gestão. Quem vai pagar a conta O financiamento é o ponto ainda pendente. Inicialmente, a autarquia dependerá de recursos do Orçamento da União, o que exige definição antes da criação formal da estrutura. No futuro, o próprio mercado deve ajudar a custear a governança do sistema. Pela legislação, 15% das receitas arrecadadas por meio de leilões e outros mecanismos de cobrança poderão ser destinados à governança, o que inclui a manutenção da autarquia. Para onde vai o restante do dinheiro A mesma regra define o destino das demais receitas. Outros 75% serão direcionados ao Fundo Clima, e 10% poderão financiar projetos de interesse público, especialmente iniciativas sociais envolvendo comunidades tradicionais e povos indígenas. Para a Amazônia, esse último ponto é o que mais tende a ter efeito direto. A região concentra grande parte dos territórios indígenas e das comunidades tradicionais do país, potenciais beneficiárias dessa fatia, embora os critérios de acesso dependam da regulamentação que o novo órgão terá de conduzir. Os próximos passos O primeiro passo é a discussão da proposta com o presidente Lula, prevista para este ano. Se houver aprovação, a medida provisória que criaria a autarquia deve ser editada, na estimativa da secretária, no começo de 2027, enquanto a definição do financiamento segue em aberto. artigo.texto: The BMX SolidSafe 20K combines semi-solid-state battery tech with a high capacity and plenty of power When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. - The BMX SolidSafe 20K uses semi-solid-state battery tech for safer, longer-lasting power - It has a 20,000mAh capacity and 100W of power - It's priced at $109.99 (roughly £85 / AU$160) Semi-solid-state batteries are the big new thing in power banks, delivering increased capacities without a bigger footprint. They're also slower to degrade — so they won't need replacing as fast — and are even deemed to be safer than conventional lithium-ion power banks, as most of the liquid found in those devices is replaced with a solid or gel electrolyte, which is less flammable. That last point is one of the big features BMX is pushing about its new 20,000mAh SolidSafe power bank, an accessory notable for being semi-solid-state and having a higher capacity than most battery packs of its kind. While many rival products with this battery tech are most suited to charging phones and tablets, the SolidSafe 20K can comfortably charge a laptop, with BMX claiming — via Gadgeteer — that it's good for one full charge of a 13.6-inch MacBook Air M3 with power left over. Three ports so you can charge everything Of course, it can charge phones and tablets too, and it has up to 100W of charging power. You'll get that much power if you just plug one thing in via its primary USB-C port, but it also has a secondary USB-C port, which individually can manage 65W, and a USB-A port, capable of 22.5W. Use all three ports at once, and you'll get 65W from the primary one and 7.5W from the other two. The SolidSafe 20K also has a tiny color LCD screen that shows the battery percentage and wattage on each port, and it comes in at 147.4 x 90.3 x 18mm and 375g, making it a lot slimmer than many laptop power banks — so it's ideal for travel, especially as it falls under the 100W carry-on limit for spare batteries on most airlines. If you like the sound of it, it's out now in the US, costing $109.99 (roughly £85 / AU$160). It's not yet available in the UK or Australia, but BMX does have a presence in both regions, so it might just be a matter of time.

RAIO accepts 11.52 kW of solar input, starts under $8,000, expands to 73.5 kWh, and carries a 12-year limited warranty. Commerce, Texas, Nov. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BigBattery today announced RAIO, a residential all-in-one energy storage system certified to UL 9540 that combines a 14.7 kWh LiFePO4 home battery and a 7.68 kW hybrid inverter in a single enclosure. RAIO enters the U.S. market as BigBattery's first all-in-one system, pairing an integrated battery and inverter with a separate smart gateway to provide solar energy storage, reduce reliance on the grid, and support whole-home battery backup during outages. BigBattery UL 9540 Certified RAIO (Residential All-In-One) RAIO, short for Residential All-In-One, provides 14.7 kWh of nominal storage, delivers 7.68 kW of continuous 120/240 V split-phase AC power, and accepts up to 11.52 kW of solar input through three independent maximum power point tracking (MPPT) inputs. It pairs with the separate RAIO Smart Energy Gateway, which manages the utility grid connection and transfers designated household loads to battery power during an outage. "Homeowners shouldn't have to piece together a battery, an inverter, and a transfer switch to own their power," said Eric Lundgren, CEO of BigBattery. "RAIO puts the battery and the inverter in one enclosure, certified to UL 9540 and backed for 12 years. It is the most complete home energy system we have released." What is BigBattery RAIO? BigBattery RAIO is an all-in-one home energy storage system that combines a solar battery and hybrid inverter in one main unit, with an accompanying smart gateway. The main enclosure contains the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack, the battery control unit, a bidirectional power conversion system that functions as a hybrid inverter, and a wiring cabinet with circuit breakers and protection devices. The enclosure measures approximately 30 inches wide, 49 inches tall, and 5.9 inches deep. It supports wall or floor mounting and is rated IP66 and NEMA 4X for indoor or outdoor installation. RAIO uses natural convection cooling and operates at a noise level below 31 dB. It is available in Stealth Gray and Pearl White. RAIO specifications Battery: LiFePO4 (LFP) battery with 14.7 kWh of nominal capacity AC output: 7.68 kW of continuous 120/240 V split-phase AC power Solar input: Suggested maximum photovoltaic (PV) input of 11.52 kW across three independent MPPTs, with an MPPT voltage range of 90–500 V and a maximum DC voltage of 550 V Inverter efficiency: 97.5% CEC efficiency and 98% maximum efficiency Protections: Arc-fault protection (AFCI), PV rapid shutdown, isolation monitoring, anti-islanding, DC reverse-polarity protection, and AC short-circuit protection Enclosure: IP66 and NEMA 4X, natural convection cooling, 385.8 lb, and wall or floor mounting Monitoring: App-based monitoring via Wi-Fi or LAN, with RS485 and CAN communication Expansion: Up to five RAIO units connected to one gateway, providing 73.5 kWh of nominal storage and 38.4 kW of combined continuous AC power, subject to the approved system design Warranty: 12-year limited warranty Whole-home battery backup with the RAIO Smart Energy Gateway The separate RAIO Smart Energy Gateway is an automatic transfer switch that transfers household loads from grid power to battery power during an outage and prevents backfeed into utility lines. Its grid and load ports are rated for 160 A of continuous current, with a maximum rating of 200 A. A qualified installer can design the system for whole-home backup or partial-home backup of selected circuits. Backup coverage depends on the system design and connected loads. The gateway's smart ports support compatible electric vehicle (EV) charging loads and a generator connection rated up to 64 A, with automatic generator start for compatible generators. RAIO can also provide home battery backup without solar panels. It can charge from the grid and store energy in reserve. It can also be AC-coupled through the gateway to a compatible existing solar inverter. Solar battery storage with four operating modes For solar battery backup, RAIO accepts solar input directly through its built-in hybrid inverter, eliminating the need for a separate solar inverter in a properly designed new installation. Homeowners can use the app to select from four operating modes: Self-Use supplies household loads with solar energy first, stores surplus energy in the battery, and uses battery energy before drawing from the grid. Feed-in Priority supplies household loads first, then exports surplus solar energy to the grid where permitted by the utility. Backup charges the battery at scheduled times and holds it in reserve for outages while grid power is available. Time of Use schedules charging and discharging around utility rate periods. A home energy storage system that expands to 73.5 kWh Up to five RAIO units can be connected in parallel to one RAIO Smart Energy Gateway. One unit provides 14.7 kWh of nominal storage and 7.68 kW of continuous AC power. Two units provide 29.4 kWh and 15.36 kW; three units provide 44.1 kWh and 23.04 kW; four units provide 58.8 kWh and 30.72 kW; and five units provide 73.5 kWh and 38.4 kW. These storage figures represent nominal capacity. Final backup power depends on the approved configuration, connected loads, and installation design. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA A LS ELECTRIC fornecerá equipamentos de manobra para a expansão de um data center de IA nos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um… Ver mais - O novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um cliente existente de data center. - As premiações repetidas dependem do cumprimento dos cronogramas de entrega de hyperscale em suas unidades de produção na Coreia e nos EUA. - A LS ELECTRIC também está desenvolvendo sistemas de distribuição DC em sua instalação de Cheonan para futuros data centers de IA. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 16 de novembro de 2026, que havia assinado um contrato de fornecimento de sistemas de energia no valor de aproximadamente US$ 93,83 milhões (130 bilhões de KRW) para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável nos EUA de uma empresa global de tecnologia de grande porte. O contrato abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV e painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, que serão fornecidos em etapas para a rede elétrica do data center. Os equipamentos de alta tensão distribuem a eletricidade recebida às instalações individuais e protegem os equipamentos quando ocorrem anomalias no fornecimento de energia. A LS ELECTRIC participou do grande projeto de data center local do cliente desde a fase inicial de construção. O novo contrato dá continuidade às encomendas de painéis de manobra de alta tensão na fase de expansão, tornando-se um pedido subsequente de um cliente existente e vinculando diretamente a atuação da fornecedora à continuidade da construção do projeto. Capacidade de entrega sustenta o pedido de expansão A LS ELECTRIC identifica o prazo até a energização — o intervalo antes que um data center receba eletricidade e possa começar a operar — como uma preocupação competitiva central na infraestrutura de IA. A empresa atribui os pedidos recorrentes ao atendimento dos requisitos de qualidade do cliente e dos cronogramas de entrega para instalações hiperescaláveis desde as etapas iniciais do projeto. Suas bases de produção nomeadas são a fábrica inteligente de Cheongju, na Coreia do Sul, a LS ELECTRIC Utah e o Bastrop Campus, no Texas. A empresa apresenta essa presença como o alicerce de sua competitividade em entregas. Neste pedido de expansão, o requisito de entrega tem uma dimensão operacional concreta: o contrato de equipamentos depende tanto da capacidade industrial e do cronograma quanto das especificações dos produtos. Contratos recentes abrangem todo o sistema elétrico Um comunicado separado de outubro de 2026 divulgou um acordo de longo prazo no valor de 168,9 bilhões de KRW (US$ 125,23 milhões) com outra empresa de tecnologia de grande porte dos EUA, abrangendo 2027–2028. O valor anunciado corresponde aos produtos programados para entrega em 2027, enquanto a dimensão dos negócios de 2028 continua sujeita a novas discussões. Esse acordo abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV. O possível fornecimento adicional de painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, transformadores de distribuição e unidades de manobra em anel continua em discussão, criando a possibilidade de um pacote de equipamentos mais amplo em torno das entregas já comprometidas. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 1º de outubro de 2026, um contrato de 181,2 bilhões de KRW (US$ 133,41 milhões) para transformadores de tensão extra-alta de 345 kV. As entregas estão programadas em etapas para nove subestações até 2030, para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável na América do Norte. Em conjunto, os registros da empresa descrevem atividades tanto em equipamentos de distribuição para data centers quanto na infraestrutura de tensão mais alta necessária para fornecer energia a grandes projetos de IA. Negócios em corrente alternada e desenvolvimento em corrente contínua Além da distribuição convencional em corrente alternada (CA), a LS ELECTRIC está desenvolvendo sistemas de próxima geração em corrente contínua (CC) para data centers de IA. A empresa descreve sua Cheonan DC Factory como a primeira unidade fabril a comercializar a distribuição em corrente contínua. Transformadores de estado sólido, disjuntores de estado sólido e sistemas de armazenamento de energia são usados ali para testar redes elétricas de próxima geração e ambientes de data center. O contrato destaca a relação comercial entre o fornecimento de energia e a capacidade computacional de IA: não é possível energizar uma nova capacidade até que os equipamentos elétricos estejam instalados. A atuação recorrente da LS ELECTRIC vincula seu negócio de equipamentos de manobra a esse cronograma, enquanto a unidade de testes de Cheonan oferece um caminho para projetos futuros em corrente contínua, à medida que os projetos hiperescaláveis se expandem e sua arquitetura de energia evolui.

artigo.texto: SALEM — The massive, whitewashed buildings of Shetland Park loom over Salem Harbor, looking much like the cotton mills they used to be. Decades ago, with its mechanical looms and thousands of low-paid textile workers, this was probably the noisiest spot in town. Today, it’s remarkably quiet. The modern tenants — law offices, a food pantry, a medical clinic, a charter school — make good neighbors for the apartment dwellers just across Congress Street, in the low-income neighborhood known as The Point. But now Shetland Park’s owner has designs on bringing back the thrum of industry. It has proposed a small-scale data center for the complex, one that would bring the constant hum of cooling fans and the occasional roar of three big diesel generators. Many in Salem want no part of it. “There’s probably a place for data centers,” City Councilor Ty Hapworth said. “It’s probably not in a dense city like Salem.” The outcry against the Salem proposal echoes the surging nationwide resistance to giant “hyperscale” data centers. In October, public opposition halted a $4 billion project in Westfield. And in a town near Worcester, Sutton residents turned out in force last week to oppose a plan by the Kraft Group to build one of the nation’s biggest hyperscale facilities. Such massive data centers are essential for training powerful artificial intelligence systems from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Their developers are up against ferocious opposition from citizens in Massachusetts and across the country, who fear the data centers will drain local water supplies, jack up electricity rates, and generate intense noise and air pollution. The Pew Research Center estimates there are about 3,000 data centers in the United States. Most of them are relatively small — like the one that’s been sitting atop the Macy’s department store in Boston’s Downtown Crossing for nearly 30 years — and use little cooling water or electricity. We rely on them for nearly every part of our digital lives, from shopping and banking to streaming video, yet until recently, few people noticed they existed. Lately, though, anything called a “data center” draws fire, however small. In Salem, upstate New York-based Prime Group Holding, which owns the 30-acre Shetland Park, had no trouble getting a building permit in May. But in September, amid intense backlash from city residents, Salem’s zoning board of appeals canceled the permit. The about-face was driven in part by concerns that Prime Group hadn’t been entirely honest about its intentions. The company had originally proposed a much smaller facility, claiming it would be used by an unnamed “IT services company.” Only after getting the permit was the project scaled up to drugstore size, requiring three diesel generators to provide backup power instead of the single generator in the original plan. Prime Group has a less-than-transparent name for the new version, calling it a “low-latency inference point,” and insists it’s not a data center, even though it would be a roomful of computers providing artificial intelligence services to local businesses. “It did feel a bit disconcerting that they would change plans midstream and try to characterize their project as something that it clearly was not,” Salem Mayor Dominick Pangallo said. Now, the city has banned the construction of data centers, except by organizations that need them for their own use, such as hospitals or government agencies. Prime Group did not respond to requests for comment. The company has until late November to challenge the zoning board’s decision in court. Across the state line, in Concord, N.H., a similar battle is playing out. City planners are having second thoughts about an already approved plan for a small data center on vacant commercial land near Interstate 93 in East Concord. The planning board may vote later this month to halt the development. Kelly Morgan, an S&P Global analyst who tracks the data center industry, said 110 US data center projects had been canceled or delayed this year through October, with the overwhelming majority scrubbed because of citizen opposition. Most were to be large data centers, using at least 50 megawatts of electric power from the local grid. But Morgan listed the cancellation or delay of eight projects requiring 36 megawatts or less. And her list did not include the Salem and Concord data centers. “I suspect it is people hearing the word ‘data center’ and not distinguishing by size or impact, just reflexively saying, ‘No thanks,’” Morgan said. Levitate, a Bothell, Wash.-based AI infrastructure and data center company, obtained a building permit in East Concord to erect a 15-megawatt, 7,500-square-foot data facility on a parcel of undeveloped land about a quarter mile from Interstate 93. The area couldn’t be more different from Salem. There’s little nearby except trees and a few businesses, including a shipping company, a data networking contractor, and a company that repairs roads and bridges. No homes, no apartment buildings. Just trees and traffic whirring past on the interstate. During a recent visit, managers of local businesses declined to speak on the record, but expressed no concern about a possible data center in the neighborhood. One seemed mystified that anybody would object. But object they did, after Concord’s city planner ruled in June that the Levitate project was a permissible use of land zoned for industrial use. Faced with broad opposition, the board deferred final action until Nov. 18. Speaking at the hearing, Levitate chief executive Ryan Howard described the data center as “a small compact design with an intentionally low impact on public resources.” He said that local power company Unitil could deliver the needed electricity without driving up electric rates. artigo.texto: The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) has launched its second Bulk Energy Storage solicitation to procure approximately 1 GW of energy storage capacity. The solicitation is open to various eligible energy storage technologies and is part of a plan to procure 3 GW of bulk energy storage through at least three annual solicitations. The initiative is part of the state’s 2022 Energy Storage Roadmap, which aims to deploy 6 GW of energy storage by 2030. Projects supported under the programme will be required to comply with updated energy storage safety codes, including requirements for safe site selection, first responder training, and emergency response plans. NYSERDA will provide incentives through its Index Storage Credit mechanism, but payments will only begin after projects have received the necessary permits, been installed and become operational, and passed peer reviews and quality assurance inspections. NY Green Bank will also offer financing options to developers and investors to support project development. In September 2026, NYSERDA awarded contracts to eight battery storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects. Together, these projects represent 1.7 GW of new capacity and over $3.7 billion in private investment. BESS projects will add 950 MW of capacity, with durations ranging from four to eight hours while the 13 renewable energy projects will add over 719 MW of capacity and comprise solar, onshore wind, and hydropower. The projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2030.

artigo.texto: Commerce, Texas, Nov. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BigBattery today announced RAIO, a residential all-in-one energy storage system certified to UL 9540 that combines a 14.7 kWh LiFePO4 home battery and a 7.68 kW hybrid inverter in a single enclosure. RAIO enters the U.S. market as BigBattery’s first all-in-one system, pairing an integrated battery and inverter with a separate smart gateway to provide solar energy storage, reduce reliance on the grid, and support whole-home battery backup during outages. BigBattery UL 9540 Certified RAIO (Residential All-In-One) RAIO, short for Residential All-In-One, provides 14.7 kWh of nominal storage, delivers 7.68 kW of continuous 120/240 V split-phase AC power, and accepts up to 11.52 kW of solar input through three independent maximum power point tracking (MPPT) inputs. It pairs with the separate RAIO Smart Energy Gateway, which manages the utility grid connection and transfers designated household loads to battery power during an outage. “Homeowners shouldn’t have to piece together a battery, an inverter, and a transfer switch to own their power,” said Eric Lundgren, CEO of BigBattery. “RAIO puts the battery and the inverter in one enclosure, certified to UL 9540 and backed for 12 years. It is the most complete home energy system we have released.” What is BigBattery RAIO? BigBattery RAIO is an all-in-one home energy storage system that combines a solar battery and hybrid inverter in one main unit, with an accompanying smart gateway. The main enclosure contains the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack, the battery control unit, a bidirectional power conversion system that functions as a hybrid inverter, and a wiring cabinet with circuit breakers and protection devices. The enclosure measures approximately 30 inches wide, 49 inches tall, and 5.9 inches deep. It supports wall or floor mounting and is rated IP66 and NEMA 4X for indoor or outdoor installation. RAIO uses natural convection cooling and operates at a noise level below 31 dB. It is available in Stealth Gray and Pearl White. RAIO specifications Whole-home battery backup with the RAIO Smart Energy Gateway The separate RAIO Smart Energy Gateway is an automatic transfer switch that transfers household loads from grid power to battery power during an outage and prevents backfeed into utility lines. Its grid and load ports are rated for 160 A of continuous current, with a maximum rating of 200 A. A qualified installer can design the system for whole-home backup or partial-home backup of selected circuits. Backup coverage depends on the system design and connected loads. The gateway’s smart ports support compatible electric vehicle (EV) charging loads and a generator connection rated up to 64 A, with automatic generator start for compatible generators. RAIO can also provide home battery backup without solar panels. It can charge from the grid and store energy in reserve. It can also be AC-coupled through the gateway to a compatible existing solar inverter. Solar battery storage with four operating modes For solar battery backup, RAIO accepts solar input directly through its built-in hybrid inverter, eliminating the need for a separate solar inverter in a properly designed new installation. artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA* A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. *Colaboraram: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr.

artigo.texto: Samsung’s Solid-State Battery and the Shaky 64% Silver Demand Claim Key Takeaways - The 64% silver claim traces to one X post from August 2024, and its author later described the figure as "completely unverified" after Kitco, MarketWatch and Morningstar carried it. - Samsung SDI has not disclosed silver loading per cell or pack; the Ag-C layer is a five-micrometre-class coating, so a plausible range is a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack. - The claim needs 16 million vehicles, equal to four of every five EVs sold in 2025, yet Samsung targets mass production only in the second half of 2027, starting with luxury vehicles and robots. - Against the Silver Institute's 2025 data, the 16,000-tonne figure falls to about 61% of mine production and about 46% of total demand. - Silver's demand case stands without Samsung; the signals to watch are a Samsung loading disclosure, real 2027 production volumes and the pace of Toyota's 2027-2028 rollout. The most quoted number in the silver bull case right now is not a Samsung number. The claim that Samsung‘s solid-state battery could consume 64% of the world’s annual silver mine supply traces back to a single post on X in August 2024. Its author later called his own figure “completely unverified”. That admission has not slowed the figure down. Kitco, MarketWatch, Morningstar and a long tail of silver-investment sites have carried it, and each retelling made it sound more solid than the last. If you hold silver or are thinking about it, you may be pricing in a story rather than a specification. This piece separates what Samsung has disclosed from what was guessed, and gives you a method for testing the next commodity demand claim that lands in your feed. Where did the 64% silver claim come from? In August 2024, Kevin Bambrough, a retired investment professional, posted an estimate of how much silver Samsung’s planned battery might need. About ten days later, Kitco published it on 19 August 2024, and the figure began its run through financial media. His arithmetic took four steps: - Each cell might use as much as 5 g of silver. - A typical 100 kWh EV pack might hold about 200 cells, giving roughly 1 kg of silver per vehicle. - Roughly 20% of about 80 million vehicles built each year (about 16 million) might adopt the battery. - That adds up to 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. Set against a rough 25,000-tonne annual mine output, you get 64%. Use the Silver Institute’s 2025 mine production of 846.6 Moz (about 26,300 tonnes) and the figure drops to about 61%. Against total 2025 demand of 1,130.6 Moz (about 35,166 tonnes), it falls to about 46%. The viral 64% figure relies on cascading estimates, concluding that 16 million vehicles would require 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. How the caveats disappeared The original post was hedged. Bambrough said official figures were unavailable, that 5 g might be high and that the true number could be as low as 0.5 g per cell. In replies, he said he had used AI to estimate grams per cell and cells per pack, and he cited a 3-10 g range without naming its source. None of that survived the trip into headlines. By late 2025, he was pushing back on people treating it as fact: His later verdict on his own estimate: “completely unverified.” Then, in 2026, a widely circulated analysis attributed the figure to technical disclosures from Samsung SDI. No such documents have been published. The same retellings blended a 600-mile range, a 20-year life and a 9-minute charge into one battery, even though those benchmarks came from separate Samsung announcements. A headline figure that cannot be traced to a primary source is a hypothesis. You should treat it as one before it shapes any allocation decision. Readers who want the bullish framing in full can read it in our deep-dive into the solid-state battery silver thesis, which sets out the mispricing pattern commodity investors repeat. When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first What has Samsung actually disclosed about silver in its battery? Strip out the guesswork and a real technology remains. Samsung SDI describes its all-solid-state battery as anode-free, meaning the cell is built without a conventional graphite or lithium-metal anode. Instead, lithium plates onto the current collector during charging and forms the anode in place. That is where silver comes in. A thin silver-carbon (Ag-C) layer helps lithium spread evenly rather than clumping, according to Korea JoongAng Daily (1 July 2026). Reports describe it as thinner than a hair, a five-micrometre-class coating. The pouch cell matters because robot packs hold a couple of kWh, against roughly 70-75 kWh in an average EV. Silver scales with stored energy, so early robot cells would use little of it. The production timing is a company target, not a guarantee. The gaps are wider than the facts: - The silver-to-carbon ratio in the layer - Silver per cell, per kWh and per pack - Final cell size for the prismatic EV product - Whether recipes differ between pouch and prismatic formats A plausible range runs from a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack; even Bambrough’s low-end 3 g per cell gives 600 g. Because the silver sits in an interfacial layer rather than a bulk electrode, you should read 1 kg as the ceiling of that range, not the baseline. How does silver demand work, and why do adoption assumptions matter? A new use for silver only matters relative to the size of the market it enters. Mine supply is the metal dug out each year. Total demand adds industrial use, jewellery, silverware and investment buying, and the gap is filled by recycling and existing stocks. Now test the adoption assumption against those totals. The International Energy Agency (IEA) counted just over 20 million electric cars sold in 2025 (about 21 million in its Global Energy Review), roughly a quarter of new-car sales. The speculative claim of 16,000 tonnes of battery demand represents a massive share of the 846.6 Moz (~26,300 tonnes)

artigo.texto: In the process of fulfilling its commitments to address climate change, Vietnam has identified the establishment of a carbon market as one of the key solutions to create incentives for emission reduction, promote green transition, and attract investment. However, for the market to operate effectively, it is necessary to further improve the institutional framework, ensure the transparency of emission data, and enhance the participation of businesses. These issues were discussed by domestic and international experts at the side event "Promoting Vietnam's Carbon Market: Transparency, Efficiency and International Cooperation," held at the Vietnam Pavilion within the framework of the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31). Turning emission reduction into an investment driver. Mr. Bui Duc Hieu, Deputy Director of the Climate Change Department ( Ministry of Agriculture and Environment ), stated that developing a carbon market is one of the important solutions for Vietnam to fulfill its national commitments on climate change response, aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050. A carbon market provides a tool for managing greenhouse gas emissions while simultaneously encouraging businesses to innovate technology, improve energy efficiency, and proactively invest in low-emission production solutions. To concretize this direction, Vietnam is accelerating the completion of institutional frameworks and the construction of infrastructure to support market operation. In the 2025-2026 period, the Government has approved a total pilot emission quota of approximately 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent, allocated to 110 facilities in three sectors: thermal power, iron and steel production, and cement. These are all industries with high emission levels and play a crucial role in industrial production and economic development. The pilot phase of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) is expected to last until the end of 2028, laying the groundwork for the carbon market to enter its official operational phase from 2029. This phased implementation aims to help regulatory agencies gradually improve monitoring mechanisms, while also enabling businesses to adapt to new requirements for inventory, management, and emission reduction. Assessing the progress of carbon market development in Vietnam, John Robert Cotton, Director of the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) at the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS), noted that Vietnam is making rapid progress in establishing a legal framework and implementing a mandatory market mechanism. Compared to many countries, Vietnam is accelerating the transition from policy-making to the implementation of an emissions trading system at a remarkable pace. However, a major challenge for Vietnam is the enormous investment capital required for green transition and achieving net-zero emissions commitments, exceeding the capacity of the state budget alone. In this context, carbon pricing is seen as an economic tool capable of promoting investment in environmentally friendly production and business activities. John Robert Cotton analyzed that, first of all, carbon pricing helps to incorporate emission costs into a company's financial accounting and balance sheet. Instead of simply implementing emission reduction measures to meet regulatory requirements, businesses will have to calculate the economic efficiency of each investment option, in which technological innovation, energy saving, and emission reduction become factors that directly impact production costs and competitiveness. Furthermore, the implementation of an emission quota auction mechanism from 2029 is expected to generate additional revenue for the state budget. This resource can be reinvested in emission reduction programs in the industrial sector, supporting technological transformation and improving energy efficiency. In particular, through the international cooperation mechanisms stipulated in Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, the carbon market can open up opportunities to access international financing for emission reduction projects that have difficulty raising capital through traditional methods. The ability to attract these resources is crucial for developing economies like Vietnam, because the green transition requires long-term capital, while many clean technology projects have large initial investment costs and long payback periods. Establishing a transparent carbon pricing mechanism can contribute to improving the financial efficiency of projects and create further incentives for the private sector to participate in emission reduction investments. However, for these financial opportunities to translate into actual capital flows, the market needs clear operating mechanisms, a reliable data system, and effective connectivity between domestic businesses and international investors and partners. Data transparency to unlock international resources. Despite progress in establishing a legal framework, experts believe that the formation of a carbon market is only the beginning. The greater challenges lie in the ability to organize and operate it, ensure the transparency of transactions, the quality of carbon credits, and the actual effectiveness of emission reductions. One of the most pressing requirements is to further improve the greenhouse gas measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. This system plays a fundamental role in determining the emissions of production facilities, evaluating emission reduction results, and providing a basis for allocation, quota trading, and carbon credit transactions. Data quality is particularly crucial for a market where transaction values are directly tied to the amount of emissions that are identified and verified. artigo.texto: No cumprimento de seus compromissos para enfrentar as mudanças climáticas, o Vietnã identificou o estabelecimento de um mercado de carbono como uma das principais soluções para criar incentivos à redução de emissões, promover a transição verde e atrair investimentos. No entanto, para que o mercado opere de forma eficaz, é necessário aprimorar ainda mais o arcabouço institucional, garantir a transparência dos dados de emissão e aumentar a participação das empresas. Esses temas foram debatidos por especialistas nacionais e internacionais no evento paralelo "Promovendo o Mercado de Carbono do Vietnã: Transparência, Eficiência e Cooperação Internacional", realizado no Pavilhão do Vietnã no âmbito da 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31). Transformar a redução de emissões em um fator de incentivo ao investimento. O Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas ( Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente ), afirmou que o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono é uma das soluções importantes para o Vietnã cumprir seus compromissos nacionais de resposta às mudanças climáticas, visando emissões líquidas zero até 2050. Um mercado de carbono fornece uma ferramenta para gerenciar as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, ao mesmo tempo que incentiva as empresas a inovar em tecnologia, melhorar a eficiência energética e investir proativamente em soluções de produção de baixa emissão. Para concretizar essa direção, o Vietnã está acelerando a conclusão dos marcos institucionais e a construção da infraestrutura necessária para apoiar a operação do mercado. No período de 2025-2026, o Governo aprovou uma cota piloto total de emissões de aproximadamente 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente, alocada a 110 instalações em três setores: energia térmica, produção de ferro e aço e cimento. Todas essas indústrias apresentam altos níveis de emissão e desempenham um papel crucial na produção industrial e no desenvolvimento econômico . A fase piloto do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) deverá durar até o final de 2028, preparando o terreno para que o mercado de carbono entre em sua fase operacional oficial a partir de 2029. Essa implementação gradual visa ajudar as agências reguladoras a aprimorarem progressivamente os mecanismos de monitoramento, permitindo também que as empresas se adaptem às novas exigências de inventário, gestão e redução de emissões. Ao avaliar o progresso do desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no Vietnã, John Robert Cotton, Diretor da Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP) do Escritório das Nações Unidas de Serviços para Projetos (UNOPS), observou que o Vietnã está avançando rapidamente no estabelecimento de um arcabouço legal e na implementação de um mecanismo de mercado obrigatório. Comparado a muitos países, o Vietnã está acelerando a transição da formulação de políticas para a implementação de um sistema de comércio de emissões em um ritmo notável. No entanto, um grande desafio para o Vietnã é o enorme capital de investimento necessário para a transição verde e para atingir as metas de emissões líquidas zero, que excede a capacidade do orçamento estatal. Nesse contexto, a precificação do carbono é vista como uma ferramenta econômica capaz de promover investimentos em atividades produtivas e comerciais ambientalmente sustentáveis. John Robert Cotton analisou que, em primeiro lugar, a precificação do carbono ajuda a incorporar os custos de emissão na contabilidade financeira e no balanço patrimonial de uma empresa. Em vez de simplesmente implementar medidas de redução de emissões para atender aos requisitos regulatórios, as empresas terão que calcular a eficiência econômica de cada opção de investimento, na qual a inovação tecnológica, a economia de energia e a redução de emissões se tornam fatores que impactam diretamente os custos de produção e a competitividade. Além disso, espera-se que a implementação de um mecanismo de leilão de cotas de emissão a partir de 2029 gere receitas adicionais para o orçamento do Estado. Esses recursos podem ser reinvestidos em programas de redução de emissões no setor industrial, apoiando a transformação tecnológica e aprimorando a eficiência energética. Em particular, através dos mecanismos de cooperação internacional estipulados no Artigo 6.º do Acordo de Paris, o mercado de carbono pode abrir oportunidades de acesso a financiamento internacional para projetos de redução de emissões que têm dificuldade em angariar capital através de métodos tradicionais. A capacidade de atrair esses recursos é crucial para economias em desenvolvimento como a do Vietnã, pois a transição verde exige capital a longo prazo, enquanto muitos projetos de tecnologia limpa têm altos custos iniciais de investimento e longos períodos de retorno. O estabelecimento de um mecanismo transparente de precificação de carbono pode contribuir para melhorar a eficiência financeira dos projetos e criar mais incentivos para que o setor privado participe de investimentos na redução de emissões. No entanto, para que essas oportunidades financeiras se traduzam em fluxos de capital reais, o mercado precisa de mecanismos operacionais claros, um sistema de dados confiável e uma conectividade eficaz entre empresas nacionais e investidores e parceiros internacionais. Transparência de dados para desbloquear recursos internacionais. Apesar dos avanços na criação de um arcabouço legal, especialistas acreditam que a formação de um mercado de carbono é apenas o começo. artigo.texto: The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong. These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives. In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park. In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison. This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum. In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm. This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial. FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs. This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers. Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed. It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers. For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With the midterms behind us and our tech infrastructure on thin ice, now is the time for the case to be made that, one way or another, our future lies in data centers.
