artigo.texto: O Goldman Sachs prevê que os preços do cobre na Bolsa de Metais de Londres (LME) atingirão US$ 15.600 por tonelada até dezembro de 2027, representando um aumento de aproximadamente 13% em relação aos níveis atuais à vista. A previsão do banco de investimentos surge após um período de alta nos preços do cobre, com o metal sendo negociado a pouco menos de US$ 10.000 por tonelada no ano anterior. O Goldman Sachs atribuiu sua perspectiva ao aumento da demanda proveniente da eletrificação, iniciativas de segurança energética, acumulação estratégica de estoques, desenvolvimento de data centers e infraestrutura que suporta inteligência artificial. O banco também identificou as restrições à produção das minas como um fator que influencia as perspectivas para o fornecimento de cobre. As políticas das cadeias de suprimentos dos EUA e da China influenciam os mercados de cobre Segundo o Goldman Sachs, as políticas introduzidas pelos Estados Unidos e pela China no último ano para garantir as cadeias de abastecimento internas aumentaram a concorrência entre os dois países pelo cobre refinado. Ambos os países têm procurado melhorar o acesso ao metal, que é utilizado em infraestruturas elétricas, equipamentos industriais e tecnologias associadas a sistemas de energia. O banco indicou que a concorrência pelo cobre refinado contribuiu para uma redução nos estoques mantidos fora dos Estados Unidos, levando os níveis a mínimas sazonais. O Goldman Sachs afirmou que esses desenvolvimentos aumentaram a pressão sobre os preços do cobre, juntamente com as limitações estruturais já existentes no fornecimento das minas. Eletrificação e investimento em data centers apoiam a perspectiva da demanda O Goldman Sachs identificou a eletrificação e o investimento em centros de dados como importantes fatores que contribuem para o aumento projetado na demanda por cobre. O banco também citou a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial e os programas de segurança energética como fontes de consumo adicional. Além da demanda industrial, o acúmulo de estoques ligado aos objetivos de segurança de abastecimento contribuiu para a competição pelo cobre refinado disponível. O Goldman Sachs espera que esses fatores de demanda, combinados com as limitações na produção de minas e a redução dos estoques fora dos Estados Unidos, sustentem sua previsão de US$ 15.600 por tonelada até dezembro de 2027. artigo.texto: GCC and EXIST Sign Carbon Market Cooperation Agreement at COP31 The Global Carbon Council and Turkiye's Energy Exchange, Enerji Piyasalari Isletme A.S., known internationally as Energy Exchange Istanbul (EXIST), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to deepen cooperation on carbon market development and to examine trading of GCC-issued carbon credits in Turkiye, according to QNA. The agreement was signed at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by the GCC and the League of Arab States, during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkiye. The memorandum was signed by Dr. Yousef Alhorr, Founding Chairman of the GCC, and Taha Meli Arvas, CEO and Vice Chairman of the Board of EPIAS. The cooperation is intended to facilitate use of the GCC's internationally recognized carbon crediting program in Turkiye, open new paths for market participants to access high-integrity carbon credits, and reinforce technical capacity as the country builds its carbon market framework. Combining Standards Expertise with Market Operations The arrangement pairs the GCC's experience in carbon crediting standards, project registration and credit issuance with EPIAS's expertise in running organized energy and environmental markets. It aims to support transparent market mechanisms that connect credible emissions reduction projects with buyers and investors, while contributing to corporate climate strategies and national climate objectives. Under the memorandum, the two organizations will explore listing and trading of the GCC's Approved Carbon Credits on EPIAS trading platforms, subject to applicable regulations and market requirements. They will also examine whether the credits could be recognized under Turkiye's future compliance carbon market framework. The proposed cooperation could widen market access for project developers and buyers and encourage the registration, issuance and use of high-quality carbon credits through transparent trading processes. Capacity Building and Technical Support Beyond trading, the agreement emphasizes capacity building and knowledge exchange. The GCC and EPIAS intend to hold workshops, webinars, seminars and other activities to improve understanding of carbon market requirements among potential participants and local stakeholders. The GCC will also support access to publicly available information on its crediting program, registry and methodologies. The cooperation may draw on the expertise of the Gulf Organisation for Research and Development, the GCC's parent organization, to support market readiness and technical capacity development in Turkiye. Possible areas of support include training on greenhouse gas accounting, monitoring, reporting and verification, carbon border adjustment requirements, and sustainability disclosure under the Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards, which are aligned with IFRS S1 and S2. The parties may also explore applying GORD digital solutions, including SustainoAI, for greenhouse gas accounting, ESG reporting and financed-emissions calculations, along with broader technical assistance on decarbonization and energy efficiency. Positions of the Signatories Dr. Alhorr commented that credible carbon markets depend on connecting high-integrity credits with transparent, well-functioning market infrastructure, and that the cooperation with EPIAS creates an opportunity to strengthen those connections in Turkiye while supporting the knowledge and institutional capacity markets need to grow responsibly. He indicated that a broader objective is to help climate projects attract investment, deliver measurable emissions reductions and contribute to sustainable economic development. Taha Meli Arvas commented that effective carbon markets require more than trading platforms, depending instead on reliable standards, transparent processes and participants with the knowledge and capacity to engage confidently. He said the cooperation with the GCC aims to explore new opportunities for carbon credit trading, strengthen technical expertise and support market development in line with Turkiye's regulatory priorities and evolving market needs. The agreement reflects a shared interest in strengthening Turkiye's carbon market ecosystem through internationally recognized standards, technical cooperation and the exchange of expertise. artigo.texto: Supported by Congress Looks to Charge Data Centers Billions in Sweeping Energy Plan The permitting bill could make it easier to build data centers for A.I. but a novel provision would also force data centers to pay much more for power. Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities. The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers. But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers. The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and triggering anger in many communities. Voters this month approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives to restrict the facilities. Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill have cast it as a boon to tech companies, arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of a many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing. By contrast, supporters have framed the bill as an opportunity to get tough on A.I. firms. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” said Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and a co-author of the bill. “Data centers now have to pay for the extra costs that they bring to the grid when they come online. They do not get to have all that extra cost dumped out onto the utility’s rate base and picked up by all of the other ratepayers.” Related Content Advertisement

artigo.texto: Washington communities push back against massive battery storage projects despite growing electricity demands Could a technology designed to prevent power shortages create new safety concerns for nearby neighborhoods? Communities across Washington are challenging proposals for large battery storage facilities, even as utilities seek additional electricity capacity to meet growing demand. The dispute has become especially visible in Snoqualmie, where residents oppose a proposed project near homes and recreational areas. Developers say large batteries are essential for modernizing the power grid, while opponents want stronger protections against fires and other potential hazards. Washington communities challenge battery storage developments Several Washington communities have adopted temporary restrictions on large battery energy storage systems, commonly called BESS. These facilities contain extensive banks of rechargeable batteries that store electricity and release it when demand increases or generation becomes less available. Snoqualmie, North Bend, Carnation, Duvall, and other communities have approved or considered moratoriums affecting commercial battery projects. Local officials say the restrictions provide time to examine potential risks and develop appropriate safety and land-use regulations. The measures do not necessarily represent permanent bans on battery storage technology. Many communities are instead seeking additional information about emergency response, construction requirements, environmental protection, and whether proposed facilities are appropriate for their intended locations. Snoqualmie residents oppose a proposed battery project A major dispute involves Jupiter Power's proposed Cascadia Ridge Resiliency Energy Storage project near Snoqualmie Ridge in King County. The planned facility would have approximately 130 megawatts of capacity and would be located outside Snoqualmie's city limits. Residents have raised concerns about the project's proximity to housing, a playground, a waterway, and an evacuation route. They argue that an industrial battery installation could pose risks that warrant closer examination before construction is approved. Snoqualmie Councilmember Dan Murphy has emphasized the importance of studying worst-case emergencies rather than relying exclusively on typical operating conditions. Local opposition has also reflected concerns about whether residents received sufficient information early in the development process. Why battery fires concern Washington residents Large lithium-ion battery systems can experience a dangerous process known as thermal runaway when individual cells overheat. The resulting chemical reaction can spread between battery components, creating intense heat, difficult firefighting conditions, and potentially hazardous smoke. A January 2025 fire at California's Moss Landing battery storage facility intensified concerns about industrial-scale installations. The incident burned for several days, and researchers detected battery-related metal deposits in nearby wetlands, raising questions about environmental contamination and emergency preparedness. Washington residents have pointed to incidents like Moss Landing when questioning proposed facilities near populated areas. Their concerns extend beyond flames to potential exposure to smoke, contaminated firefighting runoff, evacuation difficulties, and the resources available to local emergency responders. New battery technology has improved fire safety Energy storage developers argue that modern battery facilities differ considerably from earlier installations. Newer systems commonly use separated battery containers, monitoring equipment, and safety designs intended to prevent a malfunction from spreading throughout an entire facility. The research indicates that improvements in engineering, operating practices, and safety standards have reduced the likelihood of serious incidents and helped limit their consequences. However, a lower failure rate does not eliminate the possibility of accidents, leaving communities to determine what level of risk is acceptable. Snoqualmie Mayor Jim Mayhew expressed disappointment with that decision, warning that state review could reduce local control over decisions affecting residents. The city has indicated its intent to participate in the process and communicate community concerns. The change does not mean the battery project has received construction approval. Jupiter Power's published project documents indicate that its state application has not yet been filed. Once an application is submitted, state regulators will evaluate the proposal, and residents and local officials will have opportunities to submit comments and raise concerns during the review process. Those substations are frequently located near neighborhoods, public facilities, and other developed areas. artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign Thursday and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. artigo.texto: Pakistan’s next opportunity in battery technology may lie in a mineral we have known for centuries. At Khewra, visitors marvel at the pink salt that has become one of the country’s most recognisable natural products. Less celebrated is the fact that the same town has been home to an industrial soda ash plant since 1944. As Pakistan prepares to welcome investors to the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026, this combination of mineral wealth and chemical manufacturing raises an intriguing question: could our abundant salt help Pakistan enter the emerging sodium-ion battery industry? The idea is more credible than it might initially sound. Sodium-ion batteries are attracting increasing international attention as an alternative to conventional lithium-ion technologies. Sodium is widely available, and its use could help diversify battery supply chains that remain heavily dependent on a relatively small number of countries. Pakistan certainly has the raw material. According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, the country extracted approximately 2.9 million tonnes of rock salt during FY2024-25. Lucky Core Industries, meanwhile, reports an installed soda ash manufacturing capacity of 560,000 tonnes annually at Khewra. These are not insignificant foundations for a country hoping to develop new industries around its mineral resources. Rather than rushing towards large-scale manufacturing, Pakistan should begin with a focused programme linking chemical manufacturers, universities, battery researchers and energy companies. Yet there is a fundamental distinction that must not be overlooked. Having sodium is not the same as knowing how to manufacture a sodium-ion battery. Ordinary salt is sodium chloride. A rechargeable battery, however, requires carefully engineered electrode materials, specialised electrolytes and sophisticated manufacturing processes. Its performance depends not merely on the presence of sodium but on how effectively sodium ions move between the electrodes during thousands of charging and discharging cycles. The difference is considerable. A battery’s capacity, lifespan, charging performance and safety are influenced by the chemical composition and microscopic structure of its materials. Even small impurities can affect performance. The transformation from inexpensive industrial chemicals to reliable battery components therefore demands scientific expertise, precision manufacturing and rigorous quality control. This is where Pakistan must be careful not to mistake geological abundance for industrial competitiveness. China offers an instructive example. Companies such as CATL and BYD are investing heavily in sodium-ion technology, but their progress rests on decades of experience in battery research, materials processing, manufacturing equipment and supply-chain development. Their advantage is not simply access to raw materials; it is the ability to convert scientific advances into reliable products at competitive prices. The International Energy Agency’s February 2026 assessment puts the industry’s progress into perspective. Advanced sodium-ion cells can achieve energy densities of around 175 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with up to 205 Wh/kg for lithium iron phosphate batteries. Global sodium-ion production in 2025 was still less than one per cent of lithium-ion production. The technology is advancing, but established lithium iron phosphate batteries remain difficult to beat on cost, performance and manufacturing maturity. Moreover, China already dominates sodium-ion battery production and the supply of critical components. For Pakistan, this presents both a warning and an opportunity. Entering an emerging industry is attractive, but competing directly with established manufacturers without first developing the necessary expertise would be an expensive gamble. A more promising starting point may be the materials that go into these batteries. Pakistan’s existing chemical industry could investigate producing high-purity sodium compounds and cathode precursors. Khewra’s soda ash manufacturing experience is particularly relevant, although substantial additional processing and qualification would be necessary before any product could meet battery-grade specifications. There is another possibility that deserves attention: agricultural waste. Many sodium-ion batteries use a specialised anode material known as hard carbon. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries that commonly rely on graphite, sodium-ion technology can utilise carbon materials produced from various organic feedstocks. Pakistan generates substantial agricultural residues, including rice husks and sugarcane bagasse. With appropriate research and processing, some of these materials could potentially serve as feedstocks for hard-carbon anodes. This is an area where our universities and chemical-processing industries could make a meaningful contribution. The challenge would be to develop production methods that deliver the required electrochemical performance without making the final material prohibitively expensive. High energy consumption, inconsistent feedstock quality and impurities could otherwise undermine the economics. Such research is not merely theoretical. The United States Department of Energy has supported projects investigating alternative hard-carbon production processes and advanced sodium-based cathode manufacturing. This illustrates how countries seeking a place in emerging battery supply chains are investing in specific technological capabilities. Pakistan could adopt a similarly selective approach, concentrating on the parts of the industry where its existing resources and expertise offer a realistic advantage. The domestic energy market also merits consideration. Pakistan’s growing solar installations, telecommunications infrastructure and remote electricity systems create potential applications for stationary energy storage. In such installations, battery weight is often less important than

Set us as preferred There is only one place new data centers are being built in the greater Los Angeles area: the city of Vernon. Just south of downtown L.A., it’s a city made up almost exclusively of companies. About 50,000 people commute every day into Vernon to work, but only about 300 actually live there, and the city government is famous for its friendliness to heavy industry. Numerous surrounding jurisdictions have put moratoriums on data centers as a wave of furious opposition sweeps the nation. But Vernon has courted them, with one already operating and an additional five in the works. Yet even here, the anti-data center winds are starting to blow. Most development in Vernon is allowed “by right” as part of the city’s strategy to attract businesses. But at a council meeting last month, members took a step toward zoning changes that would make data centers one of the few industries to require environmental review. “We definitely need some regulations for the data centers,” Vernon Mayor Pro Tem Jesus Rivera said at the meeting. The first indication the city might be reconsidering its approach came last December when its public utility announced it would stop processing new requests from data centers to connect to its grid. The subsequent zoning review was prompted by community concerns about the demand data centers place on electric systems and water supplies, emissions and noise from their backup generators, and the relatively few permanent jobs they create, city staff said. “Even the Vernon employers, residents, businesses, those who work in Vernon,” are concerned, Chamber of Commerce president Marisa Olguin said at the meeting. “I think we should all do well to have more education and understanding about each development.” Data centers need to be up and running 99.99% of the time, so they require backup power, usually from diesel-burning generators that emit soot, harmful nitrogen oxide and carbon dioxide. The South Coast Air Quality Management District has already approved 52 diesel generators for three data centers within a four-block radius in Vernon. Air pollution rules allow the generators to run during grid emergencies, such as when blackouts are imminent, as well as 50 hours a year for testing. Boyle Heights and Southeast L.A. communities such as Maywood and Huntington Park have long fought against polluting industry in neighboring Vernon, most famously with the Exide lead-battery recycling plant, which they successfully shut down in 2015. But historically Vernon has seen very little opposition from within the city itself. The few people who live here are often employed by the city or live in city-owned housing. “It’s a company town in every sense of the word,” said Felipe Aguirre, director of Comité Pro Uno, an environmental justice nonprofit in Maywood. “People don’t want to say anything.” But data centers are changing that. The Los Angeles Unified School District, the second-largest in the country, has weighed in. It is fighting a data center planned for across the street from Vernon City Elementary School. Demolition at the site is already underway. The school district has repeatedly asked Vernon to block the construction of Texas-based Digital Realty’s 217,800-square foot project until it goes through a full environmental review, according to letters reviewed by The Times. “It’s about being informed about the potential impacts of a development near one of our schools,” Deputy Supt. Pedro Salcido said in an interview, citing a desire to know more about noise from the facility, pollution from any generators, and dust from demolition and construction. The authors of a UC Riverside report last year estimated that the health cost of running data center backup generators in California was approximately $33 million in 2023, about a third of that coming from the Los Angeles region. VCES, the only school in Vernon, sits at the loud and busy intersection of South Sante Fe Avenue and East Vernon Avenue surrounded by a paper mill, warehouses, cold storage facilities, manufacturing and other heavy industry. Its K-6 classrooms serve 144 students with special needs, most of them Latino. Just down the block, Prime Data Centers’ 242,500-square-foot facility has permits for 20 diesel generators and draws up to 49.5 megawatts, enough to serve more than 26,000 homes for a year. Vernon and Digital Realty say the new data center next to the school is permitted by right under city zoning, which means it doesn’t have to go through any formal environmental review process. In response to questions about the project’s backup generator plans, Digital Realty spokesperson Richard Hartnett said the company has “worked hard to communicate openly and transparently” with the city, the school and other community stakeholders “to understand concerns and identify opportunities to reduce potential impacts associated with construction activities.” City spokesperson Diana Figueroa said the developer has requested 49 megawatts of power. The other four centers being developed are an approximately 50-megawatt one by CoreSite Real Estate under construction a half mile from VCES at Vernon Avenue and Alameda Street, a 49-megawatt project planned by SCIND Fruitland Point LLC for its warehouse site at 2761 Fruitland Ave., and two large projects by Goodman Group by the L.A. River at Vernon Avenue and Soto Street. One of them, another nearly 50-megawatt project that appears to be almost complete, expects to start operation in February. The other, the massive 99-megawatt Goodman Energy Park, is planned for the site of the former Farmer John slaughterhouse and is seeking to exempt 40 diesel backup generators from the California Energy Commission’s regulations on small power plants, which would bring the city’s approved data center generator count to 92. “Vernon’s current approval process does not protect people’s health,”

artigo.texto: Chinese automaker BAIC’s electric vehicle brand Arcfox has launched two new battery-swappable models in China, expanding the technology into a more affordable segment of the market. The Beta S3 535 Ultra+ LiDAR Swappable Edition and Beta T1 Swappable Edition both use CATL’s Chocolate battery-swapping network, with prices starting at 52,000 yuan ($7,800) under a battery-leasing arrangement. The launch builds on a partnership between BAIC and CATL to develop a shared battery-swapping ecosystem. Both cars can swap depleted battery packs in about 99 seconds, allowing drivers to resume their journeys without waiting for conventional charging. Beta S3 gets LiDAR and 535-km range According to Car News China, the Beta S3 535 Ultra+ is a front-wheel-drive electric sedan powered by a permanent-magnet synchronous motor producing 159 kW (213 hp) and 250 Nm of torque. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (62 mph) in 7.1 seconds and has a top speed of 165 km/h (103 mph). Its battery delivers a claimed range of 535 km (332 miles) under China’s CLTC testing cycle. The vehicle also supports conventional fast charging. The new edition’s main technology highlight is its driver-assistance system. It combines a 192-line LiDAR sensor with Horizon Robotics’ Journey J6M computing chip to support highway and urban navigation assistance, as well as automated parking. More from Transportation See All Inside, the sedan features a 15.6-inch central touchscreen, an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8155 cockpit processor. Its starting price is 78,800 yuan ($11,800) with battery leasing. Beta T1 brings swapping to a lower price The smaller Beta T1 targets buyers looking for a more affordable electric car. It measures 4,337 mm (170.7 in) long, 1,860 mm (73.2 in) wide, and 1,572 mm (61.9 in) tall, with a 2,770-mm (109.1 in) wheelbase. Its electric motor produces 95 kW (127 hp), while its CATL-manufactured lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supports the swapping system. The car has a top speed of 150 km/h (93 mph), although Arcfox has not disclosed the range of this new edition. The T1 starts at 52,000 yuan ($7,800), with a higher trim priced at 60,000 yuan ($9,000), both under battery-leasing plans. CATL expands its battery-swapping network The two launches are part of CATL’s wider effort to make battery swapping available across multiple vehicle brands. BAIC, CATL, and service partner CAES signed a cooperation agreement in April 2026 covering compatible vehicle development and battery-swapping infrastructure. CATL reported that its Chocolate network had more than 1,470 stations across 99 Chinese cities at the time, with a target of exceeding 3,000 stations by the end of 2026. In October, BAIC and CATL also announced a broader partnership targeting one million battery-swapping vehicles. Under battery leasing, customers purchase the car without owning its battery outright, paying a recurring fee to use a pack maintained within the swapping network. For the new Arcfox models, monthly plans start at 399 yuan ($60) for a 5,000-km (about 6,200 miles) allowance, while unlimited monthly mileage costs 599 yuan ($90). Arcfox is also offering buyers 10,000 km (about 3,100 miles) of free battery-swapping mileage through 20 vouchers. The promotion applies to Beta S3 swapping-edition purchases made by January 31, 2027, and to Beta T1 customers. The challenge for the technology will be expanding station availability. A battery exchange that takes just 99 seconds is useful only when compatible infrastructure is accessible. By bringing more affordable vehicles into the same network, BAIC and CATL are betting that shared infrastructure can make battery swapping a more practical alternative to conventional EV charging.

artigo.texto: Industrial Manufacturing Norway Halts Data Center Projects as AI Booms Norway says stoppage is necessary to ensure 'proper operation' of the power system Released Monday, November 16, 2026 Written by Martin Lynch, European News Editor for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary As global AI data center growth accelerates, Norway has opted to press pause on related grid connection applications in an effort to regulate the kinds of data centers it wants built in the future. Stemming the AI Boom Norway's government has introduced a halt to grid connection applications for data center projects in an attempt to regulate the growing demands on its power grid. Statnett, the national grid operator, has introduced a "temporary suspension of further reservation of network capacity for data centers" and claimed the stoppage is necessary to ensure "proper operation" of the power system. It said it wants to ensure a "controlled growth of data centers in Norway and that they are as beneficial to society as possible". The government is now working on a number of measures and aims to introduce a licensing scheme for data centers in the coming year. The ban could stay in place until August 2027. According to Industrial Info Resources data, there are 74 active data center projects planned worth more than US$39 billion in investment. The Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Industrial Manufacturing Project Database offers a list of detailed project reports. The Government Take "We are facilitating more and faster development of power and networks, but it is neither desirable nor possible to develop enough to cover the power demand that comes from data centers that want to establish themselves in Norway," said Minister of Energy Terje Aasland. "We must have enough power in the right place for socially beneficial purposes. That is why we are taking action now." Torgeir Micaelsen, minister of digitalization and public administration, added: "Data centers are part of our critical infrastructure. They contribute to value creation, secure digital services and greater digital independence for Norway. But we have been clear that we do not want all types of data centers in Norway. We need those that contribute the most social benefit. Therefore, the government is starting work on a licensing scheme that will set requirements and conditions for the establishment and operation of data centers." The Problem According to Statnett, it has so far this year received applications for around 26,000 megawatts (MW) of new consumption in Norway, with data centers accounting for three quarters of those requests. Aasland said: "That's more than all of Norway's consumption today." Statnett said that today, data centers with a total power consumption of 800 MW have been connected to the grid, 4,200 MW have been reserved grid capacity and 9,100 MW are in the capacity queue. In addition, there are requests for connection of a further 18,000 MW. In comparison, the maximum power consumption in Norway is just over 25,000 MW. Norwegian data centers used 3.2 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity last year according to a report from Menon Economics last month. That's four times more than three years ago. Proposed Measures - Licensing: The first step the government will take is to introduce a licensing scheme for establishing and operating data centers in Norway. Micaelsen said that priority in licensing will be given to data centers serving defense, police, emergency response services, healthcare services and other critical infrastructure, including mobile networks and the financial system. Norway will restrict access to land and electricity for global cloud companies and cryptocurrency businesses. Data centers that conduct crypto business will not be considered socially beneficial, according to the government. - Digital security and preparedness: Requirements and conditions that support digital security and preparedness, as well as contribute to the necessary AI computing power in Norway, the Nordic region and Europe, will be considered. - Modernize the connection obligation: The government will modernize the regulations that oblige network companies to connect consumption to the electricity grid, so that it is better adapted to the actual situation where the grid queue far exceeds what is possible to handle. - Get more of the costs covered: The government wants large new power consumers to contribute more to covering the costs of developing a new grid and costs incurred in system operation. It is assessing whether a distinction can be made between new large consumption and large expansion of existing consumption. - New contributions to power production: The government will talk to the data center industry about how it can help build new power sources to deal with increased demand using gas-fired power plants with carbon capture and storage, and offshore wind. - Consider state ownership: The government will investigate different models for state ownership in data center projects of particular societal benefit. Unhappy Industry Reaction The Norwegian Data Center Industry (NDI) has reacted by claiming the move by the government and Statnett will create uncertainty for billions of dollars in investment. "Billions of kroner are invested every month in Norwegian data centers, with most of it going to the supplier industry," said NDI Chief Executive Officer Reynir Johannesson. "This is about construction workers, electricians and engineers all over the country. They deserve to know what rules apply in both the short and long term." He added: "The government uses the electricity queue as a justification, but does not launch a single measure that clears the queue. Poland cut its queue by 90% in a few months earlier this year by requiring applicants to put money on the table. It is unfortunate that the government chooses to go straight to a licensing scheme that will take years to introduce before you know how big the challenges really are. T

artigo.texto: KP Group has announced plans to establish a battery cell manufacturing facility with a capacity of 10 GWh, involving an investment of over Rs 50 billion. The first phase of the facility is expected to become operational by March 2028. Furthermore, the group plans to seek incentives under relevant government schemes to support the project's financial viability. It is working with three consultants to assess the applicable incentives and their role in achieving the targeted internal rate of return. Separately, it is exploring opportunities to expand its battery energy storage system (BESS) development business internationally, with a 5 GWh project pipeline in Botswana and plans to enter the European market after 2030. Other target markets include Zambia, Tanzania, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. In November 2026, KPI Green Energy Limited signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with SJVN Limited for a 300 MW inter-state transmission system (ISTS)-connected wind power project. The project has been awarded under SJVN's 600 MW ISTS-connected wind power projects (WIND-3) programme. Furthermore, under the PPA, a fixed tariff of Rs 3.64 per unit has been set for a tenure of 25 years.

artigo.texto: Na Cúpula do Clima das Nações Unidas COP31, em Antalya, Turquia, o Vietnã lançou oficialmente o portal público CarbonVN. Este evento marca um ponto de virada na infraestrutura digital, ajudando o mercado de carbono doméstico a acelerar a integração e a antecipar os fluxos globais de financiamento climático. Segundo informações do PNUD Vietnam, o portal de informações públicas CarbonVN foi desenvolvido sob os auspícios do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , implementado diretamente pelo Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas (DCC) com o apoio do PNUD. Esta plataforma permite que empresas, investidores, instituições financeiras e cidadãos acessem facilmente dados sobre cotas de emissão, créditos de carbono, listas de projetos registrados e políticas relacionadas. O Vietnã lançou o portal de informações públicas CarbonVN na COP31, fornecendo cotas de carbono transparentes e dados de mercado para investidores (Foto: PNUD Vietnã). Os sistemas de informação pública e os sistemas nacionais de registo constituem a infraestrutura digital essencial. Para os investidores financeiros, a transparência e a rastreabilidade dos dados são pré-requisitos para a avaliação de ativos e o investimento. Essa iniciativa coincide com o lançamento, pelo Vietnã, de uma plataforma piloto de negociação de carbono na Bolsa de Valores de Hanói (HNX), um passo rumo à meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050. A digitalização de todos os dados de transações e cotas ajuda a suprir a lacuna de informações, aumentando a confiança das instituições financeiras internacionais que buscam projetos de redução de emissões no Vietnã. A onda de conectividade global e a oportunidade para fluxos de investimento de bilhões de dólares. Paralelamente ao progresso do Vietnã, na COP31, a Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Comércio e Desenvolvimento (UNCTAD) lançou oficialmente a Rede Global do Mercado de Carbono. Essa iniciativa reúne importantes bolsas de valores, bancos e instituições financeiras internacionais, como a Climate Impact X ( Singapura ), a Bolsa de Valores da Indonésia, a Verra e o Conselho de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Financeiros de Hong Kong (China). Segundo a UNCTAD, os mecanismos de precificação de carbono estão se expandindo rapidamente em todo o mundo. Os sistemas de comércio de emissões (SCE) e os impostos sobre o carbono agora abrangem quase 30% das emissões globais, gerando mais de US$ 107 bilhões em receita pública até 2025. A maioria dos créditos de carbono voluntários gerados atualmente é fornecida por países em desenvolvimento a compradores em países desenvolvidos. Ao comentar sobre o papel do mercado, Nan Li Collins, Diretora de Investimento e Empreendedorismo da UNCTAD e Presidente da Iniciativa das Nações Unidas para Bolsas de Valores Sustentáveis, enfatizou que os mercados de carbono podem contribuir para a precificação das emissões e para a mobilização de financiamento para atividades de resposta às mudanças climáticas. No entanto, a eficácia do mercado depende de confiança, integridade e uma infraestrutura de mercado que funcione de forma eficiente. A rede da UNCTAD concentra-se na padronização de tecnologias digitais , medição e verificação para minimizar os custos de transações transfronteiriças. A sincronização da infraestrutura digital CarbonVN do Vietname com os padrões internacionais oferece aos projetos verdes nacionais uma oportunidade significativa de acesso a uma rede global de compradores. As instalações de produção industrial estão intensificando a redução de emissões para aproveitar as oportunidades do mercado internacional de créditos de carbono (Foto: MASI). Antecipando mecanismos internacionais e fluxos de financiamento verde. De acordo com o Relatório de Políticas sobre Precificação de Carbono, o quadro legal do Vietnã abriu importantes vias para atrair investimentos internacionais. O Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP estabeleceu três métodos para a transferência de resultados de redução de emissões para o exterior, em conformidade com o Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris e com padrões independentes. Em nível bilateral, o Vietnã assinou um acordo de implementação nos termos do Artigo 6.2 com Singapura e um Memorando de Cooperação sobre o Mecanismo Conjunto de Crédito (JCM) com o Japão, além de conduzir negociações com a Coreia do Sul e a Suíça . Esses acordos permitem a transferência dos resultados de redução de emissões licenciados e a implementação dos mecanismos de ajuste correspondentes. Juntamente com o mercado de crédito, os fluxos de crédito verde doméstico estão ganhando uma base mais sólida graças à Decisão 21/2025 sobre a lista de classificação verde, que inclui 45 tipos de projetos em 7 setores. Com a verificação transparente dos dados de emissões por meio do Portal CarbonVN, as empresas que reduzem efetivamente as emissões terão uma vantagem significativa no acesso a crédito verde e na emissão de títulos verdes. A infraestrutura transparente da CarbonVN, combinada com os mecanismos de cooperação internacional previstos no Artigo 6, está gradualmente transformando a redução de emissões em recursos financeiros concretos. Este é um pré-requisito fundamental para que o Vietnã avance para a fase operacional de um mercado formal de carbono com leilões até 2029, trazendo gradualmente capital verde global diretamente para projetos nacionais de transição energética e tecnologias de baixo carbono.

artigo.texto: A Moura, marca que os brasileiros conhecem das baterias de partida de carro, vai aplicar R$ 200 milhões numa operação que estoca eletricidade e a devolve ao sistema elétrico. O aporte, segundo a Exame, vai para o complexo industrial de Belo Jardim, no Agreste de Pernambuco. O investimento prepara a companhia para fornecer equipamentos aos projetos que disputarão o primeiro leilão brasileiro dedicado ao armazenamento de energia em baterias. A capacidade de fornecimento anunciada passa de 8 GWh em sistemas BESS, sigla em inglês de battery energy storage system. O equipamento carrega energia nas horas de sobra e devolve a eletricidade à rede quando o consumo aperta. Segundo a Exame, a chinesa CATL aporta a tecnologia, enquanto a Moura responde pela industrialização e pela integração local dos sistemas. No caso das baterias, a CATL assume a venda dos sistemas, por acumular experiência em disputas de leilões em diversos países, incluindo a América Latina. Os detalhes da sociedade foram dados por Spartacus Pedrosa, diretor de operações de lítio do grupo, segundo a Exame. A aliança com a CATL não começa agora e se estende a outras áreas, como a eletrificação de veículos. O investimento já está em execução e inclui obras, linha nova de produção, transferência de tecnologia e formação de profissionais. O valor inclui uma expansão recente da fábrica e um novo ciclo de ampliação, conforme o Movimento Econômico. A empresa, que atua há décadas com tecnologias de acumulação de energia, começou a desenvolver o BESS em meados da década de 2010. O primeiro sistema próprio, o Moura BESS, foi apresentado em 2019 e é produzido em Belo Jardim. O movimento abre uma nova frente para um grupo que registrou receita líquida de R$ 5,04 bilhões em 2025. A estratégia é levar o conhecimento acumulado em baterias para mercados que vão de pequenos negócios à infraestrutura elétrica nacional. Elisa Correia, diretora-presidente da Rede Moura, disse à Exame que a empresa cresceu em ritmo chinês nos últimos anos. Segundo ela, os negócios fora do segmento automotivo têm avançado mais rapidamente, enquanto a empresa já ocupa posição consolidada nas baterias para carros. Os dois falaram à Exame no Recife, durante o REC’n’Play, festival de tecnologia, inovação e negócios.

artigo.texto: HiTHIUM Partners with the University of Cambridge to Advance International Industry-Academia Collaboration in Long-Duration Energy Storage XIAMEN, China, Nov. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On November 12, the Global Energy Storage Colloquium was held in Xiamen. During the colloquium, HiTHIUM and the University of Cambridge signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU), establishing a strategic partnership. The two parties will collaborate on frontier scientific research, key technology innovation and industrial applications in battery energy storage, bringing academic research into closer alignment with industry needs and exploring new models for international industry-academia collaboration. The partnership aims to contribute to the advancement of global energy storage technology and the industry. The UK has a strong track record in the development of modern battery technologies and fundamental research. The University of Cambridge is one of the world's leading universities, with internationally recognized expertise in engineering, materials science and fundamental research. As a leading global energy storage technology company, HiTHIUM has long focused on energy storage technology development and commercialization. It continues to advance integrated research and innovation across the value chain, from high-capacity energy storage cells to long-duration energy storage systems and grid integration technologies. The collaboration is intended to bring internationally leading academic research into closer engagement with innovation across China's energy storage industry. The University of Cambridge's strengths in fundamental science, materials research and engineering will offer new perspectives and approaches to key scientific questions and emerging technologies in energy storage. HiTHIUM will bring its experience in long-duration energy storage (LDES), product development and large-scale deployment, connecting research with real industry needs and application scenarios, and supporting the engineering validation and commercialization of research outcomes. By drawing on the strengths of both research and industry, the partnership will strengthen the links between frontier innovation and practical applications. Under the cooperation plan, the two parties will establish joint management and research collaboration mechanisms, bringing together academic resources and corporate R&D capabilities. They will work together to plan research projects, facilitate scientific exchange and support the translation of research outcomes, strengthening connections between fundamental research, technology development and industrial applications so that innovation in energy storage can better serve industry needs. The partnership also marks an important step in HiTHIUM's efforts to expand its international innovation network. Building on this collaboration with the University of Cambridge, HiTHIUM will further strengthen academic exchanges and research partnerships with leading universities and research institutions around the world. By bringing together international research resources and talent, the company aims to encourage collaboration across disciplines and technology fields, explore the development of technologies such as LDES from a global perspective, and bring technical challenges and application needs from the front lines of industry into research and innovation. This will help research and industrial practice reinforce one another. SOURCE HiTHIUM

artigo.texto: NeoVolta, a U.S.-based energy technology company delivering scalable energy storage solutions, said its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power, has entered into a $116-million master purchase agreement with a leading energy solutions provider. Under the agreement announced November 13, NeoVolta Power will supply FEOC-compliant battery energy storage systems (BESS), with product deliveries scheduled for 2027. The agreement establishes a substantial base of contracted business, providing increased visibility into NeoVolta’s near-term manufacturing activity and supporting the company’s continued commercial expansion. The purchase orders would provide a substantial foundation for NeoVolta’s manufacturing ramp in Pendergrass, Georgia, supporting increased production volumes as the company expands its domestic energy storage operations. As demand for FEOC-compliant domestic supply chains continue to grow, NeoVolta believes its U.S. manufacturing capabilities position the company to play an increasingly important role in the rapidly expanding energy storage market. “Securing this $116-million agreement represents a major milestone for NeoVolta, and we believe this is only the beginning of a much larger growth trajectory for our company,” said Ardes Johnson, CEO of NeoVolta. “As we scale production in Georgia and fulfill these commitments, we are building the foundation for rapid, sustained growth while positioning NeoVolta to meet the accelerating demand for domestically manufactured battery energy storage systems and become one of the leading U.S. suppliers in the industry.” NeoVolta is an innovator in energy storage solutions dedicated to advancing reliable, high-performance power infrastructure for residential, commercial, and utility applications. With a focus on scalable technology, domestic manufacturing, and strategic partnerships, NeoVolta is positioned to support the accelerating transition toward resilient energy systems. —This content was contributed by the communications team for NeoVolta. artigo.texto: Regional carbon market leaders gather for the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) collaboration at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, with the Philippines joining as an Observer through Aboitiz Foundation, representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group. From left: Steven Marcelino, Deputy Chair for International Affairs, ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets; Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF Co-Chair and CEO of Climate Impact X; Dr. Renard Siew, President of the Malaysia Carbon Market Association; Khun Gloyta Nathalang, Chair of the Thailand Carbon Markets Club; and Faiha Azka Azzahira, Vice Head of Community Development, Indonesia Carbon Trade Association. The Philippines is strengthening its participation in Southeast Asia’s emerging carbon markets through private-sector engagement with the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), contributing to regional efforts to promote carbon market integrity, cooperation, and climate finance. Aboitiz Foundation, representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, is joining the ACCF as an Observer and participating in the signing of its Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The engagement provides an opportunity to bring Philippine perspectives and experience to regional discussions on carbon market standards, financing, and cross-border cooperation. It also highlights the growing role of Philippine private-sector initiatives in advancing forest restoration, nature-based climate solutions, and sustainable investment opportunities. The signing coincides with the renewal of the ACCF’s Memorandum of Collaboration for another two years, reaffirming regional commitments to developing connected, transparent, and high-integrity carbon markets across ASEAN. “ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz Chief Reputation and Sustainability Officer and President of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines’ participation builds on ongoing private-sector efforts to strengthen the country’s emerging carbon market ecosystem through industry collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and capacity building. Among these initiatives is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Complementing these efforts, both CarbonPH Coalition and NbS Group have a long-term nature-based solutions initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection, community development and recommended governance frameworks. These efforts highlight the Philippines’ potential to develop nature-based carbon projects that support environmental protection, attract climate financing, and create economic opportunities for local communities. They also provide practical experience that Philippine stakeholders can bring to regional discussions as ASEAN works toward a more connected and credible carbon market. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand, alongside the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to strengthen regional coordination and advance the development of high-integrity carbon markets. Under its 2026–2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure, and technical cooperation to support credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. This representation creates an avenue for Philippine private-sector stakeholders to contribute local perspectives, share practical experience, and learn from regional carbon market initiatives. For the Philippines, the engagement marks another opportunity to strengthen regional partnerships, support the development of credible carbon market mechanisms, and attract investment in climate solutions that benefit both the environment and local communities.As ASEAN advances cooperation on carbon markets, Philippine private-sector participation can help connect regional climate financing opportunities with local conservation efforts, sustainable livelihoods, and long-term environmental resilience.

artigo.texto: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark. Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW. The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes. “We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.” All about the all in one Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power. If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away. Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! artigo.texto: GCC e EXIST assinam acordo de cooperação para o mercado de carbono na COP31 O Global Carbon Council e a bolsa de energia da Turquia, Enerji Piyasalari Isletme A.S., conhecida internacionalmente como Energy Exchange Istanbul (EXIST), assinaram um Memorando de Entendimento para aprofundar a cooperação no desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e examinar a negociação de créditos de carbono emitidos pelo GCC na Turquia, segundo a QNA. O acordo foi assinado no Pavilhão Climático Árabe, organizado conjuntamente pelo GCC e pela Liga dos Estados Árabes, durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, em Antália, na Turquia. O memorando foi assinado pelo Dr. Yousef Alhorr, presidente fundador do GCC, e por Taha Meli Arvas, CEO e vice-presidente do Conselho de Administração da EPIAS. A cooperação tem como objetivo facilitar o uso do programa de certificação de carbono do GCC, reconhecido internacionalmente, na Turquia, abrir novos caminhos para que os participantes do mercado acessem créditos de carbono de alta integridade e reforçar a capacidade técnica à medida que o país constrói seu marco regulatório de mercado de carbono. Unir expertise em padrões à operação de mercados O arranjo combina a experiência do GCC em padrões de certificação de carbono, registro de projetos e emissão de créditos com a expertise da EPIAS na operação de mercados organizados de energia e ambientais. O objetivo é apoiar mecanismos de mercado transparentes que conectem projetos confiáveis de redução de emissões a compradores e investidores, contribuindo ao mesmo tempo para as estratégias climáticas corporativas e para os objetivos climáticos nacionais. Nos termos do memorando, as duas organizações vão explorar a listagem e a negociação dos Créditos de Carbono Aprovados do GCC nas plataformas de negociação da EPIAS, sujeitas às regulamentações e aos requisitos de mercado aplicáveis. Também vão examinar se os créditos poderiam ser reconhecidos no futuro marco regulatório de mercado de carbono regulado da Turquia. A cooperação proposta poderia ampliar o acesso ao mercado para desenvolvedores de projetos e compradores e incentivar o registro, a emissão e o uso de créditos de carbono de alta qualidade por meio de processos de negociação transparentes. Capacitação e apoio técnico Além da negociação, o acordo enfatiza a capacitação e o intercâmbio de conhecimento. O GCC e a EPIAS pretendem realizar workshops, webinars, seminários e outras atividades para melhorar a compreensão dos requisitos do mercado de carbono entre potenciais participantes e partes interessadas locais. O GCC também apoiará o acesso a informações disponíveis publicamente sobre seu programa de certificação, seu registro e suas metodologias. A cooperação poderá contar com a expertise da Gulf Organisation for Research and Development, organização-mãe do GCC, para apoiar a preparação do mercado e o desenvolvimento de capacidade técnica na Turquia. Entre as possíveis áreas de apoio estão o treinamento em contabilidade de gases de efeito estufa, monitoramento, relato e verificação, requisitos de ajuste de carbono na fronteira e divulgação de sustentabilidade segundo os Padrões Turcos de Relato de Sustentabilidade, alinhados às normas IFRS S1 e S2. As partes também poderão explorar a aplicação de soluções digitais da GORD, incluindo a SustainoAI, para contabilidade de gases de efeito estufa, relatos ESG e cálculos de emissões financiadas, além de assistência técnica mais ampla em descarbonização e eficiência energética. Posições dos signatários O Dr. Alhorr comentou que mercados de carbono confiáveis dependem da conexão entre créditos de alta integridade e uma infraestrutura de mercado transparente e bem estruturada, e que a cooperação com a EPIAS cria uma oportunidade de fortalecer essas conexões na Turquia, ao mesmo tempo que apoia o conhecimento e a capacidade institucional de que os mercados precisam para crescer de forma responsável. Ele indicou que um objetivo mais amplo é ajudar projetos climáticos a atrair investimentos, entregar reduções de emissões mensuráveis e contribuir para o desenvolvimento econômico sustentável. Taha Meli Arvas comentou que mercados de carbono eficazes exigem mais do que plataformas de negociação, dependendo, em vez disso, de padrões confiáveis, processos transparentes e participantes com conhecimento e capacidade para atuar com segurança. Ele afirmou que a cooperação com o GCC visa explorar novas oportunidades de negociação de créditos de carbono, fortalecer a expertise técnica e apoiar o desenvolvimento do mercado em linha com as prioridades regulatórias da Turquia e as necessidades cambiantes do mercado. O acordo reflete um interesse comum em fortalecer o ecossistema de mercado de carbono da Turquia por meio de padrões reconhecidos internacionalmente, cooperação técnica e intercâmbio de expertise. Ao combinar a certificação de carbono com a operação de mercados organizados, o GCC e a EPIAS buscam apoiar mecanismos de mercado confiáveis e acessíveis capazes de traduzir compromissos climáticos em resultados mensuráveis.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI – AI data center backup battery wins CES 2027 Innovation Award Samsung SDI’s space-saving UPS battery for AI data centers earned a 2027 CES Innovation Award for power, energy density and fire safety. Samsung SDI’s prismatic battery solution for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems won the 2027 CES Innovation Award for the world’s largest electronics trade show set to take place in Las Vegas in January. The Korean battery maker said Tuesday its SDI U8A3-UPS, an uninterruptible power supply that provides emergency power to critical facilities like AI data centers during blackouts, won in the enterprise tech category. The system was recognized for its very high power output, high energy density and fire safety, Samsung SDI said. It uses prismatic cells made with lithium manganese oxide, which makes it 33 percent more space-efficient than conventional products, so fewer units are needed to deliver stable power. It can also supply backup power during sudden surges in demand from AI computing, which helps prevent server failures and data loss. artigo.texto: O leilão de reserva de capacidade marcado para 2 e 4 de dezembro coloca a sobra de eletricidade renovável no centro de uma disputa comercial entre Tesla, Petrobras e fabricantes chineses. Em 2025, o Brasil cortou ao menos 20% da geração eólica e solar, segundo a S&P Global, em um corte forçado conhecido como curtailment, provocado por falta de demanda ou de linhas para escoar a produção. O mundo instalou 108 GW em baterias em 2025, alta de 40% sobre o ano anterior, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA). Esse avanço alimenta a corrida de grupos chineses contra Tesla e Petrobras num mercado estratégico para a transição elétrica da América do Sul. No Brasil, a matriz predominantemente hidráulica também conta com usinas reversíveis, que possuem dois reservatórios e cumprem papel semelhante ao de grandes baterias. O Ministério de Minas e Energia separou os certames: em 2 de dezembro, o leilão com exigência de conteúdo local; em 4 de dezembro, o aberto a todos os fornecedores. O relatório global do Schneider Electric Research Institute (SERI), “System Costs of Electricity: A new Baseline for the 21st Century Economy”, analisou 40.500 combinações de custos envolvendo geração solar, baterias e rede elétrica. A conclusão é que a integração entre painéis e armazenamento pode diminuir o gasto total do sistema em até 40% nos anos 2030, com os custos projetados, desde que a eletrificação da demanda avance junto, com data centers, veículos elétricos e bombas de calor. Quando a nova demanda ocupa a capacidade liberada pelas baterias, os custos fixos se dividem por um volume maior de energia vendida, derrubando o preço por megawatt-hora. Se oferta e consumo não crescerem em sintonia, os custos podem subir temporariamente antes de cair. O relatório ainda mostra que a duração dos equipamentos importa. Se os tempos de armazenamento empregados em diferentes ativos forem incompatíveis, o gasto total do sistema pode ficar até 35% acima do patamar atual. Tesla e BYD confirmaram interesse no leilão, que também terá Petrobras, Auren, Eneva e Weg, segundo o portal Zigg. Mais de 6 mil projetos foram cadastrados. No mercado brasileiro, a Voltxs aposta na locação de sistemas de armazenamento (BESS), em vez da venda, para reduzir o custo inicial das empresas. O modelo, segundo a empresa, permite adotar baterias sem grande desembolso inicial. Nos períodos de tarifa reduzida, o sistema guarda eletricidade e a entrega quando o preço aumenta, diminuindo a fatura de demanda contratada. Entre os clientes potenciais estão indústrias, data centers, shoppings, hospitais, aeroportos, agronegócio, mineração e centros logísticos. A disputa agendada para 2 e 4 de dezembro será o primeiro teste em escala nacional desse arranjo. O sucesso dependerá de alinhar oferta, consumo e financiamento, enquanto o setor acompanha se as baterias convertem o excedente em ativo econômico.

artigo.texto: Why Greenpeace Interrupted Jensen Huang’s Keynote Greenpeace used Huang’s Berlin keynote to spotlight Nvidia’s role in supply-chain emissions and data center growth – and to signal more protests ahead. Nvidia and the wider tech sector are currently confronting the so-called key-man risk long associated with Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday, Nov. 12. That dynamic was on display at Nvidia GTC Berlin, where then-CEO Huang delivered his usual one-person show, moving from high-level vision to technical deep dives. That changed midway through the presentation, when the keynote briefly became an unscripted Q&A session. At least two Greenpeace protesters unfurled a banner and projected a message onto the stage reading, “Clean Up Your Dirty Business.” They also shouted questions about Nvidia technology reportedly found in Russian drones, as well as the environmental effects of data center expansion. Huang remained calm during the interruption and asked security not to overreact as the protesters were escorted from the hall. “Everybody has a chance to say something,” Huang said. “I'll talk to you later. But let me get through my keynote.” Greenpeace later said it was behind the protest and posted a statement on its website. “While Nvidia is building an unchecked AI empire no one consented to, people are paying the price,” Benjamin Stephan, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in the statement. “Around the world, communities face damage to water supplies and soil, alongside rising electricity bills because of unchecked expansion of data centers.” For its part, Nvidia says it is focused on sustainable growth. In the company’s 2026 Sustainability Report, Huang wrote: “For the second consecutive year, Nvidia matched 100% of our global electricity consumption with clean energy. We continue to work to reduce emissions, improve efficiency across our operations, and design platforms like Vera Rubin so that powerful computing and sustainability advance together.” Arguably, Nvidia has more immediate concerns at the moment than scrutiny and potential direct action tied to its sustainability efforts. But its data center operator customers are facing more pressure than ever on issues such as environmental impact and water use. Why Nvidia Became a Protest Target Data Center Knowledge caught up with Greenpeace’s Stephan to learn more about the motivations behind the protest and whether further direct action targeting data centers and the wider tech sector is likely. The interview has been edited for length and clarity. Data Center Knowledge: What happened in the immediate aftermath of the protest? I was sitting a couple of rows behind and saw the activists being escorted out by security. Did Huang deliver on his promise to speak to the protesters after his keynote? Benjamin Stephan: They didn't get arrested. They were taken outside, banned from re-entering the building, and then they left. I personally waited outside for Jensen Huang to talk to him when he came out. Data Center Knowledge: So you put yourself in a position to have that follow-up discussion, but it sounds like Jensen did not follow through? Stephan: Yes. I waited for him outside by his car and let his security detail know that he had said onstage that he wanted to talk afterward. But they did not enable this; instead, they had his car drive off empty. Data Center Knowledge: Were you a coordinator of that particular direct action? It must have been hard to smuggle the banner past what I thought was very tight security. Stephan: No. Because I am based in Berlin, I was there as a spokesperson and Big Tech campaigner for Greenpeace International, seeking a direct conversation with Huang. This action was part of Greenpeace’s sustained effort to hold Nvidia accountable, involving several Greenpeace organizations. Previous actions included a five-layered cake topped with wind turbines that Greenpeace East Asia activists gave to Huang in Taipei. They used his metaphor [that AI is a five-layered cake] to illustrate the point that AI, in general, and Nvidia, in particular, are missing renewable energy. Confronted with the question, “Can you invest in renewable energy together with your suppliers in Taiwan?” Huang replied positively. We were in Berlin to hold him accountable, because nothing had happened yet. At Nvidia’s GTC Taipei conference, Greenpeace East Asia activists confronted Jensen Huang, calling on Nvidia to take responsibility for the growing energy demands and carbon emissions throughout its supply chain. (Image Credit: Greenpeace / Chong Kok Yew) Data Center Knowledge: What were you hoping to achieve at the GTC Berlin protest and in other actions at Nvidia events? Stephan: The goal was simple: let the public know and remind Jensen Huang that Nvidia needs to clean up its dirty business. That was the message on the banner and in the projection. Security cut the activists short when they started elaborating, but the criticism is twofold. First, Nvidia’s chips have reportedly been found in autonomous Russian drones deployed in Ukraine. That is unacceptable. The company needs to implement independent auditing across all global distributors, subsidiaries, and third-party vendors to guarantee that no Nvidia technology is used in ways that violate human rights or is diverted into military equipment or autonomous weapons. Second, Nvidia’s supply chain largely runs on fossil fuels, exacerbating the climate crisis. This also creates significant hardship for communities in Taiwan, where Nvidia relies on TSMC to manufacture its chips. All of this is happening even though it would only take a fraction of Nvidia’s gigantic profits to switch its supply chain to renewables.
