artigo.texto: S’pore steps up carbon market push forward with grants, new initiatives at COP31 ANTALYA, Turkey — Singapore’s push for carbon markets as a way for it to contribute to global climate action and channel funds into developing countries is gaining momentum, with a slew of initiatives announced at the UN climate conference COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya. The announcements, made over several days since the opening of the summit on Nov 9, include the disbursement of grant funding from the Singapore Government to two organisations to help establish carbon projects in South-east Asia. These projects – announced on Nov 12 – include ventures to protect forests and mangroves as sources of carbon credits. The set-up of a new Singapore office by a global carbon credit registry, Climate Action Reserve, was also announced on Nov 12. The environmental non-profit will help to ensure that carbon credit projects in the region are trustworthy and have a true positive impact on the climate. Two other initiatives were launched to ensure demand for carbon credits. On Nov 10, a new platform was launched to allow companies in Singapore to buy credits in a more straightforward manner, without having to build their own sourcing, contracting and settlement capabilities. The other initiative, which is supported by Enterprise Singapore, aims to aggregate demand among companies for carbon credits. The Action for a Resilient Climate Coalition said on Nov 12 that it aims to buy at least 10 million tonnes of carbon credits by 2030. It will issue its first call for proposals for one million tonnes of nature-based credits in the first half of 2027. One carbon credit represents one tonne of carbon dioxide that is either prevented from being released – by saving a forest from the axe, for example – or removed from the atmosphere, such as from a direct air capture plant. Large emitters, such as countries or companies, can buy these credits to offset their carbon footprint and meet their climate targets. Singapore has identified the growth of this sector as a driver of its green economy. But this has been hampered by allegations of fraud, where carbon projects do not actually result in true benefits to the climate. The recent announcements signal a step forward for Singapore to become a regional hub for high-integrity carbon markets, said Rueban Manokara, global lead of the carbon finance and markets taskforce at environmental group WWF. High-integrity carbon credits refer to those whose climate benefit can be trusted and verified. Manokara added that in South-east Asia, carbon markets have not reached their full potential. Funding is another obstacle. For instance, nature-based solution projects need upfront financing as such projects may not generate revenue until their first credits are issued, typically five to seven years after they begin, he added. The new initiatives could help close that gap, and funnel funds into the protection and restoration of nature, while supporting local communities, Manokara said. Frederick Teo, the chief executive of Temasek-backed investment firm GenZero added that the new initiatives can help develop the infrastructure and capabilities to attract investment and boost the supply of credits. “While the supply of Singapore-eligible credits will not increase overnight, these efforts… reflect the consistent, long-term approach that Singapore has taken to grow an important capability to address our decarbonisation challenges and to do so in an economically sustainable way,” he said. The global trade in carbon credits is provided for under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, the world’s climate pact that aims to limit global warming to 1.5 deg C above pre-industrial levels. Carbon markets can promote climate action as it allows countries to cooperate to achieve their climate targets. For instance, large emitters can buy carbon credits generated in other jurisdictions to meet their climate targets, instead of relying solely on efforts to cut emissions within their own borders. This is an important avenue for countries like Singapore to meet its climate targets, due to its lack of low-carbon energy alternatives that would enable it to reduce its emissions. At COP31, Singapore joined 13 other countries including Switzerland and Zambia in signing the Antalya Statement, which called for the need to grow high-integrity carbon credit markets to attract private investment. A policy playbook was launched alongside the statement with levers to guide governments to drive demand for such credits. For example, policymakers should set clear expectations for the use of carbon credits in corporate climate strategies. Another lever is to pool buyer demand through centralised platforms to reduce cost and risk. Developing carbon projects One of Singapore’s efforts to grow the carbon market is to increase the pipeline of projects. On Nov 12, Singapore’s Economic Development Board (EDB) announced that it will be providing grants to two organisations that could help in the development of carbon projects in the region. Swiss firm myclimate will from 2027 establish a presence in Singapore, and develop a dedicated local team of five specialists with the skills to develop carbon projects, in areas such as carbon accounting. Non-profit Conservation International will use the funds to develop nature-based carbon projects in South-east Asia. The grant, which EDB declined to reveal due to commercial sensitivities, will support the early development of projects that protect and restore carbon-rich ecosystems such as forests and mangroves in Asia-Pacific. These projects could be in the form of conserving and restoring forests in Philippines, Bhutan and Cambodia, although CI’s director for regulated natural climate solutions market Anirudh Krishnan said the projects have yet to be identified. artigo.texto: Fed alerta que a dívida dos data centers de IA pode superar a exposição dos balanços em uma desaceleração O Federal Reserve está acompanhando a alavancagem no boom acelerado de construção de data centers e alerta que inadimplências em uma desaceleração da inteligência artificial podem superar o que os balanços atuais sugerem, segundo um relatório de estabilidade financeira divulgado na sexta-feira pelo banco central. De acordo com o relatório do Federal Reserve, as hyperscalers inicialmente financiaram os data centers com recursos próprios, mas a emissão de dívida ultrapassou US$ 680 bilhões em outubro, um aumento de cinco vezes em relação aos US$ 130 bilhões de todo o ano de 2023. A composição desse endividamento também está mudando, passando de títulos corporativos em sua maioria para uma combinação de dívida pública e privada, além de crédito estruturado. Grandes empresas de tecnologia estão simultaneamente adicionando compromissos de arrendamento futuros, garantias de suporte concedidas a outras empresas e outras obrigações contingentes complexas em ritmo acelerado. O relatório descreve um padrão de financiamento circular que está se consolidando e o compara à crise financeira de 2008, quando a dívida se acumulava fora dos balanços das empresas. As evidências indicam que as empresas de IA podem enfrentar uma exposição econômica maior em uma desaceleração do que seus balanços atuais sugeririam. As hyperscalers frequentemente assinam arrendamentos de longo prazo para capacidade de data centers com desenvolvedores terceirizados, e esses desenvolvedores usam os arrendamentos para obter financiamento de construção. Separadamente, os fabricantes de unidades de processamento gráfico costumam garantir um valor residual para a garantia de GPU, a fim de apoiar a compra de seus chips por empresas de computação avançada e de modelos de linguagem de grande porte. Esses arranjos de dívida, que ligam hyperscalers e projetistas de GPU a empresas menores, são frequentemente combinados com investimentos em participação acionária das hyperscalers e dos projetistas de GPU, produzindo a dinâmica de financiamento circular. Esse padrão está estreitando os laços entre grandes hyperscalers e empresas menores e mais arriscadas, com menos acesso ao crédito. O Fed estima que os arrendamentos futuros e as garantias de suporte vinculados à construção de data centers somam agora cerca de US$ 3 trilhões. As saídas de caixa para despesas de capital sugerem que o atual ciclo de investimento pode em breve superar em velocidade o ciclo das telecomunicações da década de 1990. Ao mesmo tempo, as avaliações estão elevadas em todas as classes de ativos, incluindo ações, títulos corporativos e imóveis, e os fundos hedge carregam a maior alavancagem desde 2013, observou o relatório.

artigo.texto: SpaceX anuncia investimento de US$ 74 bilhões em data centers nos Estados Unidos | Vero NotíciasSpaceX anuncia investimento de US$ 74 bilhões em data centers nos Estados Unidos A SpaceX, empresa de Elon Musk, anunciou planos de investir US$ 74 bilhões (R$ 417,82 bilhões) na construção de complexos de data centers nos estados do Texas e do Arizona, nos Estados Unidos. No Texas, o projeto prevê investimento de US$ 24 bilhões em uma área próxima à base de lançamentos Starbase, com geração própria de energia. Já no Arizona, a empresa pretende aplicar US$ 50 bilhões em um empreendimento que poderá criar 5.500 empregos durante as obras e mil postos permanentes. A expansão ocorre após o crescimento dos negócios de fornecimento de capacidade computacional da SpaceX para empresas como Anthropic e Google. Segundo a companhia, sua divisão de inteligência artificial já representava mais da metade da receita em outubro. O secretário de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, Howard Lutnick, enfrenta críticas de integrantes do governo Trump por sua relação com Jensen Huang, ex-CEO da Nvidia, e pela demora em restringir exportações de chips avançados à China. Autoridades questionam a decisão de não incluir a empresa Megaspeed, suspeita de repassar tecnologia americana ao mercado chinês, em uma lista de restrições comerciais. Os Correios registraram prejuízo de R$ 1,9 bilhão no terceiro trimestre de 2026, alta de 19% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. Entre janeiro e setembro, as perdas acumuladas chegaram a R$ 7,48 bilhões, crescimento de 27%. A estatal atribui parte das dificuldades à queda nas receitas com encomendas e entregas internacionais, além do aumento de despesas judiciais e financeiras. O Brasil poderá receber até R$ 1 trilhão em investimentos em data centers até 2036, segundo estimativa da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). O crescimento é impulsionado pela inteligência artificial, por incentivos fiscais e pela oferta de energia renovável. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) projeta que o setor responderá por cerca de 3% do consumo nacional de eletricidade em 2036, aumentando a necessidade de fontes capazes de garantir fornecimento contínuo. Cinco economistas avaliam que o ajuste fiscal do governo Lula, voltado a alcançar superávit de 0,5% do PIB em 2027, é insuficiente para conter o crescimento da dívida pública, próxima de 83% do PIB. Entre as propostas estão mudanças na correção do salário mínimo, revisão dos pisos de gastos com saúde e educação e maior controle das despesas obrigatórias. As medidas buscam estabilizar a dívida e abrir espaço para a redução dos juros. O presidente do Federal Reserve de Kansas City, Jeff Schmid, afirmou neste domingo (15) que a inflação nos Estados Unidos permanece acima da meta de 2% e apresenta uma trajetória preocupante. Durante uma conferência no Havaí, Schmid destacou que o banco central possui instrumentos para controlar a alta dos preços, mas não defendeu explicitamente novos aumentos dos juros.

artigo.texto: As a developer works to ease intense public pushback to its potential data center in Cromwell, residents in a town 30 miles to the north are campaigning to block similar operations from even being proposed in their community. Even though no center is proposed there, the new Simsbury Citizens Against Datacenters organization — SCAD — is looking to change zoning regulations to ban data centers permanently in its town. “We want to take proactive, protective action to ensure the resources and the quality of life in our town are not threatened. I’d rather be ahead of the issue than behind it,” said Don Massey, a longtime resident and founder of the campaign. SCAD plans to present a citizen petition at the Zoning Commission’s meeting Monday evening calling for a zoning amendment to prohibit any new high-density data processing facilities anywhere in Simsbury. “The community initiative aims to protect Simsbury’s natural resources, water supply, residential neighborhoods, and electrical grid from the rapid, uncoordinated expansion of industrial-scale data center development across Connecticut,” according to a statement from SCAD. The group expects commissioners to scheduled a public hearing by mid-January. “Temporary moratoria are not the best way to deal with datacenter risk,” Massey said. “By filing a permanent prohibition text amendment, we put the decision directly where it belongs — in a public hearing where all Simsbury residents will have the right to be heard.” Beacon Falls and Trumbull are both engaged in public debates about data center planned for their towns, with some residents supporting the prospect of construction jobs and new tax revenue while others say they fear environmental damage, noise, a strain on water and power resources, and the advance of unwanted development. For many opponents, concerns about the extraordinary spread of artificial intelligence are also a factor. In Cromwell, there has been a wave of grassroots dissatisfaction with Long Island-based Global Common LLC’s plan for an enormous 300-megawatt center next to Watrous Park and the new middle school. After hearing parents’ concerns this week, the Board of Education on Thursday put out a statement calling for the local zoning board to carefully review any formal proposal. “We want to express concerns about the proposed data center,” the board said. “Any development located in close proximity to a school deserves careful consideration, particularly when questions remain about the potential environmental and health impacts and noise pollution, all of which may impact learning. “We recognize that there is more research to be done and that there are many unknowns about the impact of data centers on communities,” it continued. “However, we have heard significant concerns that the location of the proposed data center, in very close proximity to Cromwell Middle School and Woodside Intermediate School, may jeopardize students’ ability to learn in a peaceful and safe environment.” Also this week, numerous Cromwell homeowners reported on social media that Global Common is inviting townspeople to its roughly 160-acre site next Tuesday afternoon to hear details about its plan. Global Common did not respond Thursday to a request for confirmation of that plan. Mayor James Demetriades said Thursday that neither he nor the Town Council were invited to that session. Demetriades has repeatedly emphasized that Global Common has filed no formal request with the town to move forward. Demetriades plans to propose an ordinance to the town council Nov. 18 that would prohibit any local tax incentives for data centers in the future. He wants state lawmakers to repeal Public Act 21-1, which created the option for local communities to provide tax incentives for data centers. The law was written five years ago when the public and political consensus on data centers was favorable; it passed the state House and Senate with wide bipartisan support. But the mood about data centers and AI has turned negative in both liberal and conservative circles. The Planning and Zoning Commission on Dec. 3 will formally receive a proposal for a six-month moratorium on data centers, and will also receive a resident’s proposal to modify zoning regulations to become much more restrictive about the size, location and operations of any future data center. Opponents are posting social media messages urging residents to turn out on Dec. 3. However, all of the proposed measures would require public hearings followed by a vote and a brief period for appeals, so officials believe none could take effect before New Year’s at soonest. Global Common wants to build a 1.2 million-square-foot center on former Gardner’s Nurseries farmland along Geer Road, and has begun promoting a promise to reduce residents’ electricity bills if it’s allowed to go forward. The company argues that much of the opposition is based on wrong or insufficient information, and contends that its operation wouldn’t drain resources or damage the environment, but would produce a hefty tax revenue boost for Cromwell. “Unlike most data centers, it would generate its own power on-site with fuel cells instead of drawing from the local grid,” the company said this week in a Facebook post. “The proposal includes revenue for the town, lower electric bills for Cromwell households, and 20 acres donated to the town.”

artigo.texto: Waaree Energy Storage Solutions Private Limited, a subsidiary of Waaree Energies Limited, has successfully commissioned a new battery pack manufacturing line. The newly established facility, boasting an annual installed capacity of 5.15 GWh, is located at the company's factory in Rola, Valsad, Gujarat. The announcement was made on 14 November 2026, as per a regulatory filing with the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE). This move marks a significant milestone for Waaree Energies, positioning the company to enhance its capacity in the rapidly growing energy storage sector. The addition of this facility is expected to bolster the company's production capabilities and meet the rising demand for energy storage solutions. Waaree Energies Limited is known for its strong presence in the renewable energy sector, particularly in solar power. The expansion into battery manufacturing further diversifies its portfolio and aligns with the broader vision to support clean energy initiatives. The establishment of the manufacturing line at the Valsad facility could potentially lead to increased operational efficiency and expand Waaree's market reach. The move underscores Waaree's commitment to innovation and sustainability in energy storage technology, driving forward India's ambitions in renewable energy. Stakeholders and industry experts view this development as a strategic step that could have a positive impact on the company's growth trajectory. By expanding its manufacturing capabilities, Waaree Energies is poised to play a pivotal role in the evolution of energy storage infrastructure in India. More information regarding this development can be found on the company's official website, www.waaree.com. Disclaimer: This article is based on a regulatory filing submitted to the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE).

artigo.texto: Publicidade Com a vitória dos democratas nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos, o desenvolvimento das estruturas para inteligência artificial, em especial, os data centers, devem sofrer uma pausa nos estados. Estimativas da XP Investimentos calculam que essas pausas estaduais reduzam de 1% a 5% o capex de inteligência artificial das oito empresas que lideram a construção nos EUA. Segundo os analistas, esse efeito seria causado por atrasos e custos e não por algum movimento na demanda. Após as votações, 40 dos 41 plebiscitos locais realizados em dez estados durante as eleições de meio de mandato, terminaram com a rejeição popular aos projetos das big techs. No Texas, a pausa no estado já existe e deve durar cerca de 13 meses, até uma nova lei estadual passar a vigorar, a partir de agosto de 2027. Apesar de outros estados prometerem pausas parecidas, ainda não há decretos em vigor. Até 2027, não há expectativas de mudanças significativas na produção, uma vez que obras e encomendas já estão sendo executadas e parte da capacidade que atrasaria pode voltar em outros estados ou com geração própria nos próprios data centers. Já de e 2028 a 2030, os caminhos estaduais tiram de 1,2% a 4,9% do capex das empresas e de 4 a 15 GW de capacidade ligada em 2030. De acordo com a XP, o investimento soma US$ 5,1 trilhões neste período, com US$ 1,8 trilhão no último ano, no cenário base. Continua depois da publicidade Conforme os analistas, uma moratória federal, abordada pela casa como cenário de estresse/sensibilidade, mudaria drasticamente a escala, com um corte de cerca de 26% sobre o capex projetado. Impacto nas empresas De acordo com a XP, cada empresa deve sentir as mudanças com base no lugar onde constrói e a perda vai depender de quantos projetos elas têm nos estados com pausa. O grande desafio diz respeito à essas grandes estruturas e todo o sistema para colocá-las em operação. Segundo os analistas, gerar energia no próprio terreno seria a saída natural, mas turbinas e motores já estão vendidos por anos e não resolveriam completamente o problema. Continua depois da publicidade Entre as empresas, Alphabet está melhor posicionada, por ter um maior plano de investimento, afirmam os analistas. Atualmente, a companhia tem o maior plano de investimentos entre as principais empresas e é a que mais deixa de colocar capacidade em operação em números absolutos, com cerca de 2,3 GW a menos em 2030 no caso de vários estados. Por outro lado, SpaceX e CoreWeave perdem mais em proporção, por terem uma fatia maior da expansão nos estados com possibilidade de pausas. Pelo ROIC, métrica de retorno sobre o capital investido, os data centers que entram em operação em 2030 rendem 21,3% mesmo com custo alto, acima dos 15% que consideramos como retorno mínimo. Segundo os analistas, independente de moratórias, os retornos seguem acima da régua mínima de 15% porque a escassez ajuda a compensar. Continua depois da publicidade A XP reiterou a nossa preferência em nomes com menor impacto esperado em cenário de estresse de crédito, como Alphabet, Amazon e Microsoft.

artigo.texto: An energy flow simulation evaluating the German electricity system reveals that expanding wind and solar generating capacity cannot establish an autarkic, reliable electricity supply without deploying complementary battery and hydrogen storage infrastructures to offset production shortfalls during seasonal Dunkelflaute periods. The investigation, conducted by researchers Sönke Gößling and Florian Dennewitz using empirical hourly generation and demand records from 2023, assesses how a self-sufficient domestic network lacking inter-European electricity trade and devoid of conventional fossil or nuclear generators behaves under various renewable scale-up trajectories. Although renewable sources covered more than fifty percent of total German electricity production for the first time in 2023, severe meteorological fluctuations routinely created critical gaps between real-time production and consumption, which depressed spot market prices into negative values across 301 distinct hours and repeatedly forced conventional facilities to sustain grid stability during extended low-yield spans. To explore the fundamental systemic dynamics governing complete decarbonization, the researchers constructed an hourly energy flow model in MATLAB and Simulink, subsequently validating the computational dynamics through the Python-based open-source PyPSA power system architecture using the HighWays solver. The empirical input dataset was acquired from Agora Energiewende and incorporated full hourly time series spanning electricity demand alongside generation data from onshore wind, offshore wind, photovoltaic installations, biomass, and run-of-river hydropower across Germany. In the baseline operational dataset for 2023, maximum recorded peak outputs reached 44.09 gigawatts for solar systems and 50.09 gigawatts for combined wind installations, whereas biomass and run-of-river generation remained essentially invariant across the year. The mathematical model intentionally excluded cross-border trade, sector coupling, and conventional generation units to isolate how purely domestic renewable installations would interact with localized storage assets under strict self-sufficiency assumptions. Initial modeling examined a direct scaling of renewable installations, determining that in 2023 biomass and hydropower accounted for 12.1 percent of gross demand while existing wind and solar installations delivered 38.5 percent. Under the idealized scenario of matching annual gross consumption purely through renewable energy generation without storage, the mathematical formulation derived a scaling factor of 2.28 applied uniformly to installed wind and solar assets. However, running the simulation across the 8760 hourly increments of the year demonstrated that applying this 2.28 multiplier failed to alleviate supply deficits during periods characterized by minimal wind and solar activity, such as the extended winter stretch observed between January 18 and February 19. Even when testing hypothetical scaling factors ranging from 1 up to 20, the persistent residual demand could not be resolved during unfavorable meteorological conditions, as multiplying zero or near-zero production leaves massive deficits while creating extreme, unmanageable generation surpluses during midday summer intervals and windy year-end spans. Addressing the inherent mismatch between generation patterns and customer demand necessitated the numerical integration of storage assets into the primary energy flow system, beginning with a dedicated battery-only architecture. The authors modeled large-scale utility batteries operating at a round-trip efficiency of approximately 90 percent, established via symmetrical 95 percent charging and 95 percent discharging efficiencies while self-discharge losses were set aside. To satisfy total power demand continuously and guarantee that the final state of charge at year-end equaled initial storage reserves, the required renewable scaling factor increased from 2.28 to 2.34 to compensate for round-trip thermodynamic losses. Under this configuration, the required battery storage volume reached an unprecedented 22.35 terawatt-hours, with the operational state of charge collapsing from its full 22.35 terawatt-hour peak on January 17 down to 1.744 terawatt-hours by March 10, representing a single continuous seasonal drawdown of 20.61 terawatt-hours. A granular histogram evaluation tracking individual charge and discharge cycles throughout the simulated year illustrated distinct functional bifurcations in operational storage utilization across different seasonal timeframes. High-frequency cyclical demands requiring less than 600 gigawatt-hours occurred regularly between 20 and 100 times annually, primarily supporting rapid diurnal buffering during summer months when solar peaks charged batteries during daylight to discharge over nocturnal cycles. Conversely, massive multi-terawatt-hour discharge cycles exceeding 2.2 terawatt-hours took place only once per calendar year, with four of the seven largest prolonged drawdowns clustered exclusively within the winter span between January 17 and March 10. These empirical distributions confirmed that attempting to bridge deep seasonal winter deficits exclusively through battery cells would impose prohibitive capacity requirements for storage units that cycle only once annually, thereby establishing the technical rationale for integrating chemical energy storage. To establish a balanced, dual-tier technological configuration, the researchers bounded battery capacity at exactly 600 gigawatt-hours, a threshold derived from the empirical boundary of ten complete charging cycles annually. Within this hybrid configuration, the battery operates strictly as a short-term buffer, delivering peak charging and discharging outputs of 81.7 gigawatts and 52.6 gigawatts, corresponding to c-rates of 0.14 and 0.09 respectively. artigo.texto: Pesquisadores João Cassino e Uirá Porã debatem soberania digital em podcast do SINDPD-PE. Participantes de debate do Rec'n'Play falam de data centers por Otávio Gaudêncio Publicado em 13/11/2026, às 09h56 - Atualizado às 12h35 Os pesquisadores João Cassino (UFABC) e Uirá Porã debateram o desenvolvimento de data centers e a soberania digital do Brasil no podcast do SINDPD-PE, antes do painel realizado nesta sexta-feira (13) no REC'n'Play, na Cesar School. Segundo os especialistas, a falta de produção nacional de hardware e o armazenamento de dados públicos em servidores no exterior submetem informações do Estado brasileiro a leis e interesses políticos de empresas estrangeiras. João Cassino alertou que empresas norte-americanas compram prioridade na distribuição elétrica em cidades com parques eólicos no Nordeste, o que pode deixar municípios sem energia em momentos de alta demanda dos data centers. O pesquisador também apontou que o alto consumo de água para resfriar os equipamentos ameaça esgotar rios e alterar o microclima das regiões onde as estruturas funcionam. Uirá Porã criticou os projetos de hiperescala e defendeu o planejamento de data centers menores e distribuídos pelo território brasileiro para gerar mais empregos e reduzir danos ambientais. Palestrantes em painel do Rec'n Play nesta sexta-feira (13), o pesquisador do Laboratório de Tecnologias Livres da UFABC, João Cassino, e o especialista em Governança Colaborativa e Tecnologias Livres, Uirá Porã, discutiram o cenário de desenvolvimento de data centers no Brasil no podcast do SINDPD-PE. Para ambos, o Brasil cresceu na ala tecnológica por meio da capacitação de profissionais para trabalharem em áreas ligadas à computação. O avanço, porém, não rende quantidade de inovações satisfatórias para o setor no país, devido à falta de desenvolvimento nas áreas de hardwares. "A gente teria hoje capacidade e tem capacidade humana para poder desenvolver os próprios algoritmos e os próprios modelos de inteligência artificial. Mas aí, a gente, tem uma barreira muito grande que é de infraestrutura", afirma Uirá Porã. A falta de tecnologia própria na elaboração de hardwares, no entender de Porã, é um dos pontos que fazem com que o Brasil perca soberania no ambiente digital. "Mesmo você conseguindo ter instalado [datacenters] no país e que, por exemplo, rodem pelo menos softwares nossos [...] software que controla o data center, o conjunto maquinário ali, hoje ele é todo, por exemplo, quando você compra um data center da Google, ele é todo da Google", diz. Sobre esse cenário, João Cassino comenta sobre dados estatais brasileiros que ficam armazenados em equipamentos de nuvens em outros países. Para ele, a submissão dos data centers às leis estrangeiras enfraquece a soberania do país sul-americano na medida em que decisões do Estado não teriam necessariamente que ser acatadas pelos entes do outro país. "Essas empresas, elas não são neutras. Elas têm interesse comercial, elas têm interesse político, ela se posiciona politicamente", pontua o pesquisador, alertando para polêmicas relacionadas ao grupo Meta durante as eleições de 2026 no Brasil. Mesmo em um cenário com necessidade de data centers para garantia da soberania do Estado brasileiro no ambiente digital tecnológico, Cassino e Porã apontam para a importância dos cuidados necessários nas áreas de implantação do equipamento. Avaliando requisitos necessários para um ambiente favorável aos data centers, João Cassino destacou o potencial energético do Brasil, mas detalha que a capacidade das hidrelétricas e dos campos eólicos deve ser utilizada com prioridade para serviços essenciais das cidades. "Tem casos de grandes empresas norte-americanas que estão indo nas cidades do Nordeste, que tem parque eólico, e comprando a prioridade da distribuição de energia. Ou seja, se o data center demandar a energia e a cidade demanda a energia, eu transfiro a energia para o data center e deixa a cidade no escuro", detalha Cassino. Ele ainda fala sobre a necessidade de grandes volumes de água para resfriar os equipamentos dos datacenters. Segundo João Cassino, a prática pode causar esgotamento em rios e gerar mudança no microclima. Já Porã critica o modelo de data centers de hiperescala, questionando se o modelo popularizado pelo mercado é realmente o que gera mais empregos e que diminui o impacto ambiental. "Será que é um data center hiper de 50 bilhões é muitíssimo mais eficiente do que 50 data centers de 1 bilhão espalhados no Brasil [...] para mim hoje a a gente precisava pensar no Brasil um planejamento de infraestrutura de data center que fosse distribuído por território. Onde tem gente, eu preciso de data center", pontua.

artigo.texto: Singapore is stepping up carbon market cooperation with several countries at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, signing an implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation with Kenya and renewing a memorandum of understanding with Colombia on Monday (16 November). The signing ceremony took place at the Singapore Pavilion at the conference venue. Since signing its first memorandum of understanding on carbon credit trading in 2022, Singapore has established cooperation with more than 30 countries. According to a statement from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, the implementation agreement with Kenya establishes a legally binding bilateral mechanism for transferring high-quality carbon credits with corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Businesses are expected to be able to submit carbon credit projects for government authorisation from 2027. “Corresponding adjustments” refer to an accounting mechanism that ensures the same emissions reductions are not counted by both the buyer and the seller. This is Singapore’s 13th implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation, and its third with an African country, after Ghana and Rwanda. In her speech, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said: “We meet amid global headwinds, but Singapore remains steadfast in our commitment to climate action. No country can tackle climate change alone.” She said it was heartening for Singapore to work with like-minded countries, and praised Kenya for demonstrating considerable leadership in the green transition. In 2024, over 90% of Kenya's electricity was generated from renewable sources. In 2024, Kenyan projects accounted for about one fifth of voluntary carbon market revenues across Africa. Singapore and Kenya signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation in 2023. Typically, the two sides first sign a memorandum of understanding to set the direction for cooperation, before entering substantive negotiations and eventually signing a legally binding implementation agreement. Singapore and Kenya, both founding members of the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, have actively advocated the development of high-quality carbon markets. Fu noted that Singapore and Kenya have complementary strengths. Kenya is one of Africa’s most established carbon markets, with a clear legal framework in place, while Singapore is a financial and carbon services hub. Together, this can help credible projects in Kenya attract the investment they need. Expanding cooperation with Colombia This is Singapore’s second memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation with Colombia. The first memorandum, signed with the South American country in 2022, has expired. The new memorandum of understanding not only continues the partnership but also broadens its scope. It establishes a framework for dialogue, technical cooperation, exchanges of experience and the exploration of opportunities for cooperation in carbon markets and areas related to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Fu stressed that the two countries would work towards a legally binding implementation agreement that could take their cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to the next stage. “Colombia has tremendous potential for high-quality climate action – in its forests and natural ecosystems, in energy and industry, and in waste.” Besides its cooperation with Kenya and Colombia, Singapore also approved its first carbon credit project from Rwanda last Saturday (14 November) and signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon market cooperation with Bangladesh.

artigo.texto: BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya (UM) are taking their second-life EV battery initiative a step further. After rolling out a solar-powered mobile device charging station at UM Sentral in August, the collaboration has now deployed a larger Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) solution to power an Orang Asli village in Pahang. As part of the RE:GENERATE x Universiti Malaya initiative, the latest project uses retired BMW EV batteries and repurposed solar panels to provide 24-hour electricity to 20 households in the Semai Orang Asli community at Kampung Saweh, Pos Sinderut, Kuala Lipis. The new system not only reduces reliance on fuel-powered generators but also provides a practical example of how EV batteries can continue to serve a useful purpose beyond their automotive lifespan. From four hours of electricity to 24-hour power supply Prior to this, residents at Kampung Saweh relied on petrol and diesel generators, which typically operated for about four hours each night. Electricity usage was largely limited to basic needs such as lighting and fans, and each household were spending about RM10 per day on generator fuel. With the new solar-powered battery storage system, all 20 households now have access to electricity throughout the day and night, at a significantly lower operating cost. More importantly, the continuous power supply opens up possibilities for appliances such as refrigerators, which can make a practical difference to the community. According to BMW Group Malaysia, families who hunt or gather food previously had no reliable means of preserving perishable items such as meat. These items had to be consumed or shared with neighbours immediately to prevent spoilage. The system has been designed to support refrigerators as households acquire them. At the moment, televisions represent the highest individual electricity load in most homes. How does the second-life BMW EV battery system work? The energy storage system was developed by Associate Professor Dr. Tan Chia Kwang and his team of researchers and students at Universiti Malaya’s Power Energy Dedicated Advanced Centre (UMPEDAC). It consists of 30 repurposed BMW EV battery modules, supported by a combined 8kW of inverter power. The system supplies electricity to all 20 households from a single centralised point, with each household allocated 3kWh of energy per day. Instead of having separate battery storage systems for individual homes, the centralised setup allows available capacity to be shared between households based on their current demand. Besides reusing old EV batteries, the solution also utilises second-life solar panels that were retired early from commercial solar farms which still has considerable usable life. During the day, the solar panels charge the batteries, which store energy for use after sunset when household electricity demand is highest. The battery modules are housed in a structure built using wood and bamboo sourced from the surrounding environment. According to BMW Group Malaysia, the repurposed batteries are expected to serve the village for at least another five years under the current system design. This is comparable to or longer than the lifespan of new lead-acid batteries commonly used for rural electrification. The installation was carried out over five days from 23 to 27 October 2026, with the system going live during the team’s visit. Not all retired EV batteries are equal One of the challenges of repurposing EV batteries is that not every battery has the same remaining capacity or condition. According to Universiti Malaya, the research team has spent two years developing a methodology to evaluate and reconfigure used batteries for second-life applications. Each battery undergoes State of Health (SoH) testing at the cell level. Cells that have significantly degraded are removed, while those that meet the required performance thresholds are reassembled into new battery packs. The researchers found that newer-generation BMW batteries typically retain more usable energy, averaging 1.6kWh per pack, while older-generation batteries average around 0.5kWh. This allows the team to match battery packs to different applications based on their remaining capacity. Higher-capacity packs are used for more demanding applications such as rural electrification to power home appliances in off-grid villages. Meanwhile, lower-capacity packs can be used for simpler tasks such as charging smartphones. In August 2026, BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya deployed their first real-world installation under the partnership, a solar-powered smartphone charging station at the UM Sentral bus stop. The station uses three repurposed BMW battery modules with a combined capacity of 1.5kWh. These modules had retained just 30-40% of their original capacity, demonstrating that even heavily degraded EV batteries can still be useful for less demanding applications. BMW previously repurposed EV batteries for mobile EV charging This isn’t BMW Group Malaysia’s first attempt at giving retired EV batteries a second life. Back in May 2023, BMW Group Malaysia worked with EV Connection to introduce what it described as Malaysia’s first Mobile Charging Vehicle powered by repurposed BMW and MINI EV batteries. Unveiled at the Malaysia Autoshow 2023, the mobile charging solution uses 16 repurposed battery modules with approximately 70% State of Health. The latest rural electrification project builds on this concept by using retired EV batteries as a stationary energy storage solution for an off-grid community. According to Universiti Malaya, repurposing used EV batteries requires extensive testing, grading and modification due to differences in battery condition. The university also highlighted that the cost of supporting components remains substantial, despite receiving retired EV batteries from BMW and donated solar panels. artigo.texto: No Juspod, Ricardo Alpire e Tiago Trentinella explicam os desafios jurídicos, ambientais e de distribuição de energia para instalar grandes data centers no Brasil Data centers, ou centros de processamento de dados, são estruturas físicas que abrigam servidores e equipamentos de rede para processar, organizar e transmitir informações digitais. Eles são a base de sustentação da internet, de aplicativos, de serviços bancários online e de tecnologias de inteligência artificial. No último episódio do Juspod, podcast jurídico do Bahia Notícias, que foi ao ar nesta quinta-feira (12), os apresentadores Karina Calixto e Matheus Biset receberam Tiago Trentinella, especialista em Direito Ambiental, e Ricardo Alpire, especialista em regulação do setor elétrico, para uma conversa sobre o universo dos data centers. No debate, eles analisaram os impactos da inteligência artificial, o processamento de dados fora do país e os desafios de infraestrutura e energia elétrica. Segundo Tiago Trentinella, o Brasil enfrenta um cenário em que cerca de 60% da capacidade computacional nacional é processada no exterior. Ele explica que o governo busca incentivar a instalação de data centers no território brasileiro para aumentar a soberania de dados, fortalecer a segurança nacional e reduzir custos operacionais, que podem ser até 25% menores com a infraestrutura local. "A instalação de grandes data centers exige altos investimentos e recursos críticos, como energia elétrica, especialmente redes de distribuição e transmissão, e água para sistemas de resfriamento", explica Ricardo Alpire. O debate destaca que o Brasil vive um paradoxo: embora haja uma geração significativa de energia renovável, a infraestrutura de escoamento e distribuição ainda é precária. "Por mais que o Redata determine que o data center, para ter os incentivos fiscais, tenha fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, no fundo o Brasil tem uma carência não de fonte de energia, mas de acesso aos pontos de distribuição, e isso prejudica o escoamento da energia produzida", completa Alpire. Os convidados também discutiram o papel das normas ambientais e da regulação. Trentinella ressalta a importância do licenciamento ambiental e do princípio da precaução na escolha das localizações, enquanto Alpire defende o potencial dos Edge Data Centers — centros menores, distribuídos estrategicamente — como solução para interiorizar a modernização e o desenvolvimento tecnológico dos municípios brasileiros, sem causar os impactos severos de grandes estruturas concentradas. CONVIDADO Tiago Trentinella é PhD. Professor. Advogado. Especialista em Direito Ambiental pela Faculdade de Saúde Pública, USP (2005). Mestre (2012) e Doutor (2016) em Direito pela Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Osaka, Japão. Pesquisador (2014 – 2019) e professor assistente (2017) na Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Osaka, Japão. Professor Visitante na Faculdade de Direito de Ribeirão Preto, USP (2017). Professor, pós-graduado em Direito Ambiental e Urbanístico pela Faculdade de Direito de Ribeirão Preto, USP (2022-2024). Professor de Direito Ambiental na Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Mogi das Cruzes (2024). Autor de artigos científicos publicados internacionalmente. Ricardo Alpire é advogado. Especialista em Direito Empresarial pela Fundação de Comércio Alvares Penteado – 2005. Autor de artigos jurídicos na área de regulação de energia elétrica. Especialista em Mercado Regulado de Energia Elétrica desde 2008. Consultor da Associação de Dirigentes do Mercado Imobiliário – ADEMI - BA em regulação de energia elétrica. Atuação no mercado imobiliário com foco em conexão de unidades imobiliárias à rede de distribuição de energia. APRESENTADORES Liderado por Karina Calixto e Matheus Biset, o JusPod - podcast jurídico do Bahia Notícias - vai ao ar quizenalmente, sempre às 19h, às quintas-feiras. Todos os episódios estão disponíveis no canal do YouTube do Bahia Notícias. Apresentadora do JusPod - Podcast Jurídico do Bahia Notícias - desde a sua criação, em 2023, Karina Calixto é advogada. Mestranda em Direito pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Ensino, Desenvolvimento e Pesquisa - IDP, é Especialista em Ciências Criminais pela Faculdade Baiana de Direito; Professora da Fundação Visconde de Cairú (BA); Conselheira Seccional da OAB-BA; e Presidente da Comissão de Estágio e Exame de Ordem da OAB-BA. Já o co-host é o advogado Matheus Biset, sócio do escritório Matheus Biset Advocacia. Pós-graduado em Ciências Criminais pela Universidade Cândido Mendes – UCAM/RJ); Pós-graduado em Direito Penal Econômico pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais – PUC/MG; e Pós-graduando em Direito Esportivo pela Confederação Brasileira de Futebol (CBF). Membro do Instituto Baiano de Direito Processual Penal (IBADPP), é Professor de Ética, Direito Processual Penal e Prática Penal. Também é palestrante e autor do livro "Ética para OAB - Somente o Necessário para Gabaritar".

Data centers and artificial intelligence had a “huge impact, huge impact,” state Rep.-elect Ryan Kominakis, D-Valparaiso, said. More than 500 state legislative seats were flipped nationwide, he said. “I’ve been in this for a while, and I’ve never seen anything like this ever,” state Rep. Chuck Moseley, D-Portage, said. “I find it hard to believe that that many people could be wrong,” his wife told him. Utilities and data centers were the main topic that came up when Kominakis was knocking on doors in his campaign to unseat incumbent Republican Ed Soliday. “A lot of people are frustrated with the data centers,” Kominakis said, with voters citing the one that had been proposed near Wheeler High School in Union Township and another whether Valparaiso had initially proposed a sports complex. “All these horror stories,” he said, and no regulations made voters wary. Adding to that is the $655 million and counting in tax revenue loss from state economic development giveaways to data center developers. “We’ve got to repeal that law or at bare minimum amend it,” Kominakis said. He has a Dec. 11 deadline to give the Legislative Services Agency, which drafts legislation, his proposal to repeal those tax breaks, require project labor agreements for union wages for data centers that receive scaled-back tax breaks, limit their locations so they can’t be near schools or neighborhoods, and require environmental protection. Kominakis, a Democrat, plans to seek his caucus leadership for advice on the direction his legislation takes. “I want to make sure we’re doing the right thing, making the correct strategic moves,” he said. He credits his Nov. 3 victory to Republicans staying home or switching sides as well as Democrats showing up. “Voters talked about it at the door. Not every door I knocked talked about data centers, but some did,” Moseley said. The Democratic incumbent won re-election. artigo.texto: A multi-metallic oxide composite synthesized from nickel cobalt bimetallic oxide and magnesium-copper oxide has demonstrated high electrochemical activity for both water oxidation and asymmetric supercapacitor energy storage in alkaline environments. Synthesized as NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO, the material addresses limitations in the chemical fabrication of multi-metallic oxides for water electrolysis while leveraging the versatile redox properties recognized in transition metal oxides containing nickel and cobalt. The research team developed the composite using a chemical synthesis strategy combined with a modified hydrothermal process. This fabrication method utilized phytochemicals derived from lemon peel extract to facilitate the in situ growth of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite directly onto a nickel foam substrate, creating an integrated electrode structure intended for oxygen evolution reaction half-cell water splitting and asymmetric supercapacitor devices. The introduction of multi-metallic ions into the composite architecture induced electronic disorder and surface defects throughout the material. According to the study, the resulting presence of oxygen surface vacancies alongside trivalent cobalt (Co3+) and trivalent nickel (Ni3+) species contributed significantly to the material’s electrochemical performance and reaction kinetics in alkaline media. Structural validation of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite was carried out using multiple complementary characterization techniques. The researchers employed scanning electron microscopy, powder X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, which together confirmed the multi-metal oxide composition and the tailor-made structural features of the synthesized electrode material. When evaluated for the oxygen evolution reaction in a 1 M potassium hydroxide electrolyte, the composite exhibited a low overpotential of 370 millivolts at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimeter. In addition to its catalytic efficiency during water oxidation testing, the electrode demonstrated operational durability by sustaining the same catalytic function over 40 continuous hours under alkaline conditions. In asymmetric supercapacitor testing conducted in 3 M potassium hydroxide, the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite delivered a specific capacitance of 551.73 farads per gram. The assembled device attained an energy density of 193.97 watt-hours per kilogram at an applied current density of 1 ampere per gram, while exhibiting high cycling stability by retaining 96.9 percent of its original capacitance after 40,000 galvanic charge-discharge cycles. artigo.texto: How AI Is Rewriting the Rules of Data Center Cooling AI and high-performance workloads are forcing operators to rethink how data centers are powered, cooled, and scaled. Cooling, in particular, presents challenges as AI workload generate more heat than air cooling alone can efficiently support. As a result, hybrid architectures — that include both air and liquid cooling — are increasingly being adopted. Why AI is Forcing a Rethink of Data Center Cooling Design, a new special report featuring Trane, examines the technologies, design strategies, and operational realities shaping AI-ready infrastructure, including Trane’s role in helping operators integrate air, chilled-water, and liquid cooling strategies in practical, scalable ways. Check out our recent article series focused on the special report: The AI Cooling Inflection Point: AI-era cooling is not just about moving more air. It is about building a balanced thermal strategy that supports density, reliability, and long-term scalability. This article explores why airflow management is becoming increasingly important in supporting higher-density AI and HPC workloads. Cooling at the Edge of Capability: Liquid cooling is not a single design choice. It is a family of approaches that must be aligned to workload requirements, facility constraints, service models, and long-term growth plans. This article examines how many operators are augmenting proven air-cooling foundations with additional thermal management approaches to improve precision, efficiency, and scalability. Designing Cooling for the AI Data Center: Designing for AI ultimately requires a shift in mindset. Cooling must be engineered as an integrated system that supports both current workloads and future growth while remaining operationally practical at scale. This article outlines key design implications when integrating liquid cooling into a broader, resilient, hybrid operating model. Designing for Greenfield, Brownfield, and Operational Reality: As workloads intensify, cooling is evolving from a supporting utility into a more engineered, workload-aware system. This article outlines practical strategies when designing for greenfield, brownfield and operational realities. Download the full report, Why AI is Forcing a Rethink of Data Center Cooling Design, featuring Trane, to learn more. About the Author Kathy Hitchens Kathy Hitchens has been writing professionally for more than 30 years. She focuses on the renewable energy, electric vehicle, utility, data center, and financial services sectors. Kathy has a BFA from the University of Arizona and a MBA from the University of Denver.

artigo.texto: Expansão dos data centers deve diminuir após resultado das midterms Democratas no Congresso ameaçam impor moratória sobre novos data centers de IA; medida pode impactar mercado e demais setores de tecnologia A rápida expansão dos data centers de inteligência artificial se tornou uma das questões centrais nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos. Campanhas populares surgiram em diversas comunidades ao longo do país, levantando preocupações sobre os impactos locais desses grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos. Durante o programa "Resenha do Dinheiro", os apresentadores destacaram que os democratas se posicionam contrariamente à expansão acelerada dos data centers. Entre as principais preocupações levantadas estão o elevado consumo de energia, o encarecimento das tarifas energéticas para a população local, a poluição sonora e a desvalorização imobiliária nas regiões onde essas estruturas são instaladas. Alguns governadores chegaram a sinalizar a intenção de limitar o número de novas instalações por meio de moratórias. Elizabeth Warren, senadora dos Estados Unidos, declarou que pretende implementar uma moratória sobre os data centers como medida prioritária. Essa postura foi interpretada pelo mercado financeiro como um sinal negativo para as empresas de tecnologia e de IA. "É um baque e isso terá uma forte queda nos resultados da Nasdaq", ressalta Bernardo Pascowitch, apresentador do Resenha do Dinheiro. Impactos para mercado O cenário gerado pelas eleições também trouxe reflexões sobre os efeitos no câmbio. Thiago Godoy, educador financeiro, aponta que, caso os juros nos Estados Unidos recuem, a atratividade do dólar como investimento diminuiria, o que poderia representar um fator positivo para o Brasil, com a valorização do real. "Porém, esse movimento depende somente da condução política fiscal americana, de como o Fed vai reagir nas próximas reuniões", pondera Godoy. Além disso, a desaceleração dos investimentos em data centers e IA pode representar o início da bolha no setor. Marilia Fontes, sócia-fundadora da Nord Investimentos avalia que esse processo já havia sido iniciado com o aumento da taxa de juros nos Estados Unidos e que a renda fixa americana, com taxas próximas a 5% no longo prazo, se torna um investimento extremamente atrativo em comparação com ações de tecnologia. "Com o cenário de atratividade um pouco menor por conta do capex em investimentos em data centers, a renda fixa passa a ser um baita investimento. Os EUA estão na vanguarda do crescimento da tecnologia, com o PIB resiliente mas a taxa de juros e os treasuries estão ganhando cada vez mais atratividade", afirma Fontes. Resenha do Dinheiro O programa é apresentado por Marilia Fontes, sócia-fundadora da Nord Investimentos, Bernardo Pascowitch, fundador e CEO do Yubb e Thiago Godoy, o “Papai Financeiro”; e propõe uma abordagem leve, direta e descomplicada sobre temas ligados à educação financeira e investimentos. A atração aborda semanalmente os principais temas da economia com a informalidade de uma conversa entre amigos — sem abrir mão da análise. O Resenha do Dinheiro vai ao ar todas as sextas-feiras, às 19h, no canal do CNN Money no YouTube e aos domingos, às 15h, na CNN Brasil.

artigo.texto: Trending SNOQUALMIE, Wash. -- In the race to meet the nation's growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new "battery farms" that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it's projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger -- along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers -- could threaten an industry that's becoming integral to the nation's energy future. 'Meteoric growth' Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion -- a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. "The meteoric growth is continuing," said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. "For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential." Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours -- but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it's needed, instead of firing up more costly "peaker" gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. "As we're dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we've already paid for," Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry's growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. "It's basically a no-regret path," Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. "Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there's battery storage." Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they've met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. "They're making us collateral damage," said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. "We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we're going to do in our backyard." The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. Indust

artigo.texto: A aprovação do projeto de lei (PL) nº 3.716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos de contratação de baterias como reserva de capacidade, pode ser viabilizada com a manutenção do foco na proposta original, sem a inclusão de outros temas do setor elétrico. A avaliação é do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania – SP), autor do PL. O texto tramita na Câmara sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), que pretende incorporar questões adicionais ao projeto, como adicionalidade, ressarcimento do curtailment e retorno do desconto pelo uso da rede. Jardim diz que trabalha para convencer o relator a restringir o alcance do texto, pois entende que a ampliação pode dificultar a construção de apoio político para a votação. “Em vez de você agregar apoio, você torna mais complexa a decisão”, afirmou Jardim nesta sexta-feira, 13 de novembro, durante a Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia (Coniben) 2026, em Lisboa, Portugal. Assim, a estratégia do autor do PL é buscar uma sinalização favorável do governo e concentrar a negociação na alteração do rateio dos custos das baterias, atualmente atribuídos aos agentes de geração. Arnaldo Jardim afirmou que, caso não seja possível chegar a um entendimento sobre as mudanças pretendidas pelo relator, poderá apoiar a aprovação do projeto original. Ele acredita ter maioria para essa aprovação. O PL está pronto para inclusão na pauta do Plenário da Câmara, após entrar em regime de urgência, o que liberou a discussão da matéria pelas comissões. Leilões estão marcados para início de dezembro As discussões ocorrem a menos de um mês da data marcada para a realização dos leilões de bateria, agendados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. O diretor-geral da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), Sandoval Feitosa, já declarou que, caso a legislação seja modificada antes dos certames, será necessário republicar os editais e remarcar as sessões públicas. Se confirmada, esta situação deve inviabilizar a realização dos certames ainda em 2026, já que a Aneel trabalha com prazo mínimo de 30 dias entre a publicação dos editais e a realização dos leilões. Em paralelo aos editais, a Aneel conduz outro processo para regulamentar o rateio do encargo entre os geradores. A incerteza regulatória sobre as regras tem deixado até mesmo empreendedores que cadastraram projetos no leilão em compasso de espera sobre participar ou não do certame. O que pode mudar no rateio das baterias Apresentado em julho, o PL 3.716/2026 revoga um dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que estabeleceu o rateio dos custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade com baterias exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Aneel. Assim, se o projeto de lei for aprovado, as baterias passarão a seguir a regra geral de rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade, com cobrança dos consumidores de energia elétrica. Associações ligadas à geração hídrica, eólica e solar, junto a entidades que representam o setor de baterias e hidrogênio verde, manifestaram apoio ao PL. As associações afirmam que os custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias serão repassados aos consumidores de qualquer forma, mesmo que a cobrança seja concentrada nos agentes de geração.

artigo.texto: Masdar has completed its $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California as the Abu Dhabi clean energy company continues to expand its renewable energy portfolio in the US. With 365 megawatts of solar generation and 173.7MW of battery storage, the project can produce electricity to meet the annual needs of about 350,000 homes and businesses, Masdar said on Friday. The project was developed by Terra-Gen, which is owned jointly by Masdar and Igneo Infrastructure Partners. It has offtake agreements with corporate buyers and long-term power purchase agreements with California load-serving entities to help meet their energy needs. “We are delivering reliable, affordable power, creating skilled jobs and supporting economic growth,” said Khaleefa Almheiri, president and chief executive of Masdar Americas. Engineering and construction of the complex is expected to generate more than 1,000 on-site jobs. The plant is also expected to generate more than $40 million in property tax revenue over its operating life, along with additional contributions and benefits to the local community. “As electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI, advanced manufacturing and wider economic growth, Masdar is proud to be a long-term partner in powering America’s future,” Mr Almheiri said. There has been a growing demand for power from the US and other countries amid the AI-driven data centre boom. “Solar is one of the most economical sources of new electricity and storage extends its value by making that energy available when it’s needed most,” said John O’Connor, chief executive at Terra-Gen. Masdar has invested about $3 billion in the US and plans to invest a further $20 billion over the next decade, with an ambition to grow its US portfolio to up to 25GW by 2030. Owned jointly by Abu Dhabi's Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, Masdar is targeting a portfolio capacity of 100GW by 2030 as it continues to develop new renewable projects globally.

artigo.texto: Carregamento bidirecional: Audi A2 e-tron como sistema de armazenamento de energia móvel A bateria de alta tensão de um carro elétrico não só fornece energia para a condução, como também pode ser utilizada especificamente como fonte de energia fora de estrada. Com funções de carregamento bidirecional, o Audi A2 e-tron permite o fornecimento de energia a dispositivos externos através da tecnologia Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) e a utilização da energia armazenada em casa através da tecnologia Vehicle-to-Home (V2H). autonews.pt @ 13-11-2026 12:46:06 No futuro, será adicionada a tecnologia Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) para injetar energia de volta na rede elétrica pública. Sistema de baterias com gestão térmica e eletrónica de carregamento coordenadas Com o A2 e-tron, a Audi oferece pela primeira vez um modelo totalmente elétrico de entrada na classe compacta. Dependendo da versão, são utilizados diferentes sistemas de armazenamento de energia: uma bateria de níquel-manganês-cobalto de 84 kWh ou uma bateria de fosfato de ferro-lítio (LFP) com capacidade de 52 ou 61 kWh. Nos sistemas de armazenamento LFP, as células são integradas diretamente na bateria, num design célula-para-pacote. Devido à maior densidade de empacotamento possibilitada por este design, o conteúdo energético e a densidade de energia do sistema de alta tensão podem ser aumentados com uma menor necessidade de espaço. Foco na gestão térmica e na eficiência de carregamento A estratégia de temperatura e arrefecimento da bateria de alta tensão foi uma área central de desenvolvimento do A2 e-tron. O sistema de gestão térmica coordena continuamente a temperatura da bateria, o fluxo de corrente e o estado de carga durante os processos de carga e descarga. A estratégia de controlo foi concebida para operar a bateria dentro de intervalos de temperatura definidos e permitir um comportamento de carregamento reprodutível. Um controlo de temperatura mais preciso durante a carga e a descarga contribui significativamente para um comportamento mais estável da bateria. Para os clientes, isto significa não só um tempo de carregamento curto no dia a dia, mas também um comportamento de carga e descarga estável, compreensível e reprodutível. A bateria do A2 e-tron não foi apenas concebida para um pico de potência a curto prazo. O foco para o uso diário está num processo de carregamento planeável, controlado e prático. Para tal, é utilizado um componente avançado que combina carregadores de bordo e conversores CC/CC, o chamado OCDC 2.0. Inclui um maior número de transístores de efeito de campo metal-óxido-semicondutor (MOSFETs), gestão de saída CA adaptada e ajustes de software correspondentes. Gestão da bateria Um controlador de gestão da bateria assume a monitorização e a regulação da bateria. Nas baterias LFP, em particular, uma curva característica de tensão de circuito aberto (OCV) mais plana das células torna mais difícil determinar com precisão o estado de carga e envelhecimento. Por esse motivo, a Audi utiliza um algoritmo adaptado. A informação obtida é incorporada no cálculo da autonomia, comportamento de carregamento e estratégia de operação. Uso de energia alargado A bateria do A2 e-tron não é apenas utilizada como sistema de armazenamento de energia para a condução, mas também pode gerar benefícios adicionais fora do veículo, dependendo da aplicação. O Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) permite fornecer energia elétrica a consumidores externos adequados através do veículo. Isto torna o A2 e-tron uma fonte de energia móvel e flexível. A função Vehicle-to-Home (V2H) utiliza o A2 e-tron como um sistema de armazenamento de energia de grande capacidade e, em conjunto com um carregador de parede CC bidirecional compatível, permite a utilização da eletricidade armazenada para fins domésticos. Dependendo do mercado, do equipamento do veículo, da infraestrutura de carregamento compatível, da instalação residencial, dos requisitos regulamentares e, se necessário, de uma tarifa de eletricidade adequada, o Audi compacto poderá, no futuro, oferecer a função Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G). A energia da bateria do veículo é fornecida à rede elétrica pública, integrando a bateria num sistema energético mais amplo. Conclusão Com o A2 e-tron, a Audi procura o objetivo de tornar a mobilidade elétrica no segmento compacto adequada para uma utilização diária, eficiente e flexível. A interação entre a gestão térmica coordenada, a eletrónica de carregamento inteligente e a gestão avançada da bateria garante um comportamento de carregamento estável e consistente. Ao mesmo tempo, as funções de carregamento bidirecional alargam o leque de aplicações da bateria para além da condução, tornando o veículo parte ativa do sistema energético. Desta forma, o A2 e-tron combina um carregamento eficiente, uma utilização inteligente de energia e um elevado nível de usabilidade diária num conceito geral orientado para o futuro. autonews.pt @ 13-11-2026 12:46:06 Clique aqui para ver mais sobre: Auto News, Mercado Automóvel e Novidades

artigo.texto: Stars could disappear from the night sky because of space data centers – scientists warn of a threat Kyiv • UNN Tens of thousands of space data centers could change the appearance of the night sky and make astronomers’ work more difficult. Scientists also warn of collisions and orbital debris. The mass deployment of artificial intelligence data centers in Earth's orbit could radically change the appearance of the night sky. Scientists warn that satellites could become more visible than stars and create serious problems for astronomical observations. Axios reports this, citing a new scientific study, writes UNN. Details According to researchers' estimates, the deployment of tens of thousands of orbital data centers could result in artificial satellites becoming the brightest objects in the night sky across most regions of the world. In addition to light pollution, scientists warn of the risk of collisions between spacecraft traveling at about 27,000 km/h and an increase in the amount of orbital debris. Companies plan to launch tens of thousands of satellites According to Quilty Space, investment in space data centers increased from $197 million in 2025 to $1.11 billion in 2026. SpaceX has applied to create a network of 1 million satellites. Meanwhile, the Starcloud and Blue Origin projects envisage the potential deployment of 88,000 and 51,600 spacecraft, respectively. However, experts emphasize that the announced figures do not mean that all the satellites will actually be launched. The study's lead author, David Sandalow, urged companies to act cautiously, as the consequences of the mass deployment of data centers in space have yet to be sufficiently studied.
