artigo.texto: ‘Estado do Pará está prestes a vender R$ 1 bilhão em créditos de carbono’, diz pesquisador Em entrevista ao VEJA+Verde, o americano Daniel Nepstad explica vantagens do mercado jurisdicional para o Brasil O Pará está prestes a fechar a primeira grande venda de créditos de carbono do mercado jurisdicional brasileiro: 12 milhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente evitadas, a 15 dólares a tonelada, o que deve render cerca de 180 milhões de dólares (ou 1 bilhão de reais). A compradora é a Amazon, multinacional de tecnologia e comércio eletrônico de Jeff Bezos, por meio da coalizão LEAF, uma iniciativa global público-privada de proteção às florestas. A informação é do cientista americano Daniel Nepstad, presidente do Earth Innovation Institute, instituto de pesquisa que trabalha com governos estaduais e setores do agro pela transição para um novo modelo de desenvolvimento rural sustentável na Amazônia. O mercado de carbono jurisdicional, também conhecido como REDD+ Jurisdicional é a aplicação do mecanismo de Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação florestal (incluindo conservação, manejo sustentável e aumento de estoques de carbono) em uma escala territorial ampla — seja nacional ou subnacional, como um estado, província ou município — em vez de ficar restrito a projetos isolados em propriedades privadas específicas. O contrato no estado amazônico depende da conclusão da validação do programa e a grande incógnita, segundo Nepstad, é se o próximo governo paraense vai manter o mecanismo, que levou 18 anos para sair do papel. O dinheiro, ressalva Nepstad, exige gestão criteriosa: “É muita grana, mas não é suficiente para cada produtor ou comunidade receber individualmente valores elevados. Por isso os investimentos precsam ser muito bem pensados, para gerar mais reduções de emissoes e mais vendas de crédito no futuro.” Lucrar com preservação No modelo estadual do REDD+ jurisdicional, o governo faz uma contabilidade coletiva de todas as emissões — do desmatamento, dos incêndios, da degradação florestal e da exploração madeireira. As reduções abaixo do nível de referência, calculado com a média das emissões dos cinco anos anteriores, geram créditos divididos entre os setores: comunidades indígenas, quilombolas, madeireiros, agricultura familiar e pecuária. São dez estados brasileiros participando do mecanismo, com Mato Grosso e Acre mais avançados e Goiás entrando agora. O Pará já reduziu muito suas emissões, mas perdeu créditos por causa dos incêndios de 2024. Nos projetos privados, parte da receita vai para a empresa desenvolvedora; no jurisdicional, diz Nepstad, “basicamente tudo fica ou com o governo ou com os beneficiários”. Cada crédito emitido por um projeto privado, porém, é descontado do saldo estadual — quanto mais projetos, menos créditos para o programa jurisdicional. E a regra de ouro é inegociável: “Se não tiver redução de emissões, esquece: entra aquele dinheiro inicial e depois volta tudo ao normal.” O piloto do projeto está em Paragominas, no nordeste do Pará, num programa que o instituto de Nepstad chama de “municípios inovadores”, com a participação da prefeitura, da assistência técnica e da extensão rural. O setor pecuário do estado escolheu concentrar os recursos na prevenção de incêndios, cicatriz dos grandes fogos de 2024. Nepstad também rebate a desinformação que circula sobre o mecanismo, como a ideia de que o estado estaria “roubando o carbono” do proprietário rural ou das comunidades — a participação é voluntária. “O que importa é se as emissões de CO2, causadas pelo desmatamento, pelos incêndios e pela exploração madeireira, estão caindo. Enquanto estiverem caindo, o dinheiro vai chegar”, diz o ambientalista. Rios voadores Considerado um dos mais relevantes cientistas do ambiente amazônico, onde desenvolveu pesquisas durante décadas, Nepstad defende que a preservação da floresta é uma questão econômica: a evapotranspiração das árvores fornece o vapor que forma as nuvens e esfria o ar, e parte dele viaja para o Cerrado e o Sul do continente. “Onde tem mais floresta, tem mais chuva confiável e a temperatura é um, dois, até três graus menor”, diz. O cientista cita dados da Universidade Federal de Viçosa: no sudeste da Amazônia, o período seco anual é cinco semanas maior agora do que 20 anos atrás. “Isso está medido, não é teórico.” Há saída, e ela tem prazo: a mata secundária, aos 15 anos, já recupera o papel da floresta madura — e cada ano que uma floresta não pega fogo, ela fica mais alta e mais resistente ao fogo. Para o produtor rural, a reserva legal funciona como seguro: cercado de floresta num raio de 20, 30 quilômetros, o risco de perder safra, peso dos animais e pastagens na próxima megasseca é menor. Vitória ambiental A avaliação de Nepstad sobre as políticas ambientais brasileiras é positiva. O PPCDAm, plano de combate ao desmatamento lançado no primeiro governo Lula, com Marina Silva no Ministério do Meio Ambiente, combinou comando e controle, áreas protegidas e restrição de crédito a municípios desmatadores: a taxa de desmatamento caiu quase 80% até 2012, voltou a subir nos governos Dilma, Temer e Bolsonaro e caiu de novo. Este ano, o Brasil registrou a menor taxa da série histórica do INPE (Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais), que começa na década de 1980. A próxima onda, na avaliação de Nepstad, deve ser a colaboração entre setores, e a Lei do Manejo Integrado do Fogo, de 2024, é o instrumento ideal: em vez de punir quem usa o fogo, promove o manejo adequado. “Não conheço ninguém que defenda incêndio. Todo mundo sofre com incêndio — perde cerca, perde animais, perde pasto.” Protecionismo europeu No comércio exterior, Nepstad alerta para dois movimentos quase opostos. A moratória da soja no Brasil, criada em 2006, foi praticamente suspensa no início deste ano — e o desmatamento seguiu caindo, o que, para ele, mostra que políticas construídas com participação da própria sociedade são mais sólidas. artigo.texto: Mettler-Toledo Leading in lab-grade OCV testers According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Open Circuit Voltage Graders market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) Graders market is entering a transformative phase as battery manufacturing scales up to meet electric vehicle and energy storage demand. OCV graders, which measure resting voltage to sort cells for consistency and safety, have become indispensable in gigafactory quality control. The market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 6.8% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 192 (2025=100). Growth is driven by capacity additions in lithium-ion battery production, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America, and by tightening quality standards that demand 100% cell grading. However, cyclical oversupply in battery manufacturing and high capital costs pose restraints. This report provides a data-driven outlook on market size, segmentation, competitive landscape, and regional dynamics, equipping stakeholders with actionable insights for strategic planning through 2035. The baseline scenario for the Open Circuit Voltage Graders market anticipates steady expansion over 2026-2035, underpinned by global battery manufacturing capacity growth. As gigafactories ramp up production, the need for precise cell grading intensifies to ensure pack performance and safety. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 6.8%, with demand peaking in the late 2020s as new plants come online. Technological shifts toward higher-throughput automated graders and integration with manufacturing execution systems will shape product demand. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest market, while North America and Europe show accelerated growth due to local battery supply chain investments. Restraints include potential delays in gigafactory construction and price pressure from battery makers. Overall, the outlook remains positive, with the market index reaching 192 by 2035. Lithium-ion battery manufacturing is the dominant end-use sector for OCV graders, accounting for over half of global demand. As gigafactories scale production for electric vehicles and energy storage, the need for 100% cell grading becomes critical to ensure safety and performance. OCV graders measure resting voltage after formation and aging, sorting cells into precise bins for pack assembly. The shift toward higher nickel chemistries and larger cell formats increases sensitivity to voltage variations, driving demand for more accurate and faster graders. Through 2035, as global battery capacity multiplies, this segment will remain the primary growth engine, with demand-side indicators such as EV production volumes and battery plant utilization rates directly influencing grader sales. Current trend: Growing rapidly. Major trends: Ramp-up of gigafactory capacity worldwide, Increasing cell size and capacity, Integration with automated production lines, and Adoption of smart grading software. Representative participants: Arbin Instruments, Maccor, Bitrode, Digatron, and Chroma ATE. In solar panel production, OCV graders are used to test photovoltaic modules for voltage output and consistency, ensuring performance guarantees. As solar installations accelerate globally, manufacturers require reliable grading to minimize mismatch losses in modules. The trend toward larger wafers and higher-efficiency cells increases the importance of precise voltage measurement. Demand is supported by capacity expansions in Asia-Pacific and the United States, though growth is tempered by overcapacity in module manufacturing. Through 2035, demand will be driven by technological upgrades and quality standards, with indicators such as solar capacity additions and module efficiency targets shaping the market. Current trend: Moderate growth. Major trends: Shift to larger wafer sizes, Growth in bifacial module production, Automation of module testing, and Stringent performance warranties. Representative participants: Hioki, Keysight Technologies, Chroma ATE, and National Instruments. Electronics component quality control utilizes OCV graders for testing capacitors, sensors, and other components where voltage characteristics are critical. As electronics become more complex and miniaturized, the need for precise voltage grading in production increases. This sector benefits from the ongoing digitalization and IoT device proliferation, which drive demand for reliable components. OCV graders in this segment are often benchtop or automated systems integrated into production lines. Through 2035, growth will be steady, supported by trends in consumer electronics and automotive electronics, with demand indicators including semiconductor production volumes and quality failure rates. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Miniaturization of electronic components, Growth in automotive electronics, Increasing automation in QC, and Adoption of Industry 4.0 practices. Representative participants: Keysight Technologies, National Instruments, Ametek, and Hioki. Battery recycling and second-life assessment is a fast-growing end-use sector for OCV graders. As the first wave of EV batteries reaches end-of-life, the need to rapidly assess state-of-health and residual value becomes paramount. OCV grading provides a quick, non-destructive method to sort cells for reuse or recycling. The sector is supported by regulatory pressures for battery recycling and the economic value of recovered materials. Through 2035, demand will surge as recycling infrastructure expands, particularly in Europe and North America. Key indicators include EV battery retirement volumes and recycling capacity investments. artigo.texto: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is seeking a stronger foothold in Southeast Asia’s emerging carbon markets, with Aboitiz Foundation joining a regional framework as an Observer in a move that could open up opportunities for climate financing, carbon trading and investments in nature-based projects. Representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, Aboitiz Foundation has joined the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) as an Observer, marking a step toward greater Philippine participation in regional carbon market development. The engagement coincided with the signing of the framework’s Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, and the renewal of the agreement for another two years. The move provides Philippine stakeholders an avenue to contribute to discussions on carbon market standards, financing mechanisms and regional cooperation as Southeast Asian economies work toward more interconnected and credible carbon markets. “ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz chief reputation and sustainability officer and president of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines’ participation comes as the country works to strengthen its carbon market ecosystem through private-sector collaboration, knowledge-sharing and capacity-building initiatives. One such initiative is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together industry stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Together with the NbS Group, the coalition is also advancing a long-term initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection and community development, alongside the development of recommended governance frameworks. These efforts aim to position the Philippines to develop nature-based carbon projects that can attract climate financing while creating economic opportunities for communities involved in conservation and restoration. The country has significant potential given its extensive natural resources, but turning this natural capital into viable carbon assets will require credible project standards, transparent governance and mechanisms to ensure measurable environmental and social benefits. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, along with the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to coordinate regional initiatives and promote high-integrity carbon market development. Under its 2026-2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure and technical cooperation to facilitate credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. The inclusion of Philippine private-sector stakeholders as Observers provides an opportunity to exchange expertise with established regional initiatives while bringing local experience in conservation, restoration and sustainable investment into the discussions. For the Philippines, the engagement could help bridge the gap between its natural capital and emerging financing opportunities in regional carbon markets. As ASEAN moves toward greater market connectivity, the challenge will be to ensure that carbon trading delivers more than emissions offsets by supporting investable climate solutions that protect ecosystems, strengthen local livelihoods and build long-term environmental resilience.

artigo.texto: Powering the AI era: Building Resilience Beyond the Data Center As AI drives unprecedented demand for compute, data centers are becoming larger, denser and more complex. Long gone are the days when 20 megawatts represented the energy ceiling for a supercomputer. Today, some projects are approaching gigawatt scale, reshaping decisions about where data centers can be built and how they are designed and operated. Energy access has overtaken land availability and fiber connectivity as a primary constraint on development. Increasingly, data center operators have to go where the power is or find new ways to generate and manage it themselves. That makes energy resilience an imperative from the earliest stages of development. “Energy resilience has become the make-or-break parameter for success in the AI compute ecosystem,” said Sandor Becz, senior vice president of research at FM. A changing power equation Data centers are developing a new, two-way relationship with the electricity grid. They can adjust consumption, generate power and help balance supply and demand. Developers are also considering hybrid energy strategies that combine grid connections with behind-the-meter generation, renewable energy and battery storage. At gigawatt scale, that relationship brings new responsibilities. Data centers place significant pressure on existing grids, requiring closer coordination with utilities and government to support grid stability. Power disruption presents the greatest resilience challenge. Conventional backup strategies may no longer be sufficient at this scale. “The business model needs to support the idea that you’re not going to have 100% backup all the time,” said Adrian Oxley, principal engineer at FM. Developers and operators need to understand what happens when part of the system becomes unavailable. Can failures be contained? Which operations take priority? How quickly can full operations be restored? Finding those answers should start long before a facility comes online. Designing resilience into the ecosystem FM helps clients address these questions early with FM Intellium, combining insurance capacity, engineering expertise and scientific research in one solution to manage risk across the data ecosystem. Developed specifically for data centers and their interconnected infrastructure, FM Intellium draws on more than 25 years of data center insurance and engineering experience. Today, FM engineers help protect more than 1,500 data centers valued at approximately US$620 billion. Its whole-system approach starts with three fundamentals: place, protection and people. Where a facility is built, how its interconnected systems are protected and how prepared its operators are can all determine its ability to withstand disruption. FM Intellium supports clients across the data center lifecycle, beginning with site selection and construction, when there is the greatest opportunity to mitigate risk. FM engineers work closely with clients to understand each facility's goals, constraints and operating environment. By examining dependencies across data, power and renewable energy infrastructure, they can identify vulnerabilities, anticipate how disruption could spread and develop practical measures to strengthen resilience. This collaborative approach brings together the client's knowledge of its business and FM's engineering expertise to help shape resilience strategies tailored to each project. That expertise is informed by scientific research into technologies reshaping data center operations, including liquid cooling, uninterruptible power supply systems, lithium-ion battery safety and automation. People are equally critical. Human factors contribute to as many as half of data center outages. FM Intellium helps clients evaluate operational risks alongside physical infrastructure, including the people and processes responsible for keeping these advanced systems running. From energy consumer to energy resource Considering community needs and opportunities early in development can help operators identify ways to deliver tangible benefits and build stronger relationships with the people who live and work there. With careful planning, the considerable heat generated by data centers can become one such resource. Siting facilities near homes and businesses creates opportunities to share that excess heat with the surrounding community. The same site-specific thinking applies across data center resilience. Grid reliability, natural-hazard exposure, access to resources and regulation all vary by location, making these factors critical considerations from site selection onward. Becz suggested that policymakers avoid blanket regulation, preserving the flexibility for data centers to address site-specific risks and respond to local needs. FM Intellium draws on FM’s global experience across these disciplines to help clients assess the specific combination of natural hazards, power and water availability, infrastructure dependencies and operational challenges each site presents. Building resilience for what comes next Today’s data center operates within a complex, interconnected ecosystem of data and compute, power generation, utilities, renewable energy, cooling systems, supply chains and communities. As the industry races to build the infrastructure for what comes next, resilience will help determine how far and how sustainably it can grow. FM Intellium works with developers and operators across the lifecycle of that ecosystem, helping them identify risks early, strengthen resilience and prepare for the demands ahead. You can learn more about FM Intellium here. About the Author FM Intellium Team FM Intellium delivers data-driven risk management, engineering expertise, and scalable solutions to protect data centers, AI systems, and power infrastructure. artigo.texto: Ireland’s Data-Center Lawsuit Puts Energy Policy Under Scrutiny (Bloomberg) -- With its temperate climate, sparse population and pro-business government, Ireland seemed for years like a perfect location for building data centers. Now, the country is becoming a test bed for legal opposition to those centers on climate grounds. This week, Ireland’s energy and water regulator faces a case in the High Court over its rules for new data centers. The case, brought by environmental law charity ClientEarth and Irish environmental groups, argues that the regulator’s latest policy for connecting large energy users to the electricity grid fails to comply with Irish and European law and risks locking Ireland into years of fossil-fuel use, undermining its ability to meet legally binding emissions targets. It’s part of a recent wave of action against data centers on climate grounds in Ireland — one of Europe’s largest data hubs — and around the world. Concern and anger about the energy and land demanded by the buildout is already high, but with global energy use by these centers expected to almost quadruple by 2035, according to BloombergNEF, the potential impact on emissions and man-made climate change is huge. The Irish case is significant because it targets overall policy rather than an individual development. It could also have implications for data-center construction in Europe more broadly. While European laws won’t change off the back of a domestic case, its outcome may guide decision-making in any similar challenges that come up in other EU states. “Ireland has a really robust legal framework when it comes to its climate targets,” said Eoin Jackson, a researcher at the London School of Economics whose work identifies Ireland as a hotspot for litigation against data centers on climate change grounds. Its data-center boom was also early, so “there were already a lot of challenges underway to data centers that kind of precede the concerns driven by AI.” As a result, he said, “Ireland has become a little bit of a canary in the coal mine when it comes to data-center litigation taken on climate grounds.” Obvious Choice In recent decades, tech companies including Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms Inc. and TikTok have all established their European headquarters in Ireland, attracted by a favorable tax regime and highly educated, English-speaking workforce. Corporation taxes paid by US multinationals are of huge economic importance to the country, allowing it to run a budget surplus. Ireland was also the obvious choice for many of the tech giants’ data centers, at least to begin with. It now hosts approximately 89 data centers — about 10 times more than the European per-capita average — most of which are in industrial areas surrounding the capital, Dublin, and along the east coast. In 2025, data centers accounted for 23% of metered electricity use in Ireland, more than all urban households and up from just 5% a decade ago. In a recent report, a United Nations academic body warned that Ireland offers a “cautionary example” of grid stress from concentrated digital infrastructure. Concerns about grid capacity and blackouts brought new construction to a halt in 2021. That November, the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) implemented a de facto ban on connecting new centers to the grid by introducing strict criteria around the location of data centers and their ability to provide on-site energy generation or energy storage. While the process didn’t amount to an outright ban, securing new connections became close to impossible. Industry groups argued that Ireland was missing out on the global capital pouring into AI infrastructure. However, the freeze was celebrated by environmentalists and Irish residents worried about energy costs alike. Ireland is far behind on meeting its legally binding climate targets. Its EU target is to reduce emissions by 42% by 2030 compared with 2005 levels; it is currently on track to achieve 13%, according to estimates by Ireland’s Environmental Protection Agency. The country got 47% of its electricity from gas-fired generation in 2025 and is heavily reliant on gas imports, mostly from the UK. It has ambitions to tap its significant offshore wind resources, but for now, it’s relying on smaller renewable inputs from onshore wind, solar power and batteries. Those may not be enough to keep up with the demand from hyperscalers. In December — at a time when various countries had or were considering pauses on data-center development — the CRU published a new policy on grid connections, bringing the de facto moratorium on grid connections to an end. Under the regulator’s new policy, any data center seeking a grid connection must install on-site generation or battery systems capable of meeting its full electricity demand, as well as providing power back to the national grid when needed. The CRU rules also allow for data centers to run on non-renewable energy for six years, after which point their energy supply must be 80% renewable. However, the renewable calculation does not take into account back-up generation. artigo.texto: SAN JOSE IS CONSIDERING a temporary pause on data center projects before development standards to guide limits on water use and other environmental impacts are finalized in December. Mayor Matt Mahan and Councilmembers Pamela Campos, David Cohen, Peter Ortiz and Domingo Candelas on Thursday announced a proposal to halt land use approvals for data centers, putting a pause on any related projects before the City Council votes on uniform standards on Dec. 8. This move comes after San José Spotlight reported that Google’s data center in Alviso could be approved ahead of the standards. The project located at 5087 Disk Drive would require 250 megawatts — enough to power 250,000 households. “After many months of community engagement and research, we are preparing to vote on the strictest proposed regulations for data centers in the country, which include requirements for 100% clean energy, closed loop water systems, union labor, monitoring and enforcement of noise restrictions, and bans on NDAs and any public subsidy,” Mahan told San José Spotlight. “But none of that matters if we allow projects to slip through just before these standards are adopted. The action we’re proposing is about holding every project to the same high bar — short of that would be an unacceptable betrayal of public trust.” In the proposed standards, data center developers will be encouraged to enroll with San Jose Clean Energy, which supplies renewable power. Diesel backup generators must follow the strictest federal emission standards, and can only run when there are power outages. The San Jose Planning Commission will consider the latest version of the proposed standards on Nov. 18. For months, residents have been demanding the city implement a moratorium on data centers before standards get put in place. But advocates such as Linda Hutchins-Knowles, co-founder of environmental nonprofit Mothers Out Front Silicon Valley, said the proposed pause still falls short. “After many months of community engagement and research, we are preparing to vote on the strictest proposed regulations for data centers in the country. … But none of that matters if we allow projects to slip through just before these standards are adopted.” Mayor Matt Mahan “I definitely appreciate there being a pause put now to stop any more getting through, but I still think that needs to be extended beyond their current timeline,” Hutchins-Knowles told San José Spotlight. “We believe that it would also be a betrayal of trust to not impose an actual moratorium in order to ensure that the standards are truly robust and that the community is on board. (The) city’s community engagement process was rushed and insufficient.” San Jose began the process of drafting the development standards in June. When officials presented the draft proposal last month, residents decried how the standards fell short of covering the heat island effect and studying how low-frequency infrasound will affect the community. What impact will new projects have? Advocates have asked city officials to consult with state and county agencies to study the cumulative effects of bringing on the 16 data center projects in San Jose’s development pipeline. They have noted that the city’s efforts to become the world’s artificial intelligence capital is in conflict with developing standards to regulate the industry it wants to attract. “The moratorium should be long enough to allow the city to conduct studies of the long-term cumulative impacts of the massive scale of data center development contemplated by the city, which are anticipated to triple our energy use,” a joint statement from eight environmental and advocate groups, including Green Foothills, the Sierra Club Loma Prieta Chapter and Alviso in Action, reads. The People Over Data Centers San Jose Coalition, a group comprised of neighbors and community organizations, has organized meetings and town halls in every council district to educate residents on data centers. The city has also conducted its own outreach and incorporated some of the feedback it has received from residents, including prohibiting open loop cooling systems that use drinkable water and can consume millions of gallons of water a year. Instead, the city will require data centers to use recycled water or a closed loop system that circulates water through pipes to absorb heat from the electronics. “The city must strike a balance between securing economic development and ensuring that growth is responsibly built,” a Nov. 6 memo from Planning Director Chris Burton said. “While the proposed standards do not address every concern raised through the community engagement process, they represent that balance.” Ortiz, who oversees District 5 in East San Jose, said the city is seeing unprecedented interest from developers for data center projects, and San Jose has a responsibility to ensure growth will benefit residents. “This proposed pause is not about stopping development. It’s about establishing responsible standards, protecting our communities and ensuring that industries benefiting from our city’s resources also contribute to addressing challenges like affordability,” Ortiz told San José Spotlight. “Economic growth should not come at the expense of our residents. It should improve their quality of life.” Contact Joyce Chu at [email protected] or @joyce_speaks on X. This story originally appeared in San Jose Spotlight.

artigo.texto: Bloomington to consider extending data center moratorium, seek feedback on revised regulations BLOOMINGTON (25News Now) - Monday is likely not to be the final chance for the public to sound off on data centers in Bloomington as city officials want more time to consider regulations. Bloomington’s planning commission is being asked to recommend the city council extend the moratorium another six months as staff revises rules first proposed on Oct. 9. Changes contained in planning commission documents include requirements for air quality and noise control. Developers would be banned from entering into non-disclosure agreements for any size data centers, when the initial proposal said it would apply to only hyperscale facilities. Also, higher fines would be imposed for developers who violate city regulations. The city council’s six-month moratorium on data centers is set to expire at the end of this month. A second half-year pause would run until May. The planning commission’s second public hearing is scheduled for Monday at 4 p.m. at the Bloomington Center for Performing Arts. Another hearing would follow after staff reviews public testimony and prepares an ordinance for final city council approval. artigo.texto: A Samsung Electronics está em negociações para adquirir a Modine Manufacturing, fabricante americana de sistemas de refrigeração para data centers, segundo reportagem publicada pela Bloomberg News na quinta-feira, 12. De acordo com pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto ouvidas pelo veículo, as empresas discutem um possível acordo que poderá ser concluído nas próximas semanas. As conversas, no entanto, ainda não resultaram em uma decisão definitiva. Segundo a Bloomberg, as negociações podem fracassar e existe a possibilidade de outro interessado apresentar uma proposta pela companhia. A Reuters informou que não conseguiu verificar imediatamente a informação e que não obteve comentários da Samsung nem da Modine. Ações da fabricante sobem após notícia A notícia sobre a possível aquisição provocou uma forte reação no mercado financeiro. As ações da Modine subiram 29% nas negociações realizadas após o fechamento do mercado na quinta-feira. Na mesma data, a empresa tinha valor de mercado estimado em US$ 5,6 bilhões, segundo dados compilados pela LSEG. A Modine é especializada em soluções de gerenciamento térmico, incluindo equipamentos utilizados para controlar a temperatura de instalações industriais e centros de processamento de dados. Esse tipo de infraestrutura é necessário para manter servidores em funcionamento e evitar o superaquecimento dos equipamentos, especialmente em instalações que demandam grande capacidade computacional. A possível aquisição representaria uma movimentação da Samsung no segmento de infraestrutura para data centers, mercado que ganha importância com a expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) e o aumento da demanda por capacidade de processamento. Até o momento, porém, as empresas não anunciaram oficialmente um acordo.

artigo.texto: Buffalo Township is moving forward with a data center ordinance that’s designed so that the public won’t “hear, smell or see” any data center that would be built. During Wednesday evening’s Nov. 11 meeting, township Solicitor Brian Farrington provided an overview of the 22-page draft data center ordinance. “This has been in the works for some time,” Farrington said. No data center has been proposed to be built in Buffalo Township. “This is constructed for the protection of our township,” said Ron Zampogna, chairman of the township supervisors. “We don’t have anybody looking to do anything right now. But it sounds like any (developer) is going to have a lot of hoops to jump through.” The board will host a public hearing to discuss this ordinance further with the public on Dec. 9. Buffalo Township established a moratorium on all data center development in August in order to give the supervisors time to approve an ordinance that will set parameters for potential developers. The moratorium expires in February. The ordinance has moved into its final review stage. Both the Butler County and Buffalo Township planning commissions have commented on the document. A broad overview “I have tried to (make) this ordinance as comprehensive as possible,” Farrington said. Some key elements include limiting development to the manufacturing zoning district as well as requiring all developers submit site plans, utility plans and environmental impact statements. Developers must submit plans for water usage, as well as create an air-emission inventory for site emissions. In addition, any developer would need to submit reports for sound vibration, lighting, landscaping, emergency response, waste management, traffic, screening and decommissioning. Farrington proposed that any site be a minimum of 40 acres, with a 100-foot minimum building setback and 40% of the entire site covered. If the site should be in proximity of a residential district, a 300-foot buffer must be maintained for all truck parking and infrastructure. This rule applies to schools, daycare centers, hospitals, nursing homes or personal care spaces. The ordinance stipulates the main data center building cannot be taller than 45 feet, and any rooftop equipment cannot extend past 55 feet. In addition, all developers would have to submit cooling system plans and detail where they plan to get their water — whether it will be pumped in, part of the public water system, or trucked in and placed in a water tower on-site. The document states that a licensed Pennsylvania professional must certify that all utilities meet the outlined requirements. Noise emissions and buffers One of the biggest complaints Farrington found while doing research for the ordinance revolved around generators. “It’s not just the sound of the generators, but the fact that these generators create a low hum which, when mounted on a cement or steel pad, vibrates,” he said. “Because it vibrates at a low frequency, it causes disturbance — so there are some regulations here to protect residents from that,” Farrington said. Emergency generators cannot operate during an emergency outage for more than one hour. If they need to go longer, the site will have to shut down. Generators can only be tested Mondays through Fridays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and never on a federal holiday. Generators can run no more than 50 hours in a calendar year. “All of that must be maintained in a log that the township could review,” Farrington said. Buffers must also be placed to shield the data center from public view. A 100-foot buffer must be maintained around the premises, with two staggered rows of evergreen trees in front of public rights of way and residences. All power equipment must be buffered and screened by at least a 12-foot-tall opaque wall or fence on all sides, except if the main building provides adequate screening. Acoustic louvers are needed on any ventilation openings to prevent sound from leaking out. Gates need to be opaque, and all fencing must be placed inside the tree-line buffer “so people driving past don’t have to look at it,” said Farrington. The goal of the ordinance is to ensure the public cannot hear, smell or see a data center, he said.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI secures 16-GWh US battery supply deal with Jupiter Power Summary Samsung SDI America has signed a deal to supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate batteries to Jupiter Power in the United States, with deliveries scheduled over three years starting in 2029. The batteries will be made at Samsung SDI’s Indiana plant for Jupiter Power’s large-scale energy storage projects. Including an earlier contract, Samsung SDI’s orders from Jupiter Power total about 27 gigawatt-hours. The agreement follows the start of mass production of lithium iron phosphate batteries at the Indiana facility. Key Facts - The contract is estimated to be worth several trillion won. - Jupiter Power has 19,700 megawatt-hours of projects operating, under construction or committed, and another 110,000 megawatt-hours in development across the United States. - Jupiter Power is backed by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock. - Samsung SDI said it is the only non-Chinese manufacturer of prismatic batteries for battery energy storage system applications in North America. - Samsung SDI is reinforcing its lithium iron phosphate supply chain through material supply agreements with Korean companies, including POSCO Future M and L&F. Samsung SDI said Monday that its U.S. subsidiary has signed a deal to supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate batteries to Jupiter Power, a U.S. energy storage developer and operator, in a contract estimated to be worth several trillion won. Under the agreement, Samsung SDI America will supply the batteries over three years starting in 2029 for Jupiter Power's large-scale battery energy storage system projects in the United States. Including a previous contract, Samsung SDI's total orders from Jupiter Power now amount to approximately 27 gigawatt-hours, the company said. Jupiter Power, backed by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock, has a portfolio of 19,700 megawatt-hours of projects that are operating, under construction or committed, with another 110,000 megawatt-hours in development across the United States. The batteries will be manufactured at Samsung SDI's plant in Indiana. The deal comes shortly after the company began mass production of lithium iron phosphate batteries at the facility, underscoring the competitiveness of its technology as it expands its presence in the U.S. energy storage market. Samsung SDI is the only non-Chinese manufacturer of prismatic batteries for battery energy storage system applications in North America. It has also secured non-Chinese sources for key battery materials, strengthening its supply chain and appeal to U.S. energy companies seeking alternatives to Chinese suppliers. The company has recently won a series of orders as it expands its battery energy storage system portfolio beyond nickel-cobalt-aluminum-based batteries to include lithium iron phosphate products. It is also reinforcing its lithium iron phosphate supply chain through material supply agreements with Korean companies, including POSCO Future M and L&F. "This agreement reflects the competitiveness and supply capabilities of our locally produced prismatic lithium iron phosphate batteries in the U.S.," said Fabrice Hudry, president of energy storage systems at Samsung SDI America. "Building on our differentiated prismatic battery technology and stable supply chain, we will continue to expand our presence in the global battery energy storage system market." Jupiter Power CEO Andy Bowman said securing reliable, domestically manufactured equipment was central to the company's plans to reduce risks in its project development. "Samsung SDI's lithium iron phosphate batteries, produced here in the U.S., strengthen our supply chain as we continue to deliver reliable power and capacity when and where the grid needs it most," he said. artigo.texto: Weekend - Blackstone’s QTS cuts AI data center debt sale 60% as investors push back on pricing Summary - Blackstone-backed data center operator QTS cut a planned private debt sale to about $300 million from roughly $800 million after weak demand, refusing to pay higher yields. The pullback hints at limits to investor appetite for AI-related debt. For credit markets, the QTS cutback is an early sign that the price of financing AI infrastructure is starting to matter. Investors are putting limits on how much they will hold of repeat issuers and on concentrated exposure to the sector. If that spreads, data center and AI-linked borrowers could face wider spreads or smaller deals, pushing more issuance into private credit and project finance at higher cost. For equities, any rise in funding costs feeds into the capex economics behind the AI trade. That is a sensitive point for sentiment this week, with Nvidia due to report on Tuesday. The deal is small, so it is not a credit event, but it is a signal worth tracking in future AI debt deals. --- Big week for AI ahead: --- The AI build-out has had seemingly unlimited access to capital, but QTS’s shrunken deal shows that even a Blackstone-backed borrower now has to choose between paying up and settling for less. Summary: - QTS, a Blackstone-backed data center operator, cut a planned private debt sale by about 60%. - It is raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. - Some investors objected to pricing, while others were limited by QTS’s repeated use of the private placement market. - QTS has raised billions through at least two private placements in 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade sale last year. - Blackstone resisted higher yields because wider pricing could become a costlier benchmark for its other debt. - AI companies are tapping every part of the capital markets to fund investment that could reach the trillions of dollars. QTS, the data center operator backed by Blackstone, has scaled back a planned private debt sale by around 60% after struggling to find enough investor demand, and after declining to pay the much higher yields some buyers wanted, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the transaction. The company is now raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. Some investors objected to the pricing on offer, while others were constrained because QTS has already tapped the private placement market several times, according to the people. QTS has been a heavy user of that market. It has raised billions of dollars through at least two private placement deals over the past 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade bond sale last year and a separate $800 million financing. Blackstone’s reluctance to sweeten terms reflects a wider concern. Because the firm borrows frequently across many markets and through many issuers, wider pricing on the QTS deal could set a more expensive benchmark for investors weighing other Blackstone-related debt. The episode matters well beyond one borrower. Artificial intelligence companies are reaching into every corner of capital markets, from investment-grade bonds to project finance, to fund build-outs that could cost trillions of dollars over the coming years. The QTS deal suggests that appetite is not unlimited, particularly in narrower pools such as private placements, where a small group of buyers can quickly hit internal limits on exposure to a single name or sector. That leaves borrowers with an uncomfortable choice: accept higher funding costs, shrink deals or spread issuance across more markets. Each option raises the cost or complexity of financing the AI infrastructure boom. For now, the decision to cut the deal’s size rather than pay up shows that well-backed issuers can still walk away. But it is a sign that the market is starting to discriminate on price. The next test will be how other data center and AI-related borrowers do in upcoming deals, and whether investors start demanding a premium for concentrated exposure to the sector. artigo.texto: Global energy storage owner-operator, BW ESS, has entered into a partnership with French battery storage developer, Wattmen, to develop a portfolio of approximately 500 MW of battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in France over the next three years. The partnership establishes a platform for originating and progressing standalone, transmission-connected projects, supporting BW ESS’ continued growth in the French market. The collaboration brings together Wattmen’s local project origination and development capabilities with BW ESS’ international experience in energy storage investment, project design, and procurement across seven markets. The partners will work together to advance projects from greenfield to ready-to-build status, securing the land rights, grid connections, and authorisations required for construction. The partnership will focus on projects with connection capacities of at least 100 MW, prioritising sites close to grid connection points and with sufficient space to accommodate battery systems offering at least four hours of storage duration. This approach is designed to create a portfolio of large scale assets with the flexibility to respond to the evolving needs of the French electricity system. Hazel Starmer-Jones, Development Director at BW ESS, commented: “Partnering with Wattmen is an important step in building our presence in France. We take a highly considered approach to development partnerships in new markets, and Wattmen have shown a depth of technical and local expertise that makes them an ideal partner in originating and developing high-quality energy storage projects. Together, we aim to build a portfolio that delivers lasting value and helps strengthen the flexibility and resilience of the French electricity system.” Wattmen will lead local development activities, including site identification, land agreements, permitting, and grid connection co-ordination, working closely with landowners, authorities, and communities. BW ESS will contribute its international energy storage expertise, supporting project design and procurement strategy. Jean-Marc Guenée, CEO and Co-Founder of Wattmen, noted: “This partnership brings together complementary strengths and a shared ambition to develop high-quality battery storage projects in France. By combining our local knowledge and development capabilities with BW ESS’ international experience, we can progress strategically located projects and help deliver the flexible infrastructure needed for the energy transition.” The partnership reflects BW ESS’ approach of working selectively with specialist local developers to build energy storage portfolios, combining local knowledge with the capabilities of a global owner-operator. It builds on BW ESS’ recent entry into the French market through the acquisition of two 100 MW/400 MWh BESS projects. Together, these investments have created a pipeline encompassing both greenfield and advanced projects, strengthening the company’s presence in France and establishing a foundation for continued growth. artigo.texto: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks. The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws. This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September. BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. But Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. While Beshear can’t stop the data center from happening, Anozie said, local governments can still make it difficult for projects to operate once they are built. “Where the states might have a way of regulating what is going on is using state environmental laws to challenge and to say, ‘Well, you didn't get the permit for this,’” he said. “But they cannot outrightly veto or zone out that area for a data center.” Amentum And DC Blox In South Carolina The Savannah River Site was one of 16 sites identified by the DOE in April 2025 to support the construction of data centers and the power infrastructure they require. The site was used to produce plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons in the 1950s, Spectrum News reported. Efforts at the site have centered on environmental cleanup and managing nuclear materials, as well as research and development. artigo.texto: U.S. construction economists continue to marvel at the historic strength of the data-center market, with unprecedented growth in project value and industry domination never before experienced. Experts assembled for the Construction Economy Outlook Fall 2026, presented by ConstructConnect on Nov. 12, spoke in superlatives throughout the webinar. Even threats such as growing public resistance and the uncertainty of financing may only cool the pace of data-center growth, not arrest it, they suggested. “We continue to see just amazing, unprecedented growth in data centers,” said ConstructConnect chief economist Michael Guckes. “Even though we’ve seen some political pushback on data centers, I think it’s too late. I think the train has left the station. “Once you have a technology with this kind of power, and other countries are competing in this realm for it, there’s no going backwards with this.” Guckes reported in 2022, the first $1-billion data center broke ground; in 2024, the U.S. had the first project that surpassed $3 billion; the next year saw the first $10-billion project; and now, he said, “Amazingly enough, we saw more starts in just January than we did in all of 2024. This is also the first time where we’re seeing these campuses of $50 billion and greater breaking ground.” Guckes added, “So this industry is not only huge for construction, but it has completely transformed within its own ranks. “If you go back to pre-COVID, you were seeing about 10 to 12 per cent of all non-residential construction dollars heading into megaprojects and now it’s more than one out of every $4.” Guckes was joined by Ken Simonson, chief economist, Associated General Contractors of America; Richard Branch, chief economist, American Institute of Architects (AIA); and Kristy O’Brien, director of content acquisition, ConstructConnect. Paul Hart, vice-president of economic content with ConstructConnect, served as the moderator. 2027 looks brighter Overall, U.S. construction spending is expected to remain slow, Branch said. Non-residential building construction spending is forecast to decline 0.3 per cent in 2026 before increasing three per cent in 2027, he said. Commercial construction is expected to grow 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 5.8 per cent in 2027, while industrial construction is expected to decline 11.6 per cent in 2026 and 0.6 per cent in 2027. Institutional construction is forecast to rise 2.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent, respectively. The Fed is expected to raise rates in the next year. “We’re probably looking at another 50 basis points of rate hikes between now and at this point next year,” said Branch. “I do think, though, if we start to see oil prices come down, that we’ll start to see inflation peel back, and as inflation peels back, particularly if it gets closer to their two-per-cent target, I think we will start to see they’re loosening rates.” Strong commercial numbers are largely because of data centers, Branch said. Traditional office construction is expected to decline five per cent and four per cent this year and next, respectively, while warehouse spending is forecast to decline 1.7 per cent in 2026 before increasing 1.4 per cent in 2027. Guckes reported ConstructConnect’s October 2026 economic forecast projects U.S. GDP growth of 2.1 per cent in 2026, rising to 2.4 per cent in 2027 and 2.7 per cent each of the next three years. Guckes identified various headwinds facing the construction sector: Higher interest rates make it harder to build profitably, while slow labour growth restrains the economy’s expansion. Inflation hurts consumers and spending, casting a shadow over the construction economy. Costs, rates squeeze margins O’Brien reported higher costs and rates are squeezing margins even as demand holds. She said tariffs and trade disruption continues to buffet the U.S. construction sector. Steel and aluminum imports have faced 50 per cent tariffs since June 2025, while overall construction material prices are up 11.0 per cent year-over-year, the fastest spike since May 2022. Tax cuts and business-investment incentives in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act continue to support demand, O’Brien stated. Bid prices are up 5.4 per cent. According to Simonson, tariffs, immigration enforcement, federal deficits and interest rates are the four major risks to construction. The concern is tighter immigration enforcement will worsen labour shortages. The webinar wrapped up with further roundtable discussion of the topic of the day. Branch said, “I think where that moratorium issue comes more is in 2028 spending data. There again, I don’t see a decline. I don’t see a collapse. I see more of a flat market in 2028 rather than a slowdown.” O’Brien noted Texas is leading in data-center construction, followed by Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas and the Midwest states. The sheer scale of the explosion, she said, brings constraints: power and water availability, public response and the cost of capital. Guckes said public pushback can be addressed in part through engineering. “Some of the solutions you talk about, noise, water, pollution of other types, a lot of those have engineering solutions…Those things generally just take money, and so far the data centers have access to a lot of it.”

artigo.texto: Com tecnologia da chinesa CATL, a expansão industrial em Belo Jardim permitirá fornecer sistemas de armazenamento com capacidade superior a 8 GWh, preparando a fabricante brasileira para atender aos grandes projetos do setor elétrico a partir de 2028. A Moura vai investir R$ 200 milhões em Pernambuco para ampliar sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, instalada em Belo Jardim, no Agreste do estado. O projeto inclui uma nova linha industrial, transferência de tecnologia da chinesa CATL e previsão de mais de 200 contratações, com início da produção ampliada esperado para 2027. Conhecida nacionalmente pelas baterias automotivas, a empresa agora pretende disputar espaço em um mercado que ganha importância com a expansão das usinas solares e eólicas: o armazenamento de eletricidade em equipamentos de grande porte. O investimento já está em execução. Segundo reportagem da Exame, publicada em 14 de novembro de 2026, a companhia prepara seu complexo industrial para atender aos projetos que disputarão o primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento de energia em baterias. - Em apenas 81 minutos, leilões de energia movimentam R$ 14,25 bilhões, garantem eletricidade para os próximos anos e levantam uma pergunta incômoda sobre a conta de luz - Quem paga conta de luz no Nordeste pode ter alta de 9,58% em 2027, enquanto o Sul terá queda de 7,59%: a Thymos Energia projeta tarifa 2% menor na média do país - Montadores de subestação no Rio Grande do Norte esperam 2.299 vagas no Lote 7 da Axia, que tem 42 meses de obra e negocia até R$ 680 milhões com o BID para 3 compensadores síncronos em Açu e João Câmara - Operadores da Termocabo, em Pernambuco, vão trocar 250 toneladas diárias de óleo combustível por gás natural nos 3 motores da usina, convertidos pela Wärtsilä para um contrato de 10 anos A capacidade de fornecimento anunciada supera 8 gigawatts-hora (GWh), colocando a nova operação em uma escala industrial voltada ao atendimento de grandes empreendimentos do setor elétrico. Fábrica da Moura em Pernambuco receberá nova linha de produção e tecnologia chinesa A ampliação ocorre no complexo industrial de Belo Jardim, onde a Moura mantém uma de suas principais operações produtivas. O prédio destinado à expansão já está pronto, enquanto a nova linha industrial foi adquirida na China. A expectativa é iniciar a produção dos equipamentos no fim do primeiro semestre de 2027. A parceria com a CATL, uma das maiores fabricantes mundiais de baterias, divide responsabilidades entre as duas companhias. A chinesa fornece tecnologia de armazenamento e participa da comercialização dos sistemas. A Moura ficará responsável pela industrialização, montagem e integração dos equipamentos no Brasil. O processo envolve receber módulos de baterias e integrá-los em sistemas completos, instalados em contêineres industriais de aproximadamente 20 pés, equipados com refrigeração e proteção contra incêndios. De acordo com informações publicadas pelo Jornal do Commercio, a fabricação nacional também está relacionada às condições de financiamento do BNDES, que podem exigir índices de conteúdo local entre 50% e 60%. A produção em Pernambuco permitirá concentrar no Brasil atividades de engenharia, integração, testes e assistência técnica, fortalecendo a cadeia industrial brasileira de armazenamento de energia. Moura prepara mais de 200 contratações para ampliar produção de baterias em Pernambuco A ampliação da fábrica em Belo Jardim deve impulsionar a geração de empregos no Agreste pernambucano. A Moura prevê contratar e capacitar mais de 200 profissionais para atender à nova linha de produção de sistemas de armazenamento de energia, desenvolvida em parceria com a chinesa CATL. Atualmente, o grupo possui aproximadamente 7.400 funcionários, dos quais cerca de 3.500 trabalham no complexo fabril de Belo Jardim. As novas contratações acompanharão a expansão das atividades industriais, com demandas relacionadas à montagem, integração e operação de sistemas de baterias de grande porte. Com investimento de R$ 200 milhões e início da produção previsto para 2027, a expansão fortalecerá a estrutura industrial da Moura em Pernambuco, ampliará sua capacidade de fornecimento e criará novas oportunidades profissionais em um segmento estratégico para o setor elétrico brasileiro. Sistemas de armazenamento poderão alcançar mais de 8 GWh e atender grandes projetos elétricos O principal produto da expansão será o BESS (Battery Energy Storage System), sistema capaz de armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, conforme a necessidade da rede. Esses equipamentos ganham relevância com o aumento da participação de fontes renováveis na matriz elétrica. Usinas solares concentram sua geração durante o dia, enquanto parques eólicos produzem de acordo com as condições de vento. O armazenamento permite aproveitar a energia gerada nesses períodos e disponibilizá-la em horários de maior demanda. As baterias contribuem para aumentar a flexibilidade operacional do sistema elétrico e favorecer a integração das fontes renováveis. A Moura desenvolve soluções de armazenamento desde meados da década passada e apresentou seu Moura BESS em 2019. Atualmente, a companhia acumula mais de 40 projetos instalados no Brasil, atendendo segmentos como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e infraestrutura elétrica. artigo.texto: Ministry of Heavy Industries Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh ACC Battery Manufacturing Capacity The tender covers 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity for grid-scale stationary storage applications under India's ₹18,100 crore PLI scheme. The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) manufacturing capacity under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for ACC battery storage. The capacity has been earmarked for grid-scale stationary storage (GSSS) applications and forms part of India's broader target to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The bids were submitted through a global tender floated on the Central Public Procurement (CPP) Portal to select companies for setting up giga-scale ACC manufacturing facilities in India. Technical bids were opened on November 11, 2026, at the Ministry of Heavy Industries in the presence of the participating bidders. The selection process is being conducted through a two-stage Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism. The 22 bidders include ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Avaada Electro, Exide Energy Solutions, Fujiyama Power Systems, GK Energy, Godawari New Energy, JPM Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy, Lineage Power, Mahendra Sponge and Power, and Megha Engineering and Infrastructures. Other companies that submitted bids include Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Reliance Industries, Renew Photovoltaics, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Sun Drops Energia, Utex New Energy, Vikram Solar, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions and Zetsol Energy. PLI Scheme Targets 50 GWh of ACC Manufacturing Capacity The tender is part of the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage, approved by the Union Cabinet in May 2021 with a budgetary allocation of ₹18,100 crore. The programme aims to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity and encourage domestic and international companies to set up manufacturing facilities in India. The 10 GWh allocation for grid-scale stationary storage is intended to address energy-storage requirements arising from the expansion of renewable energy capacity. The programme also seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and develop the local value chain for ACC technologies. The Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued on July 15, 2026, followed by a pre-bid conference on July 29. The deadline for submitting bids was November 10, with technical bids opened the following day. artigo.texto: Form Energy has appointed Lori Goler, former Chief People Officer at Meta, and Jon McNeill, a former senior executive at Tesla and Lyft, to its Board of Directors as the energy storage company prepares to expand manufacturing and commercial deployments of its iron-air battery technology. The appointments bring experience in organizational development, operations, sales, and scaling high-growth businesses. Goler currently serves as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, while McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of venture firm DVx Ventures. The appointments follow a significant period of financial and operational expansion for Form Energy, which is developing long-duration energy storage systems designed to improve electricity grid reliability and affordability. The company closed a $750 million Series G financing round in August 2026 and secured a $270 million credit facility in September to support manufacturing expansion and working capital requirements. The financing is supporting continued development of Form Factory 1, the company’s manufacturing facility in Weirton, West Virginia. Form Energy also expanded its executive leadership team with the appointments of Navneet Govil as Chief Financial Officer and Wes Sloan as Chief Operating Officer. Lori Goler Brings Experience Scaling Global Organizations Goler has served as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative since 2025, overseeing its work across science and education. Previously, she spent 16 years at Meta, serving as Chief People Officer from 2008 through 2024. During that period, she led the company’s global workforce strategy and organizational operations through substantial growth and transformation. Earlier in her career, Goler served as General Manager of eBay Stores and led consumer marketing at eBay. She was also a founding executive at online retailer eStyle. She previously served on the board of Stanford Health Care from 2013 to 2022. Goler holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, an MBA from Harvard Business School, and a Master of Public Policy from Harvard Kennedy School. Form Energy expects her experience developing organizational structures and managing workforce expansion to support its growing manufacturing and commercial operations. Jon McNeill Brings Tesla And Lyft Operating Experience McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of DVx Ventures, a venture firm focused on creating and scaling companies addressing large market opportunities. Previously, he served as Chief Operating Officer at Lyft between 2018 and 2019 and as President of Global Sales, Delivery and Service at Tesla from 2015 through 2018. Before joining Tesla, McNeill was CEO and chairman of the board at software company Enservio, where he served from 2006 to 2015. Throughout his career, he has founded and scaled six companies, many of which were subsequently acquired by publicly traded businesses. McNeill has served on the boards of Lululemon Athletica, CrossFit, and Asurion. He also previously served on the board of General Motors from 2022 through 2026. His additional board experience includes Cruise, Stash, Tekion, TIER Mobility, and TrueMotion. McNeill graduated from Northwestern University. Expanding Long-Duration Energy Storage Form Energy is developing iron-air battery systems designed to provide approximately 100 hours of energy storage. The technology uses iron, water, and air, materials the company describes as among the most abundant and affordable resources available. The batteries are designed to store electricity and discharge it over extended periods, providing a potential solution for balancing renewable energy generation and electricity demand. Long-duration storage could help utilities manage periods when wind and solar generation are limited, while improving the resilience of electricity networks. Form Energy is manufacturing its systems at Form Factory 1 in West Virginia as it prepares to serve customers across the United States and internationally. The addition of Goler and McNeill comes as the company moves from technology development toward broader commercial production and deployment. KEY QUOTE: “Lori and Jon have each led organizations through critical periods of rapid growth and I am pleased to welcome them to the Board. Lori spent 16 years at Meta building a global workforce and culture, and as our team grows, that experience will be invaluable. Jon has scaled operations, sales, and delivery at Tesla and Lyft, which is just what we need as we continue to ramp production and deploy iron-air batteries to customers across the United States and internationally. Their perspectives will guide how we grow, and I’m looking forward to working closely with both.” Mateo Jaramillo, Co-Founder And CEO Of Form Energy

artigo.texto: Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company (Masdar), a global clean energy leader, has celebrated the completion of the $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California, marking another major milestone in the company’s growing US renewable energy portfolio. The Lockhart complex was developed by Terra-Gen, which is jointly owned by Masdar and Igneo Infrastructure Partners. The project includes more than 925,000 solar modules and 248 battery enclosures. Its 365 megawatts (MW) of solar generation and 173.7 MW of battery storage generate enough electricity to meet the annual needs of approximately 350,000 homes and businesses. Khaleefa Almheiri, President and CEO of Masdar Americas, said: "The completion of Lockhart demonstrates the scale of Masdar’s ambitions in the United States and our commitment to supporting America’s growing energy needs. By bringing together Masdar’s global expertise, investment capabilities and track record of delivering major renewable energy projects with Terra-Gen’s strong local presence, we are delivering reliable, affordable power, creating skilled jobs and supporting economic growth. As electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI, advanced manufacturing and wider economic growth, Masdar is proud to be a long-term partner in powering America’s future." The milestone was commemorated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Hinkley facility, bringing together company employees, local officials, commercial lenders, project partners and customers. "Today is about recognising the people and partnerships that brought Lockhart to life and celebrating what this project means for the region," said John O’Connor, Chief Executive Officer at Terra-Gen. "Solar is one of the most economical sources of new electricity, and storage extends its value by making that energy available when it’s needed most. At the scale of our Lockhart facility, that combination can make a meaningful difference for California’s growing electricity needs." Engineering and construction of the solar and storage complex created more than 1,000 on-site jobs with 880,000 hours worked over four years. -TradeArabia News Service Copyright 2026 Al Hilal Publishing and Marketing Group Provided by SyndiGate Media Inc.
