artigo.texto: Côte d’Ivoire and Sweden Sign Landmark Article 6 Agreement at COP31, Advancing the Country’s Carbon Market Ambitions November 13, 2026 Category ANTALYA, Türkiye, November 13, 2026 – The signing of the Bilateral Agreement between Côte d’Ivoire and Sweden under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement at COP31 marks a major diplomatic milestone and an important step forward in strengthening Côte d’Ivoire’s participation in international carbon markets. This achievement builds on the progress made since 2024 through the Article 6 Climate Cooperation Fund (ACCTIF) – hosted under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) with contribution from the Swedish Energy Agency (SEA). With this support, GGGI has contributed to strengthening the institutional, regulatory and technical foundations of Côte d’Ivoire’s carbon market. This includes supporting the Government in advancing its governance framework, building institutional capacity and preparing for the operationalization of Article 6. Beyond strengthening institutional readiness, GGGI’s CTF has helped translate this progress into concrete opportunities for climate action. Following an Expression of Interest (EoI) launched in April 2025, two promising mitigation activity ideas were selected for further development in the clean transport and bioenergy sectors, laying the groundwork for a pipeline of future carbon projects. Together, these achievements reflect Côte d’Ivoire’s growing readiness to engage in international carbon market cooperation and demonstrate GGGI’s continued commitment to supporting the country in translating its carbon market ambitions into tangible climate action, investment opportunities and sustainable development benefits. “The Republic of Côte d’Ivoire reaffirms its ambition to make the carbon market a strategic instrument in support of its ecological transition, sustainable development, and climate commitments. The signing of the bilateral Agreement with the Kingdom of Sweden under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement paves the way for high-quality climate investments, technology transfer, and the development of high-impact projects, while upholding the principles of environmental integrity, transparency, and the prevention of double counting.” – Abou BAMBA, Minister of Environment and Ecological Transition, Côte d’Ivoire “Achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement will require investment at scale and the rapid deployment of climate solutions. We are pleased to further strengthen the partnership with Côte d’Ivoire as well with the Global Green Growth Institute, a key partner for Sweden in the implementation of article 6 of the Paris Agreement,” – Caroline Asserup, Director General of the Swedish Energy Agency “Carbon markets aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement require countries to cooperate with confidence and trust. This partnership between Sweden and Côte d’Ivoire shows what that cooperation looks like in practice. GGGI is proud to have facilitated it, in line with our mandate to advance green growth through country-led action.” – Fenella Aouane, Managing Director and Head of Carbon Finance, Global Green Growth Institute About the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) was founded as a treaty-based international, intergovernmental organization in 2012 at the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development. GGGI supports its Member States in transitioning their economies toward a green growth model that simultaneously achieves poverty reduction, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and economic growth. With 54 Member States and 30 Partner countries and regional integration organizations in the process of accession, GGGI delivers programs and projects in over 57 countries. These initiatives encompass developing innovative green growth solutions, technical support, capacity building, policy planning & implementation, and assistance in building a pipeline of bankable green investment projects, project financing, investments, and knowledge sharing. GGGI’s work contributes to its Member States’ efforts to fulfill the Sustainable Development Goals and the Nationally Determined Contributions to the Paris Agreement. About the Carbon Transaction Facility The Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) is a country-driven mechanism that enables governments and private sectors – particularly in developing countries and emerging economies – to engage meaningfully in Article 6 carbon markets. By uniquely combining strong preparedness support with structured transaction facilitation, the CTF offers a full-cycle pathway – evolving readiness into results – to access and benefit from international carbon market mechanisms. The CTF facilitates partnerships, supporting host countries in implementing climate action while also helping buyers advance their climate commitments. As a technical enabler and trusted partner, the CTF helps drive forward transparent, high-integrity, and inclusive carbon transactions aligned with the Paris Agreement. The CTF is comprised of the Article 6 Readiness Facility, a multi-donor fund to provide readiness support, as well as three Carbon Funds: the Article 6 Climate Cooperation Fund (ACCTIF) opened by Sweden, the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund opened by Norway, and the Singapore Article 6 Carbon Facility (SACF) opened by Singapore. artigo.texto: Suzhou, China (ANTARA/PRNewswire)- BloombergNEF (BNEF) has released its Q4 2026 Tier 1 list of global energy storage manufacturers, with LONGi securing its 10th consecutive quarterly listing. The recognition reflects its track record in global project delivery, system integration and commercial execution. This quarter, BNEF introduced stricter project financing requirements, requiring qualifying projects to secure non-recourse financing from at least two commercial banks. The higher threshold places greater emphasis on project bankability and commercial viability, adding significance to LONGi's continued inclusion. Full-Stack Innovation Strengthens System-Level Capabilities Under its LONGi ONE strategy, LONGi has developed a full-stack, in-house 5S technology platform spanning iCCS, BMS, PCS, TMS and EMS. This enables native system integration and coordinated management across utility-scale, commercial and industrial (C&I), and microgrid applications. By combining proprietary technologies with integrated system design, this approach supports reliable performance and efficient project execution. A unified responsibility framework and Long-Term Service Agreements (LTSA) provide support throughout the project lifecycle. Global Projects Demonstrate Versatility Across Applications LONGi's global projects demonstrate the adaptability of its solutions across diverse power markets, grid requirements and operating environments. In Australia, the 5MW/20MWh Lunio Energy project in South Australia was connected to the grid in September 2026 and entered the National Electricity Market (NEM), enabling participation in electricity market trading. In Germany, a project in Stralsund integrated energy storage with an existing solar-thermal plant, delivering frequency response in under 50 milliseconds to support grid stability and power quality for critical infrastructure. LONGi also demonstrates its capabilities in challenging environments. In Finland, a microgrid solution achieved black start in under two minutes, supporting independent power supply in extreme cold. In coastal Italy, a 50.16MWh storage system integrated with a 35MWp solar plant features comprehensive anti-corrosion protection, maintaining over 99% system availability in high-salt and high-humidity conditions. Advancing Global Energy Storage Capabilities From proprietary technologies and integrated solutions to global project delivery and lifecycle services, LONGi continues to strengthen its capabilities across the energy storage value chain. The launch of its new smart manufacturing base also further enhances manufacturing and delivery capacity for global markets. Looking ahead, LONGi will continue to advance its LONGi ONE strategy, combining full-stack innovation, global project experience, smart manufacturing and localized services to deliver efficient, reliable energy storage solutions and support the global energy transition. artigo.texto: Running for City Council in Farmington this year, Ben Blomgren said voters asked him about data centers more than anything else. “This was the issue that everyone wanted to talk about,” he said. “When I went door to door, it was about the data center.” Blomgren had a clear position on the proposed Farmington Technology Park hyperscale data center project. He opposed it, and, if elected, would vote against it at every turn. On Election Day, the candidate earned the most votes out of six people running for two open seats. When he takes office in January, he’ll be one of a host of newly elected leaders in Minnesota bringing skeptical stances against data centers to local governments. A spike in voter turnout in Farmington and other cities linked to data centers helped these candidates win, according to data from the Minnesota Secretary of State. The data center effect Data centers became a new election issue in Minnesota this year. After city leaders opened doors to developments – sometimes using nondisclosure agreements to keep details out of the public eye – residents in suburban Farmington and Greater Minnesota cities like Hermantown, Faribault, Pine Island and Monticello organized against them. In the face of this loud opposition, projects mostly inched forward unless courts slowed them down. But the issue contributed to an uptick in candidates filing to run in local government elections this year. On the campaign trail, at forums and in newspaper articles, data centers dominated the discourse. Several races offered stark differences between candidates on the issue. Related: Data centers in Minnesota: The next big election issue Pine Island’s mayoral race, for example, featured an appointed incumbent who supported Google’s data center project against a candidate motivated to run against it. The latter, Mark Lang, won in a landslide. Voter turnout data showed 12% more people in Pine Island voted in the race compared with the last midterm race in 2022. The rise, though, was about in line with Minnesota’s 13% increase in voter turnout between the two years. In Hermantown, tensions flared in late October when council members approved a key step in the regulatory process for another Google-backed data center. Days later, voters ousted one of the council members involved, Andy Hjelle. Two members of Stop the Hermantown Data Center, Emma Richtman and Candi Mock, beat him in a race for two open seats, helped by an 18% increase in voter turnout. Other races had more staggering turnout spikes. Faring well in Faribault and Farmington Farmington’s city council race had 48% more voters than in 2022. Along with a robust slate of candidates, a special mayoral election drew people to the polls. But the sitting council’s data center decisions clearly played an important role, Blomgren said. He lives about 1,000 feet from where the hyperscale development could be built. There are residents who live much closer. “People built their homes to the west side of the property thinking it would be a golf course or homes,” he said. “When you build a home next to a railroad track, you know a railroad track is there. You don’t build your home thinking there will be a data center.” He isn’t opposed to data centers per se, but said he is against projects of such a massive size receiving selective rezoning near residential neighborhoods. Related: In pausing data centers, Minnesota courts did what local officials wouldn’t “The scale is really the issue,” he said. “Few people are as worried about a gas station next to them. A lot of people would be if it were a refinery.” Even more than Farmington, Faribault had the largest rise in voter turnout among cities linked to data centers. About 61% more votes were cast in the southern Minnesota city this year than in 2022. A deep field of candidates likely contributed to the uptick. Also, none of the six candidates running for three spots expressed support for data centers ahead of the election. The top vote-getter, Natalie Halverson, said she thinks opposition to data centers partly explains the huge turnout at polling places. “It is a big looming issue,” she said. “People want to know where people stand on that. I think it might have driven some people to be a little bit more engaged.” ‘A hot-button issue’ among many The election wasn’t all about data centers, however, she cautioned. Faribault faces major challenges apart from whether a data center development is worth it, including housing shortages and maintaining healthcare access. Halverson and other candidates talked about those issues and data centers during their campaigns. “It’s a hot-button issue,” she said of data centers. “But Faribault is not a one-issue town.” The same is true in other cities. Blomgren’s campaign site pointed out Farmington needs a grocery store, right under his stance on data centers. It’s reasonable to conclude data centers were not the sole driver, but rather an important driver, of voting this year. At a postelection panel at Minnesota State University in Mankato, political scientist Kevin Parsneau noted the issue featured prominently in state legislative races. A state House race in the area, District 18A covering North Mankato and St. Peter, had ads pinning a pro-data center stance on Republican incumbent Erica Schwartz. She lost to DFL challenger Leah Hanson, part of a blue wave carrying her party to legislative majorities. Stances on data centers don’t entirely fall along partisan lines, Parsneau said, but President Donald Trump’s loud support for data centers before the election may have had an impact. “Probably Donald Trump didn’t do Republicans a favor by being very much for data centers,” he said. His colleague, political scientist Fred Slocum, noticed campaign ads centered around data centers in the close 1st Congressional District race. The winning Democratic candidate, Jake Johnson, called for a moratorium on the projects, distinguishing himself from Republican incumbent Brad Fins

artigo.texto: SC26 Preview: AI-HPC Convergence Takes Center Stage in Chicago As the high-performance computing community prepares to gather in Chicago for SC26, November 15–20, the latest episode of the Data Center Frontier Show offers a timely preview of the technologies, market developments, and infrastructure challenges expected to shape this year's conference. Hosted by DCF Contributing Editor Doug Black, the conversation brings together Lois Curfman McInnes, Argonne Distinguished Fellow and senior computational scientist at Argonne National Laboratory; Addison Snell, founder and CEO of Intersect 360 Research; and Earl Joseph, CEO of Hyperion Research. The episode also inaugurates Data Center Frontier's new Frontier Computing channel, expanding DCF's coverage of the technologies and infrastructure driving the convergence of high-performance computing, AI, QC and next-generation scientific discovery. The central theme is unmistakable. AI is no longer simply an adjunct to traditional supercomputing. It is changing how scientific computing itself is performed. "We're really moving beyond focusing just on bigger machines, faster machines," McInnes observes, pointing to the growing integration of AI into scientific software development, simulations, and research workflows. Joseph underscores the acceleration, citing new Hyperion research finding that 70% of respondents are already using AI for code generation. The panel also examines the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, a sweeping effort to link supercomputers, large-scale AI infrastructure, and cloud resources in support of scientific discovery. Joseph calls Genesis "the first time I've ever seen something that's truly a broad national resource," while Snell emphasizes that investments in AI infrastructure must be matched by investments in science itself. For data center professionals, the discussion turns to increasingly consequential questions about the economics and sustainability of the AI buildout. Snell warns that the industry's focus on rapid construction has outpaced serious discussion of infrastructure lifecycles and upgrades. Joseph highlights the mounting difficulty of financing supercomputers costing $100 million or more when new GPU generations arrive roughly every 12 months. The group also considers growing public opposition to data center development, with Joseph arguing that the industry has yet to adequately communicate the societal value of its infrastructure investments. Looking ahead to the SC26 exhibition floor, the discussion touches on quantum computing's longer-term prospects, photonics, advanced cooling technologies, processor sovereignty, and the challenge of preserving traditional HPC capabilities as hardware becomes increasingly optimized for AI. Together, these issues provide a preview of an SC26 conference increasingly defined not simply by computing performance, but by the opportunities and trade-offs of building the next generation of AI and scientific infrastructure. Listen to the full DCF Show conversation for Doug Black's SC26 preview with McInnes, Snell, and Joseph. At Data Center Frontier, we talk the industry talk and walk the industry walk. In that spirit, DCF Staff members may occasionally use AI tools to assist with content. Keep pace with the fast-moving world of data centers and cloud computing by connecting with Data Center Frontier on LinkedIn, following us on X/Twitter and Facebook, as well as on BlueSky, and signing up for our weekly newsletters using the form below. About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem Private Limited, a group company of Advait Energy Transitions Limited (AETL), has appointed Bhushan Shahane as its Chief Operating Officer (COO). In a press release, Advait Energy Transitions explained that Shahane will lead the Advait Group's BESS business, overseeing its manufacturing and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) operations. His responsibilities will include accelerating business growth, strengthening operational capabilities, improving execution efficiency and supporting the company's expansion across the energy storage value chain. With nearly two decades of experience across energy infrastructure, manufacturing and large-scale project execution, Shahane's appointment marks an important step in strengthening the company's leadership as it expands its presence in India's Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) sector. The appointment comes as Advait Battery Ecosystem advances its strategy to develop integrated energy storage manufacturing and project execution capabilities. The company is focused on strengthening the technical and operational foundations required to support larger and more complex BESS deployments. Bringing Experience Across Energy Infrastructure and Storage Prior to joining Advait Battery Ecosystem, he was associated with ABB and GE Vernova, where he gained experience across power system infrastructure, manufacturing and energy-related operations. He also spent four years at Amperehour Energy, where he led key BESS infrastructure projects for electricity distribution companies and utility-scale applications. His experience in energy storage project development and execution provides a foundation for leading Advait's expanding BESS operations. Leadership Commentary Commenting on the appointment, Shalin Sheth, Founder and Managing Director of Advait Energy Transitions Limited, said, "Energy storage is becoming an increasingly important part of India's power infrastructure, and building strong manufacturing and execution capabilities will be essential to meeting the sector's evolving requirements. At Advait, our focus is on creating an integrated BESS business supported by engineering expertise, reliable technology partnerships and operational excellence".

artigo.texto: O Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (LAPIN), em cooperação com centros de pesquisa e entidades do terceiro setor, estrutura o lançamento do Observatório Latino-Americano de Data Centers para fevereiro de 2027, com foco inicial nas operações instaladas no Brasil e no México. A iniciativa, divulgada pela Fundação Heinrich Böll, propõe monitorar as externalidades socioambientais decorrentes da expansão acelerada de infraestruturas físicas de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial no continente, mapeando desde o consumo intensivo de recursos naturais até eventuais conflitos fundiários e litígios regulatórios. A estruturação da plataforma foi apresentada durante as atividades do II Seminário Inteligência Artificial, Meio Ambiente e Justiça Socioambiental, realizado em Fortaleza nos dias 9 e 10 de novembro de 2026. Conforme os organizadores, a finalidade técnica é consolidar um banco de dados regional que registre licenças ambientais, contestações judiciais e métricas de sustentabilidade, estabelecendo metodologias comparativas para avaliar o custo-benefício econômico e ecológico dos complexos tecnológicos voltados à computação em nuvem. Expansão da infraestrutura digital e pressões locais O avanço de cargas de trabalho orientadas à inteligência artificial generativa exige instalações de alta densidade computacional, o que tem direcionado investimentos globais para mercados emergentes com disponibilidade de energia renovável. No território brasileiro, o levantamento preliminar do observatório abrange projetos estratégicos, a exemplo do empreendimento associado à plataforma TikTok projetado para Caucaia (CE) e iniciativas industriais de processamento em análise para Eldorado do Sul (RS). De acordo com a Fundação Heinrich Böll, a chegada desses investimentos costuma ser acompanhada por promessas de atração de capital, modernização tributária e geração de empregos qualificados, mas gera preocupações técnicas quanto à sobrecarga da rede de distribuição elétrica e à captação em bacias hidrográficas sob estresse hídrico. A entidade e seus parceiros apontam que os modelos de resfriamento evaporativo convencionais podem competir com demandas prioritárias de abastecimento regional caso não adotem circuitos fechados ou tecnologias de resfriamento líquido avançado. Durante o seminário em Fortaleza, líderes e pesquisadores do Brasil, do México e do Chile confrontaram experiências sobre a implantação de complexos de hiperescala em seus respectivos países. As discussões indicaram padrões semelhantes nas fases de prospecção, marcadas, segundo os participantes, pela assimetria de informações técnicas disponibilizadas às comunidades lindeiras e aos órgãos de controle durante o rito de licenciamento. Demandas hídricas e desafios do licenciamento ambiental Os requisitos de resfriamento contínuo em instalações de missão crítica impõem aos operadores a necessidade de compatibilizar a eficiência de uso de energia (PUE) com a eficiência no uso da água (WUE). O LAPIN sustenta que, em localidades do semiárido e zonas costeiras, a ausência de estudos detalhados de impacto cumulativo pode gerar vulnerabilidades operacionais para as próprias mantenedoras dos data centers, além de riscos jurídicos atrelados à segurança hídrica. A diretora-presidente do LAPIN, Cynthia Picolo, afirmou no evento que os relatos colhidos no México e no Chile reproduzem a dinâmica identificada no Ceará. No caso do município de Caucaia, a organização realizou escutas com o povo indígena Anacé e interlocuções com órgãos do Ministério Público, apontando a necessidade de realização de consulta prévia, livre e informada, nos moldes da Convenção 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho. O diretor executivo do LAPIN, Felipe Silva, pontuou que os projetos de grande porte frequentemente enfrentam fragilidades na transparência dos dados de consumo e na concessão de outorgas hídricas. A entidade argumenta que o monitoramento independente auxiliará na redução de assimetrias, municiando tanto a sociedade civil quanto os investidores com parâmetros objetivos de conformidade regulatória e boas práticas de governança socioambiental (ESG). Cooperação interamericana e governança institucional Os debates promovidos no seminário envolveram a participação de Javier Palummo, relator especial sobre Direitos Econômicos, Sociais, Culturais e Ambientais da Comissão Interamericana de Direitos Humanos (CIDH), vinculada à Organização dos Estados Americanos (OEA). A presença do órgão reforça a busca das entidades civis por parâmetros internacionais de responsabilização corporativa na esteira de investimentos tecnológicos transfronteiriços. A construção do observatório conta com a atuação conjunta de organizações com histórico de incidência política e científica no continente. O LAPIN, fundado em 2016 em Brasília, atua em quatro linhas prioritárias: vigilância digital, inteligência artificial e novas tecnologias, desinformação e governança de dados, além de economia digital. A instituição integra a iniciativa ao lado do Instituto Terramar, que atua na zona costeira cearense, do projeto investigativo O Joio e O Trigo e da aliança global de financiadores Green Screen Coalition. A Fundação Heinrich Böll, organização ligada ao Partido Verde alemão com presença de mais de duas décadas e meia no Brasil, atua como parceira estratégica na estruturação da pauta. A instituição concentra esforços na interface entre direitos humanos, transição ecológica e governança tecnológica, defendendo que a transformação digital latino-americana não reproduza modelos predatórios de exploração de recursos naturais em benefício exclusivo de cadeias de valor externas. artigo.texto: Mercado global de ventilação para baterias: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de ventilação para baterias até 2035: demanda por segurança acelera com a expansão do BESS Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de ventilação para baterias, o mercado inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de ventilação para baterias entra em uma fase de expansão estrutural, impulsionado pela rápida implantação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia com baterias de íons de lítio (BESS) e pelo endurecimento de códigos de segurança que exigem mitigação certificada de fuga térmica. As aberturas de ventilação para baterias, antes tratadas como componentes de baixo custo, são hoje reconhecidas como subsistemas de segurança críticos que influenciam a bancabilidade dos projetos, as condições de seguro e as aprovações de interligação à rede. A demanda se bifurca: ventilação de alto volume e custo otimizado para células de veículos elétricos de grande consumo, e soluções de ventilação altamente projetadas e específicas para armazenamento estacionário de grande porte, onde as consequências de falha são graves. Até 2035, o crescimento será sustentado pela integração de renováveis em escala de utilidade, pela energia de reserva de data centers e por aplicações de resiliência industrial, sobretudo em regiões com metas ambiciosas de descarbonização. No entanto, o mercado enfrenta gargalos nos ciclos de qualificação, no fornecimento de materiais especializados e na necessidade de instalação junto às gigafábricas. Este relatório oferece uma análise estruturada do tamanho de mercado, da segmentação, da dinâmica competitiva e das perspectivas regionais, proporcionando aos tomadores de decisão uma visão comercialmente fundamentada do mercado de ventilação para baterias de 2026 a 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de ventilação para baterias até 2035 pressupõe a continuidade da aceleração das instalações globais de BESS, apoiada por metas de energia renovável, requisitos de estabilidade da rede e queda dos custos de baterias. Espera-se que a ventilação para baterias deixe de ser um componente secundário para se tornar um subsistema de segurança reconhecido, com demanda cada vez mais moldada por exigências regulatórias como a NFPA 855 e a IEC 62933-5-2, que requerem prevenção certificada de fuga térmica. Projeta-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta anual de 9,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 245 (2025=100). O crescimento se concentrará na Ásia-Pacífico, impulsionado pela liderança da China na fabricação de baterias, seguida pela América do Norte e pela Europa, onde códigos de segurança e incentivos à localização criam novas exigências para as cadeias de suprimento. A pressão sobre os preços persistirá no nível dos componentes, mas o valor migrará para módulos de segurança integrados e sistemas de ventilação conectados ao BMS. Entre as principais incertezas estão o ritmo de comercialização das baterias de estado sólido, que poderia alterar os requisitos de ventilação, e a disponibilidade de polímeros especializados e de capacidade de usinagem de precisão. No geral, a perspectiva é positiva, com a demanda sustentada pelo papel crítico da ventilação na prevenção da propagação térmica e na garantia de operação segura em diversos ambientes de implantação. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Rápida expansão das instalações de BESS em escala de utilidade, impulsionada pela integração de renováveis e por requisitos de estabilidade da rede - Códigos e normas de segurança rigorosos (NFPA 855, IEC 62933-5-2) que exigem prevenção certificada de fuga térmica - Adoção crescente de baterias de íons de lítio em veículos elétricos e armazenamento estacionário, ampliando a necessidade de ventilação confiável - Exigências crescentes de seguro e bancabilidade que tratam a ventilação como componente crítico de segurança - Avanços tecnológicos em acionamento de precisão e integração com o BMS para análises preditivas de segurança - Localização das cadeias de suprimento de baterias junto às gigafábricas, criando demanda por fornecedores de ventilação instalados nas proximidades Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Ciclos longos de qualificação e testes (de vários anos), que criam barreiras à entrada e retardam a troca de fornecedores - Dependência de polímeros especializados, ligas metálicas e usinagem de precisão, com fluxos limitados de materiais qualificados - Poder de precificação concentrado nos integradores de sistemas e fabricantes de células, comprimindo as margens dos componentes - Possível disrupção decorrente da comercialização de baterias de estado sólido, que poderia reduzir ou alterar os requisitos de ventilação - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimento devido à necessidade de instalação junto às gigafábricas e de entrega just-in-time Estrutura da demanda por setor de uso final Concessionárias de energia e operadores de rede (participação estimada: 35%) As concessionárias de energia e os operadores de rede formam o maior setor de uso final da ventilação para baterias, impulsionados pela expansão global dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia com baterias (BESS) em escala de utilidade para integrar a geração renovável e prestar serviços de estabilidade da rede. Nesse segmento, a ventilação é fundamental para gerenciar os riscos de fuga térmica em baterias de íons de lítio de grande porte, onde as consequências de falha são graves e o escrutínio regulatório é intenso. artigo.texto: A provedora de infraestrutura digital Ascenty anunciou, em 12 de novembro de 2026, a abertura do programa Academia Ascenty, iniciativa desenhada para selecionar e contratar 40 profissionais para o cargo de Analista de Infraestrutura. Segundo informações divulgadas pela companhia, os contratados ingressam imediatamente sob o regime da Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT) antes do início do ciclo formativo de nove meses, com início planejado para janeiro de 2027 no campus corporativo localizado em Hortolândia, no interior de São Paulo. A organização sustenta que o objetivo central da iniciativa reside em qualificar mão de obra técnica para atuar diretamente em ambientes de missão crítica sem exigir experiência prévia no segmento de centros de processamento de dados. Conforme detalhado no comunicado da empresa, o processo seletivo destina-se a candidatos com formação em áreas correlatas, tais como elétrica, refrigeração, automação predial e manutenção industrial. A empresa alega que a proposta visa atender demandas operacionais imediatas e futuras decorrentes da expansão dos parques tecnológicos na Região Metropolitana de Campinas, abrangendo os municípios de Sumaré, Vinhedo, Campinas e circunvizinhanças. Após a etapa de formação teórica e prática supervisionada, a entidade afirma que os colaboradores serão alocados prioritariamente no novo data center Sumaré 03 (SUM03), unidade atualmente em fase de obras. Demanda por capacidade computacional e adensamento regional A proliferação de serviços em nuvem, aliada à expansão acelerada de aplicações de inteligência artificial corporativa, gerou uma corrida por ativos imobiliários e energéticos de alta densidade no território brasileiro. Tradicionalmente, o estado de São Paulo concentra o maior volume de tráfego de dados e infraestrutura de telecomunicações do país. Dentro desse mapa, o eixo rodoviário entre Campinas e Hortolândia consolidou-se como um dos principais polos de acolhimento de instalações de hiperescala, beneficiando-se da proximidade com subestações elétricas de grande porte, rotas estruturadas de fibra óptica e oferta de mão de obra técnica oriunda de universidades e escolas politécnicas regionais. Contudo, operadoras globais e regionais enfrentam recorrentemente escassez de quadros especializados aptos a lidar com as peculiaridades de ambientes tolerantes a falhas. Ao contrário da manutenção predial convencional ou da indústria fabril seriada, as instalações de tecnologia exigem aderência contínua a protocolos de disponibilidade ininterrupta (uptime). A necessidade de garantir níveis de serviço de alta disponibilidade (Tier III ou superior) transforma a gestão de contingência elétrica e térmica em um ativo estratégico de conformidade contratual perante corporações dos setores financeiro, de saúde e comércio eletrônico. Estrutura curricular e metodologia de imersão técnica De acordo com a Ascenty, o modelo pedagógico formulado para a Academia Ascenty contempla uma carga de 100 horas dedicadas exclusivamente ao conteúdo teórico, seguida de módulos práticos integrados à rotina operacional do data center de Hortolândia. A entidade afirma que a grade acadêmica abrange fundamentos termodinâmicos, balanceamento de cargas em corrente contínua e alternada, protocolos de segurança de sistemas de alta tensão e metodologias para detecção precoce de incidentes físicos. A capacitação abordará os seguintes eixos tecnológicos centrais: - Sistemas elétricos de potência: Manuseio e supervisão de geradores a diesel de grande porte, no-breaks rotativos ou estáticos (UPS), quadros de transferência automática e transformadores dedicados. - Refrigeração e HVAC de precisão: Operação de chillers industriais, unidades de tratamento de ar (CRAH/CRAC), sistemas de contenção de corredores quentes e frios, além de técnicas avançadas de gerenciamento de fluxo aerodinâmico. - Automação e telemetria predial: Interação direta com plataformas de gerenciamento de infraestrutura de data center (DCIM) e sistemas SCADA para controle de variáveis físicas em tempo real. - Continuidade de negócios e segurança: Normas internacionais de gestão de riscos, procedimentos operacionais padronizados (SOPs), métodos de intervenção emergencial (EOPs) e conformidade com normas regulamentadoras nacionais. Conforme declarou Gustavo do Carmo, gerente de educação técnica da Ascenty, em material oficial de divulgação, o crescimento acelerado da infraestrutura digital abre portas para perfis multidisciplinares que anteriormente não consideravam esse ramo econômico. O porta-voz alega que o compromisso com a disciplina de procedimentos e a predisposição para o aprendizado contínuo constituem bases prioritárias para a construção da carreira na empresa, sobrepondo-se à exigência de bagagem prévia no nicho de missão crítica. Integração operacional e horizonte de expansão física A transição dos estudantes para o trabalho de campo diário ocorrerá sob mentoria direta dos engenheiros e operadores sêniores da companhia. A Ascenty sustenta que essa aproximação visa atenuar os riscos inerentes à operação de maquinário pesado e sistemas complexos, permitindo que a tomada de decisão em situações de contingência seja calibrada em conformidade com as diretrizes globais da organização. O modelo de negócios da empresa apoia-se em sua estrutura societária, sustentada por uma joint venture entre a Digital Realty e a gestora de ativos alternativos Brookfield Infrastructure. Atualmente, a operadora reporta um portfólio composto por 40 data centers operacionais ou em diferentes fases de implantação distribuídos por Brasil, Chile, México e Colômbia. Essas estruturas estão interconectadas por uma malha proprietária de aproximadamente 4.000 quilômetros de redes subterrâneas de fibra óptica. A companhia declara ainda que disponibiliza a arquitetura ServiceFabric, solução desenvolvida para viabilizar orquestração dinâmica entre múltiplas plataformas de nuvem pública, ambientes corporativos dedicados e cargas pesa

artigo.texto: A governadora de Pernambuco, Raquel Lyra (PSD), defendeu que a atração de novos investimentos tecnológicos para o Estado seja acompanhada de planejamento e contrapartidas econômicas e sociais. A declaração foi feita nesta quinta-feira (12), durante participação no REC’n’Play 2026, no Bairro do Recife, em um painel sobre inovação, inteligência artificial e desenvolvimento. Ao lado do presidente do Porto Digital, Pierre Lucena, a governadora levantou questionamentos sobre a instalação de data centers em Pernambuco, especialmente diante dos desafios relacionados ao abastecimento de água e à demanda por energia. Raquel destacou que o Estado precisa avaliar quais benefícios esses empreendimentos efetivamente deixarão para a população, considerando a geração de empregos, o desenvolvimento tecnológico e o retorno econômico. “Eu vou botar data center aqui, mas nós vamos desenvolver inteligência artificial aqui? Ou eu vou botar data center aqui para estar servindo de armazenamento para outro lugar, consumindo a minha água e a minha energia?”, questionou. A governadora também chamou atenção para a necessidade de estabelecer prioridades diante da escassez de recursos naturais. Como exemplo, citou atividades econômicas já presentes em Pernambuco, como os polos cervejeiro e de confecções, que também demandam recursos hídricos. Tecnologia e desenvolvimento econômico Durante o debate, Raquel Lyra defendeu que Pernambuco avance na construção de uma economia baseada em inovação, ciência e tecnologia. A gestora afirmou que o Estado possui potencial para ocupar posição de destaque no cenário tecnológico, mas precisa transformar suas capacidades em oportunidades concretas de desenvolvimento. A governadora também manifestou interesse em ampliar a parceria com o Porto Digital e fortalecer a participação do Governo de Pernambuco na contratação de soluções desenvolvidas por empresas do setor tecnológico. Outro ponto abordado foi a necessidade de reduzir a burocracia nos processos de contratação e ampliar a utilização da tecnologia na administração pública, especialmente em áreas como saúde e gestão de serviços. Educação e formação profissional Raquel também destacou a importância de investir na formação de profissionais para acompanhar as transformações do mercado de trabalho. Durante sua participação, chamou atenção para os desafios da educação básica, especialmente no ensino da matemática, e defendeu o fortalecimento da formação científica e tecnológica dos estudantes. A gestora ainda mencionou iniciativas estaduais de incentivo à inovação, como o Inova PE e o programa Cientista Arretado, voltado à aproximação entre pesquisadores e a gestão pública. Ao defender um planejamento de longo prazo, Raquel afirmou que Pernambuco precisa pensar seu desenvolvimento para além dos ciclos eleitorais, reunindo representantes do poder público, universidades e setor produtivo na construção de estratégias para os próximos dez anos. A participação da governadora integrou a programação da oitava edição do REC’n’Play, festival de tecnologia, inovação, criatividade e cultura realizado entre os dias 11 e 14 de novembro, no Bairro do Recife.

artigo.texto: Statkraft starts commercial operations at first phase of 750MW Neilston BESS project “Urgent action is needed to transform our electricity grid and make it fit for the future,” said Statkraft UK and Ireland country manager Kevin O’Donovan. Norwegian renewable energy developer Statkraft has started commercial operations at the first 50MW phase of its 750MW Neilston Greener Grid Park, a battery energy storage system (BESS) outside Paisley in Scotland. The project is Statkraft’s first grid-forming BESS in the UK to enter commercial operation, and follows over three years of construction, which began in August 2023. The Scottish government granted approval for Statkraft to expand the project to 750MW in August 2025, but the company did not provide a timetable for this expansion this week. While Statkraft did not disclose the duration of the project, it is likely between 1-hour and 2-hour. If it's main purpose is grid-forming applications, a relatively short duration is likely. “Innovative projects like Neilston Greener Grid Park will help us to move away from fossil fuels to a low-carbon electricity system, stabilising consumer bills and strengthening Great Britain’s energy security,” said Statkraft UK and Ireland country manager Kevin O’Donovan. “Urgent action is needed to transform our electricity grid and make it fit for the future.” The successful realisation of the first part of the project forms part of Statkraft’s investments into the UK’s renewable energy sector, which exceeds £2 billion. Already this year, the company has secured planning permission for a 32MW solar-plus-storage project in Cornwall and started commercial operations at a 20MW BESS in Cushaling. Statkraft has a number of other projects under development as part of its ‘Greener Grid Park’ portfolio, including the 50MW Coylton project, also in Scotland, at which construction began in July 2024. The company described the project this week as its “second-grid firming BESS scheme”. Ampeak receives e-STORAGE batteries for 240MW Afon Wysg 1 project In other BESS news, developer Ampeak Energy announced this week that it had received deliveries of batteries and “key components” for its 240MWh Afon Wysg 1 project. The 55 batteries for the project were supplied by e-STORAGE, the BESS subsidiary of Canadian Solar that will also be responsible for commissioning work, and were installed by Jones Bros Civil Engineering. Ampeak expects to energise the project later this month and reach full commercial operation in the first quarter of 2027. The project is part of the Uskmouth Sustainable Energy Park in Wales, which could support around 3.5GWh of BESS and at which Ampeak expects to build three BESS projects, including the 250MW/1,250MWh Afon Wysg 2 project, for which it received planning permission last year. Ampeak CEO designate David Taaffe added that the company plans to expand the Afon Wysg 1 project to 480MWh. “The progress achieved on site is testament to the commitment and expertise of everyone involved,” said Taaffe. “We will then move to rapidly financially close the expansion to 480MWh which can be implemented with minimal disruption to the 240MWh operating asset.” The news follows a number of other encouraging BESS advancements in the UK, including Danish company Ørsted completing construction at a 300MW/600MWh system near Norwich, its first in the UK, and the government offering £28 million in grant funding for ultra-long duration energy storage. This takes place in the context of the UK struggling considerably with grid connection availability for new energy projects, which has led to the National Energy System Operator (NESO) looking to reform the grid connection process in the country; prior to these reforms, NESO figures showed that the UK’s grid queue stood at over 700GW. UK prime minister Andy Burnham has also announced plans for a new publicly-owned company to invest in the UK’s grid infrastructure, and lawyer Shraiya Thapa wrote a guest blog for Solar Power Portal last month about the potential impacts of the proposed Great British Grid.

artigo.texto: A estatal mineira Cemig pretende participar dos leilões de baterias de dezembro, quando prevê uma competição acirrada, com preços agressivos diante do elevado número de projetos cadastrados. Durante teleconferência sobre os resultados do terceiro trimestre do ano, o superintendente de Expansão de Geração e Transmissão da Cemig, Fredstwon Reis Pereira, afirmou que, embora a demanda que será efetivamente contratada ainda não seja conhecida, a expectativa é de os preços sejam “bastante pressionados”. A discussão ocorre em um momento de execução de um programa de investimentos de aproximadamente R$ 7 bilhões em 2026. Até o terceiro trimestre, a companhia havia realizado cerca de 75% do montante previsto para o ano. A distribuição concentra a maior parcela dos aportes, com aproximadamente R$ 4,1 bilhões investidos. O objetivo é avançar na execução do ciclo de investimentos até a revisão tarifária da distribuidora, prevista para 2028. A transmissão recebeu quase R$ 500 milhões, principalmente em reforços e melhorias, enquanto os investimentos em geração estão relacionados, sobretudo, à manutenção dos ativos. A Cemig também destacou investimentos de R$ 132 milhões na Gasmig, voltados praticamente à conclusão do projeto Centro-Oeste, e de R$ 258 milhões na expansão da Cemig SIM, que possui participação relevante no mercado de geração distribuída em Minas Gerais. Em geração centralizada, a prioridade da empresa está na renovação da concessão da hidrelétrica de Sá Carvalho, de 78 MW, por mais de 30 anos. Agora, o foco é garantir as renovações das usinas Nova Ponte, de 510 MW, e Theodomiro Carneiro Santiago, ou Emborcação, de 1.192 MW. Em junho, a Aneel recomendou a renovação das duas usinas também pelo regime de cotas. De acordo com o vice-presidente de Finanças e Relações com Investidores, Leonardo Magalhães, a companhia está agora em tratativas com o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), responsável pela condução do processo. Questionados sobre o apetite para aquisições em um cenário de juros elevados, os executivos reconheceram que as condições financeiras tornam as operações de fusões e aquisições (M&A) mais desafiadoras. Magalhães explicou que a companhia mantém como prioridade os investimentos próprios, especialmente na distribuição e nos reforços de transmissão. Distribuição e mercado Na agenda regulatória, a Cemig apontou dois temas considerados relevantes para a próxima revisão tarifária: o reconhecimento das perdas e a definição do fator X, relacionado à produtividade da distribuidora. A companhia afirmou que atualmente mantém as perdas dentro dos limites regulatórios e espera que as discussões sobre esses parâmetros sejam concluídas até a revisão tarifária de 2028, com efeitos positivos para o negócio. A estatal mineira faturou cerca de, 9,7 milhões de clientes em setembro de 2026, com crescimento de 176 mil clientes em relação a setembro de 2025, o que equivale a um aumento de 1,9% na base de consumidores. Deste total, 9.724.583 são consumidores finais e de consumo próprio e 617 são outros agentes do setor elétrico brasileiro. O fornecimento de energia para clientes cativos somado à energia transportada para clientes livres e distribuidoras, excluindo a energia compensada de GD1, totalizou 12.151 GWh no 3T26, com aumento de 1,0% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. Esta variação decorre, principalmente, do aumento de consumo da classe residencial (+223,2 GWh ou +6,9%), refletindo o crescimento no número de clientes, e da classe comercial (+68,7 GWh ou +4,5%), devido à melhoria nas condições econômicas e a temperaturas mais elevadas, que foram compensados pelo menor consumo no mercado livre da classe industrial (-92,4 GWh ou -1,7%), em razão da queda da produção de Ferroligas e do setor de Fertilizantes. O aumento de 1% na energia distribuída, excluindo GD1, resulta do crescimento no período de 0,7% no consumo do mercado cativo e de 1,2% no uso da rede pelos clientes livres (+38,5 GWh e +77,5 GWh, respectivamente). Considerando a energia compensada de GD1, a energia total distribuída teve crescimento de 2,8% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. A energia vendida pela Cemig geração e transmissão e holding, excluindo a liquidada na Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), diminuiu 6,7% na comparação anual, sendo que a energia faturada pela Cemig GT totalizou 7.014 GWh, representando um aumento de 8,9% (+575,9 GWh) em comparação ao mesmo intervalo do ano passado. Já a Cemig holding registrou vendas de 3.769 GWh, redução de 26,4% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. Do total comercializado pela holding e cemig GT na etapa, 568,7 GWh foram vendidos no mercado varejista. Cemig no 3T26 A empresa teve lucro líquido de R$ 1,72 bilhão no terceiro trimestre de 2026, acima dos R$ 796,7 milhões contabilizados em igual etapa do ano anterior. O desempenho foi justificado pela reversão da provisão para contingências referente aos processos que discutem a incidência de contribuições previdenciárias sobre o os pagamentos de Participação nos Lucros e Resultados (PLR) no período de 1999 a 2016, com impacto positivo no resultado de R$ 774,6 milhões, crescimento do lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização (Ebitda, na sigla em inglês) da distribuição e da comercialização, parcialmente compensado pela redução do Ebitda ajustado da geração e transmissão. O resultado também foi impactado pelo crescimento dos encargos com debêntures superior em R$93,5 milhões, decorrente, principalmente, do aumento da dívida líquida. O Ebitda ajustado da companhia fechou o período em R$ 1,99 bilhão, crescimento de 31,1%. Também houve aumento de 5,12% na receita líquida, que somou R$11,16 bilhões, apoiada em aumento de 3,2% no fornecimento de energia elétrica e incremento de 16,5% na linha Tusd, a receita de uso de sistemas elétricos de distribuição.

artigo.texto: India's Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, including submissions from Reliance Industries, ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Exide Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy and Vikram Solar. Other participating companies include Avaada Electro, Fujiyama Power Systems, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions, Godawari New Energy, Renew Photovoltaics and Sun Drops Energia. MHI has earmarked the 10 GWh capacity for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage (GSSS) under its broader 50 GWh ACC manufacturing programme to address growing renewable energy storage requirements, strengthen energy security and develop domestic ACC manufacturing capabilities. The global tender was floated on the CPP Portal on July 15, 2026, and technical bids were opened on November 11 for two-stage quality and cost based selection. MHI receives 22 bids for 10 GWh ACC battery manufacturing capacity under PLI India’s MHI received 22 bids for 10 GWh of ACC battery manufacturing capacity under its PLI scheme, supporting grid-scale energy storage requirements. Huang’s Downfall Could Shake the Economy, and Detainees Have Disappeared From an ICE Database
Plus, the Friday news quiz.
- This transcript was created using speech recognition software. While it has been reviewed by human transcribers, it may contain errors. Please review the episode audio before quoting from this transcript and email transcripts@nytimes.com with any questions.
- tracy mumford
- From “The New York Times,” it’s “The Headlines.” I’m Tracy Mumford. Today’s Friday, November 13. Here’s what we’re covering.
- ben casselman
- So everything that’s going on with NVIDIA, and especially with Jensen Huang’s resignation, has just raised a lot of questions about what’s going to happen with the company, with the AI industry, and even beyond that. I spoke to an expert on Thursday who asked, can one CEO’s sex life take down the economy?
- tracy mumford
- Ben Casselman is “The Times” chief economics correspondent.
- ben casselman
- And look, the literal answer here is obviously no. But NVIDIA really does play a unique role. And that isn’t just because it makes something like 90 percent of the advanced chips that go into all of these AI models. It’s because they play this role of almost being a central bank for the AI industry. They have played this really fundamental role in financing and providing loan guarantees to their customers and suppliers, to the companies that run the data centers, to the companies that are designing these models. And every time that there starts to be a wobble in the AI story, every time the market starts to freak out a little bit, more often than not, it’s NVIDIA and it’s Jensen Huang that have stepped in to steady the ship. They provide a financial backstop, or Huang himself just comes out and reassures everybody that the AI boom is still on track. And if they stop playing that role, if they pull back in some way, that could really have profound implications for the entire AI boom. So while I don’t think it’s literally true that one sex scandal is going to bring down the US economy, financial markets are built on confidence to a significant degree, and you never what is going to be the precipitating incident that brings everything down. I wouldn’t predict that that’s what’s going to happen here, but it does really point to the degree to which these interconnected financial pieces and our reliance on AI have become a real vulnerability for the US economy. [THEME MUSIC]
- tracy mumford
- Meanwhile, a Senate committee has summoned Jensen Huang to testify over national security concerns related to his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The committee has also summoned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. In his role, Lutnick has control over government restrictions on technology sales like limits on the transfer of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China. While many top Trump administration officials have pushed for tighter restrictions to try and keep China from gaining an economic or military edge

artigo.texto: TotalEnergies acquires 450MW solar, 150MW BESS NSIP project On 31 October, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) Steeple Solar Farm Limited changed hands, with TotalEnergies taking it over from RES UK & Ireland. French integrated energy and petroleum company TotalEnergies has acquired the Steeple Renewables Project from developer RES. On 31 October, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) Steeple Solar Farm Limited changed hands, with TotalEnergies taking it over from RES UK & Ireland. Steeple Renewables Project will comprise 450MW solar energy generation and a 150MW battery energy storage system (BESS). The Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) was granted a development consent order (DCO) in early October. Due to be constructed in Nottinghamshire, the Steeple Renewables Project is located near the decommissioned West Burton Power Station and will use existing grid capacity and infrastructure in the area. As seen in the image below, taken from Solar Media Market Research's new data platform, there are currently 14 assets connected to West Burton Substation (291MW), where the Steeple project will connect. There are another 17 projects in the pipeline across solar and battery storage due to connect there. West Burton is the seventh-largest progressed pipeline in the country, with four out of those seven largest grid supply points (GSPs) in the T5 zone. Source: Solar Media Market Research. TotalEnergies did at one point have its own projects in the NSIP process: the 98MW Hedgehog Grove and 98MW North Ray Solar Farm projects. However, the capacity boundary that classifies NSIPs, requiring government approval and superseding local council planning authorities, changed to 100MW earlier this year. This saw the projects moved to be approved under the Town and Country Planning Act (TCPA), which TotalEnergies said “allows for a more locally focused consultation”. Read more about:

artigo.texto: Want an Energy-Efficient Data Center? Build It Underwater Microsoft wants to submerge data centers to keep them cool and to harvest energy from the sea When Sean James, who works on data-center technology for Microsoft, suggested that the company put server farms entirely underwater, his colleagues were a bit dubious. But for James, who had earlier served on board a submarine for the U.S. Navy, submerging whole data centers beneath the waves made perfect sense. This tactic, he argued, would not only limit the cost of cooling the machines—an enormous expense for many data-center operators—but it could also reduce construction costs, make it easier to power these facilities with renewable energy, and even improve their performance. Together with Todd Rawlings, another Microsoft engineer, James circulated an internal white paper promoting the concept. It explained how building data centers underwater could help Microsoft and other cloud providers manage today’s phenomenal growth in an environmentally sustainable way. At many large companies, such outlandish ideas might have died a quiet death. But Microsoft researchers have a history of tackling challenges of vital importance to the company in innovative ways, even if the required work is far outside of Microsoft’s core expertise. The key is to assemble engineering teams by uniting Microsoft employees with colleagues from partner companies. The four of us formed the core of just such a team, one charged with testing James’s far-out idea. So in August of 2014, we started to organize what soon came to be called Project Natick, dubbed that for no particular reason other than that our research group likes to name projects after cities in Massachusetts. And just 12 months later, we had a prototype serving up data from beneath the Pacific Ocean. Project Natick had no shortage of hurdles to overcome. The first, of course, was keeping the inside of its big steel container dry. Another was figuring out the best way to use the surrounding seawater to cool the servers inside. And finally there was the matter of how to deal with the barnacles and other forms of sea life that would inevitably cover a submerged vessel—a phenomenon that should be familiar to anyone who has ever kept a boat in the water for an extended period. Clingy crustaceans and such would be a challenge because they could interfere with the transfer of heat from the servers to the surrounding water. These issues daunted us at first, but we solved them one by one, often drawing on time-tested solutions from the marine industry. But why go to all this trouble? Sure, cooling computers with seawater would lower the air-conditioning bill and could improve operations in other ways, too, but submerging a data center comes with some obvious costs and inconveniences. Does trying to put thousands of computers beneath the sea really make sense? We think it does, for several reasons. For one, it would offer a company like ours the ability to quickly target capacity where and when it is needed. Corporate planners would be freed from the burden of having to build these facilities long before they are actually required in anticipation of later demand. For an industry that spends billions of dollars a year constructing ever-increasing numbers of data centers, quick response time could provide enormous cost savings. The reason underwater data centers could be built more quickly than land-based ones is easy enough to understand. Today, the construction of each such installation is unique. The equipment might be the same, but building codes, taxes, climate, workforce, electricity supply, and network connectivity are different everywhere. And those variables affect how long construction takes. We also observe their effects in the performance of our facilities, where otherwise identical equipment exhibits different levels of reliability depending on where it is located. As we see it, a Natick site would be made up of a collection of “pods”—steel cylinders that would each contain possibly several thousand servers. Together they’d make up an underwater data center, which would be located within a few kilometers of the coast and placed between 50 and 200 meters below the surface. The pods could either float above the seabed at some intermediate depth, moored by cables to the ocean floor, or they could rest on the seabed itself. Once we deploy a data-center pod, it would stay in place until it’s time to retire the set of servers it contains. Or perhaps market conditions would change, and we’d decide to move it somewhere else. This is a true “lights out” environment, meaning that the system’s managers would work remotely, with no one to fix things or change out parts for the operational life of the pod. Now imagine applying just-in-time manufacturing to this concept. The pods could be constructed in a factory, provisioned with servers, and made ready to ship anywhere in the world. Unlike the case on land, the ocean provides a very uniform environment wherever you are. So no customization of the pods would be needed, and we could install them quickly anywhere that computing capacity was in short supply, incrementally increasing the size of an underwater installation to meet capacity requirements as they grew. Our goal for Natick is to be able to get data centers up and running, at coastal sites anywhere in the world, within 90 days from the decision to deploy. Most new data centers are built in locations where electricity is inexpensive, the climate is reasonably cool, the land is cheap, and the facility doesn’t impose on the people living nearby. The problem with this approach is that it often puts data centers far from population centers, which limits how fast the servers can respond to requests. For interactive experiences online, these delays can be problematic. We want Web pages to load quickly and video games such as Minecraft or Halo to be snappy and lag free. artigo.texto: Every day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about. “When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts. Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery. In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says. Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy. To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.” This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling. “Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says. When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions. It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT). The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says. The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries. “If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says. CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs. CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000. The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035. In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures. One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use. “For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says. Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says. The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations.
